item.title: Filizko Went to LA for Quantum Things
item.description:
Filizko went to LA for quantum things. :)

I visited UCLA for a quantum workshop, which still sounds a little unreal to write. There was sunshine, palm trees, physics, computer science, too much coffee, and many moments where I quietly thought, “Wait, this is my life now?”

Los Angeles was beautiful, chaotic, bright, and very LA.

UCLA was lovely. The workshop was inspiring! I got to listen, learn, meet people, think about research, and feel once again that I am slowly finding my place in this strange and beautiful field.

Also, yes, I did go to Santa Monica and Venice Beach.

Because even quantum people deserve a little ocean. :)

And not only that: I have now swum on both sides of the Pacific.

Dance dance, baby. :)

P.S. Zlatko tweeted a photo from the workshop, I look so happy and I do not know why! :D https://x.com/zlatko_minev/status/2067037518294573488

item.title: On an MRI Machine, a Forgotten Memory, and the Most Important Thing I Have Learned About Myself
item.description:
Three years ago I went to a routine eye appointment.

I wear glasses. Every six months, a check-up. Nothing special.

The doctor was looking at medical images of my retina when she paused.

She asked if I got headaches.

I said yes, always! I drink a lot of caffeine, I don’t drink enough water, I have sleep problems.

I had normalized the headaches a long time ago…

Then a second doctor came into the room. Then a third.

Each one looked at the screen, said hello to me, and turned back to the images.

I watched all of this and told myself:

eyyy, filizco, it’s nothing, do not worry about it!

tabii ki böyle demedim, konuşsanıza amk diye saydırdım içimden.

One of them asked if I had numbness in my arms or hands.

I said yes, actually. I did.

They spoke quietly among themselves. Then they told me: my prescription had changed significantly, and there was inflammation of the optic nerve. An MRI would be a good idea.

I tried to get more information. They said there could be many causes. The MRI would tell us more.

I walked out of the office and went directly to a café.

This is something I inherited from my grandmother. I never go straight home after difficult news.

When I was a child, after every doctor’s appointment she would take me to my favorite restaurant.

When I grew up and she was no longer with me, I kept the habit.

Find a crowded place first. Let your mind settle. Then go home.

I sat in the café and looked up what optic nerve inflammation could mean.

The first result: MS. Multiple sclerosis.

I sat with that for a while.

Then I called my closest friends.

My friend N started crying almost immediately. It’s her thing, and it is the exact reason why I love her.

Life is so unfair, Filiz. This is so unfair.

F said, “No, I don’t think it’s anything. I really don’t.”

But his voice, his whole energy on the phone, changed completely.

I knew him well enough to know he looked it up the moment we hung up.

M was at work that day. I texted him the news.

M called me a little later, after he had done his own research.

He is deeply religious. Faith is the center of his life.

But that day he was angry (very unusual of him).

I’m angry at God, Filiz. He hasn’t given you things other people take for granted, and now this on top of everything? He shouldn’t do this!

His voice broke a little.

I have had a great life. Hard one, yes, but genuinely, fully great.

I traveled the most beautiful places on earth, tasted the foods I wanted to try, always blessed with the best people. Ben dünyada olduğum için her zaman çok mutluydum!

If today were my last day, I would have no remorse about myself!

My closest friends know this about me!

I understood why they were reacting this way. They know my life.

They know that I have navigated most of it without the safety net that most people don’t even notice they have, the people who are simply there, who you don’t have to explain anything to, who would show up.

My friends are that for me now.

But they also know what it cost to get here. And they were frightened for someone who has already carried more than her share.

I listened to all of them. I told them it would be okay. I didn’t know yet if that was true, but it felt like the right thing to say.

Only later did I notice that I had spent those conversations on the other side of the equation.

The one doing the reassuring, not the one being reassured.

I didn’t mind. That is just how I am built.

But I also knew, somewhere, that I needed to be as careful with myself as my friends were being with me.

I may never fully come to terms with how unfair life is, but I accepted that truth a long time ago.

I have always tried to live fully in whatever moment I am in.

That is how my grandmother raised me!

For the MRI, they gave me an appointment for two weeks later.

I cannot explain how vulnerable you feel being far away from home when you are having such health problems.

I was not going to sit at home for two weeks feeling sorry for myself! Not for Filizko! :)

The week after the eye appointment, we bought tickets to New York. We flew there.

We strolled the city, ate incredible East Coast cuisine, visited every bookstore I loved, spent hours in museums in front of paintings I love.

We stayed in Hoboken and every morning I woke up to the Manhattan skyline.

Most of the time, I was having fun. NYC is the kind of city that pulls you in, that makes you forget.

The MS thought came back occasionally.

If you have MS, you can collapse suddenly. That was frightening. But if I had MS, there was nothing I could do about it. I would only know when I knew.

What unsettled me more was the fear that came into M’s eyes, every now and then, when he thought I wasn’t looking.

It was chilling.

I was okay with waiting. He was not!

He was ready to do anything, to learn the truth immediately…

He was in NYC with me, but his brain had no break until exam day!

Then came the MRI day!

There was a problem.

The machine was not the kind where only your head goes in. My whole body had to be inside.

I have claustrophobia.

I undressed completely. They gave me a white garment: ugly, unironed, freshly washed.

I lay down on the table. The machine began to move slowly, pulling me inside.

A few minutes in, I said I needed to get out. I was breathing too fast.

The technician said: I don’t think we can do this, you’re not looking well.

I really couldn’t. My heart was trying to leave my chest.

It’s a terrible machine, it makes terrible sounds and you cannot move at all.

But I genuinely needed to know. Whether I had MS or not.

The uncertainty was one thing. I can tolerate uncertainty. But this uncertainty was different.

I said: I’ll do it.

I lay back down. The technician said: I don’t think this is going to work, but okay, let’s try one more time.

I closed my eyes. I did not open them for one hour.

I could feel tears wanting to come but I held them.

I was going to learn the truth, whatever it was.

My heart was beating loud enough to feel in my chest for the first four or five minutes.

And then, from somewhere, a memory came.

Something I hadn’t thought about in twenty-four years.

My grandmother had surgery once, when I was a child. I stayed with my aunt during that time.

When we went to visit her afterward, I asked: Grandma, what did they do to you?

She told me they put her in a closed machine for a long time, then operated, removed the bad things.

She had serious heart problems and had gone through open-heart surgery.

I asked: Weren’t you scared? In the closed machine?

She said: I was scared. But then I thought of you, and it passed.

That memory came to me in the machine.

I thought: She was scared too. She thought of me and it passed. I’m scared. I’ll think of her.

It will pass. A few more minutes. You’re almost there, Filiz.

When the sixty minutes ended, the white garment was soaked through.

The technician said: I thought you couldn’t do it. You’re a pretty tough lady.

A few weeks passed.

I did not pray to God. I do not know, I just could not…

Then the results came in.

It was not MS!!! (Yesss beeeh!!!)

It was something called pseudotumor cerebri.

Hypothyroidism and extra weight were putting pressure on my spine.

Not even a real tumor. There was treatment. There was a solution.

Everyone was very happy. I was happy too.

But I had learned something.

I needed to take better care of myself.

Everything outside of me, every obligation, every responsibility, every job, every person, was a fraction of my life.

The main thing was me!

Me » everything else.

I had always been sensitive to other people, always tried to help, always taken on more than I should.

But this moment was clear: I needed to take care of myself.

Physically. Psychologically. Emotionally.

I kept that promise to myself for a long time.

Then, being in a foreign country, the workload, the school, the pressure, somewhere the thread broke again.

Not as badly as before, but I still wasn’t meeting all my own needs.

A few weeks ago, my body reminded me again:

iron deficiency, heavy periods, heart palpitations, shortness of breath.

I remembered the girl in the MRI machine who held herself together for sixty minutes so she could learn the truth.

Don’t forget her, I told myself.

Your degree, your work, other people, all of it is a fraction of your life.

You come first, Filiz.

I don’t want my body to have to remind me again. And honestly, I do not know whether I am lucky enough to be reminded again. Not everyone has that chance, right?

I am grateful to God for those reminders.

So..

Everything else can wait. Everyone else can wait.

I am only going to spend my energy on things that make me happy, on things that move me toward a better version of myself.

I already don’t keep people around me who exhaust me.

But the ones I’ve felt obligated to, the ones who drain me for no real reason, I’m going to give them only what’s necessary.

Nothing more.

I love myself. I will love myself more!

I want to spend my life with the people and things that make me feel that.

No more chasing. No more fixing. No more running after things that aren’t already moving toward me.

My happiness is the most important debt I owe.

And I intend to pay it.

This essay was originally published at gulfiliz.github.io.

item.title: Erotapokriseis XI
item.description:
EN:

Helloggg my dear readers,

One of the sweetest surprises of keeping this blog has been discovering the questions that come back to me from the other side of the screen. I’ve answered most of your messages, but I wanted to save a few of them here, in this little archive of conversations.

TR:

Sevgili okurlarım,

Bu blogu yazmanın en tatlı sürprizlerinden biri, ekranın öbür tarafından bana dönen sorular oldu her zaman! İyi ki varsınız! Mesajlarınızın çoğuna cevap verdim, ama bazılarını bu küçük sohbet arşivinde saklamak istedim. :)

1) Q: Why does the renormalization group feel less like a technique in physics and more like a way of thinking? renormalization group

A: Because it isn’t a tool you reach for; it’s a lens you can’t put down. A technique answers one question. RG tells you which questions even survive once you step back far enough to see the shape of a thing. After a while you start asking it of everything, not just physics: what stays true when I stop looking so closely? That is not a method. That is a way of seeing.

2) Q: When the scale of something changes, does its truth change as well?

A: The parameters do. The electric charge you measure literally depends on how closely you look. What changes, though, is not the truth itself but which description is the honest one at that scale. The world isn’t lying to you at low resolution. It’s telling you a coarser truth, and RG is the grammar that connects the coarse one to the fine one.

3) Q: Does RG suggest that the world is understood not through details themselves, but through the way details are forgotten?

A: Yes, and that’s the part that gives me chills. RG makes forgetting rigorous: it tells you exactly which details you are allowed to throw away, and then proves the answer doesn’t depend on them. We spend our lives thinking knowledge means holding on to more. RG says the deepest understanding is knowing precisely what to let go of!

4) Q: Why does the idea of universality affect you so much: because order emerges from chaos, or because different systems seem to speak the same language?

A: The second, and it isn’t close. Order from chaos is beautiful, but I’ve made my peace with it. What undoes me is that a lump of iron and a jar of fluid near their critical points obey the exact same numbers, having never met, sharing none of the details. What they do share is the deep grammar: the same symmetry, the same dimension, the same short reach of interaction. It’s the universe rhyming with itself, and the rhyme has a reason, which somehow makes it more chilling, not less. Universality is the closest physics comes to admitting reality has only a few real ideas and endless disguises. I will write a blog post on Chaos very soon! Tbh, you inspired me to write one! Cheers. :)

5) Q: If physics tells us that the same explanation does not hold at every scale, could that also be true of human life?

A: We stopped demanding a single explanation for every scale; we use quarks for one regime and fluids for another, and nobody calls that failure… I think, I need to think about this one a little more.

I will answer this later. Sorry! Thanks for the question!

6) Q: What fascinates you most about quantum error correction?

A: I’m still a beginner in this field. Learning, and not understanding enough yet for fascination!

7) Q: When we try to protect a quantum computer, what are we really protecting: computation, information, or possibility?

A: All three, but most fundamentally, information.

Computation is what we want to do with it; possibility is the strange quantum form it takes before measurement. But what we are really protecting is fragile information from leaking into the world too soon.

A quantum computer is powerful because it can hold possibilities coherently. Error correction is our way of saying: not yet, universe. Do not turn this into history before the computation is done. :)

8) Q: Is decoherence only a physical problem, or can it also be seen as the universe’s resistance to preserving memory?

A: Physically, decoherence is not the universe “resisting” anything; it is the environment entangling with the system and carrying information about it away.

But romanticizing is free, right? :) So, poetically: yes. It feels like the universe reminding us that memory is not free, and that every preserved possibility has to be protected from a world constantly trying to read it. Cheers!

This is almost the same question as Q1, asked by two different people. I tried to answer it the way the reader asked:

9) Q: Why does the renormalization group feel less like a physics technique and more like a worldview?

A: Because the renormalization group teaches you that not every detail deserves to survive a change of scale.

Some things are relevant, some are irrelevant, and some only look important because you are standing too close. That feels less like a technical lesson in physics and more like a way of thinking about almost everything: ideas, people, pain, memory, even the self.

What remains true after you zoom out? That is the question. :)

item.title: A Manifesto Against Pseudo-Intellectualism — On the Most Dangerous People in the Room
item.description:
My favorite word in English is “pseudo”. I seriously love it. You can put it in front of anything and it just completely messes up the meaning. Anyway…

I want to talk about the most dangerous people in contemporary intellectual life.

Not the ignorant. The ignorant are not dangerous. They know they don’t know, or they don’t know they don’t know, but in either case they are not actively doing damage to the infrastructure of knowledge.

Not the stupid. Stupidity is a cognitive limitation, not a moral failure. You cannot hold someone responsible for the architecture of their brain.

I want to talk about the pseudo-intellectual.

The person who has received education, sometimes excellent education, and emerged from it not with knowledge but with the performance of knowledge.

The person who has learned not how to think but how to sound like they think.

The person who deploys vocabulary as camouflage, citations as authority, complexity as a substitute for clarity, and the appearance of rigor as a replacement for actual rigor.

This person is dangerous in a way that ignorance never is. Because they are convincing. Because they have credentials. Because they sit on committees and write reports and give talks and shape policy and teach students and review papers and make decisions that affect real people’s real lives,

while understanding, at a fundamental level, almost nothing about what they are doing.

I. The Taxonomy

Let me be precise about what I mean, because “pseudo-intellectual” is often used as a simple insult, and I want to use it as a diagnosis.

There are several distinct varieties.

The Credential Hoarder.

Collects degrees, affiliations, publications, not as byproducts of genuine inquiry but as the goal itself.

The CV is the intellectual life. The paper is the thought. The conference is the work.

They have learned to produce the outputs of intellectual labor, the paper, the grant application, the review, the talk, without the inputs.

Without genuine curiosity. Without the sustained encounter with difficulty. Without the willingness to be wrong.

The credential hoarder’s papers cite correctly. The methodology section is technically adequate. The conclusions are hedged appropriately.

And the work contributes nothing, because nothing was genuinely asked, genuinely investigated, genuinely risked.

The Jargon Welder.

Has learned that complexity signals intelligence.

Writes sentences like: “The heteronormative discursive formations that undergird the epistemological violence of neoliberal subjectification require a transgressive praxis of intersectional counter-hegemonic resistance.”

This sentence means something. Or rather, it could mean something, in the right context, with the right interlocutor, with genuine analytical work beneath it.

Usually it means nothing.

It is a performance of having thought about a subject without the inconvenience of actually thinking about it.

The jargon welder uses complexity not to illuminate but to intimidate, to make the reader feel that if they do not understand, it is their failure, not the writer’s.

This is the inversion of intellectual virtue.

Good writing makes the difficult clear. Bad writing makes the simple obscure, and calls the obscurity depth.

The Reference Dropper.

Has read, or skimmed, or read about, the important texts.

Drops names with confidence: Foucault, Derrida, Lacan, Žižek, Agamben. Or: Kahneman, Taleb, Gladwell, Peterson. Or: Feynman, Hawking, Penrose, Tegmark.

The references are real. The understanding is not.

The reference dropper has learned that Discipline and Punish is about power, that The Black Swan is about tail risk, that A Brief History of Time is about cosmology.

They have not read these books carefully. They have not tested their understanding by trying to explain the arguments to someone who has also read them carefully.

They have not asked: does this argument actually work? What are its assumptions? Its limits? Where does it fail?

They have acquired the brand without the product.

The Confident Generalist.

Has opinions on everything. Strong opinions. Stated confidently.

Speaks with authority on quantum mechanics, political economy, evolutionary psychology, the history of the Ottoman Empire, the neuroscience of addiction, the future of artificial intelligence.

Has thought seriously about none of them.

The confident generalist has learned that the appearance of confidence is socially rewarded. That hesitation reads as weakness, that “I don’t know” reads as ignorance, that the person who speaks first and loudest is perceived as the most knowledgeable.

They are exploiting a genuine cognitive bias, the Dunning-Kruger effect, but from the inside, as a strategy.

They know just enough to be convincing. They do not know enough to know what they do not know.

The Ideological Ventriloquist.

Has replaced thought with tribe.

All questions have predetermined answers, determined by political affiliation, disciplinary loyalty, institutional interest, or personal identity.

They do not investigate. They confirm. They do not argue. They signal. They do not change their minds, because their minds were never genuinely engaged in the first place.

The ideological ventriloquist is particularly dangerous in academia and in policy, where they occupy positions designed for genuine inquiry and use them for tribal warfare.

II. Why They Are Dangerous

You might ask: isn’t this just vanity? Aren’t they harmless pretenders, whose bluster affects nothing important?

No.

They occupy space.

Academic positions, editorial boards, policy committees, expert panels: these are finite resources. A pseudo-intellectual in a position of intellectual authority displaces a genuine thinker.

The mediocre paper published is the good paper rejected. The confident fool on the committee is the careful thinker silenced.

They corrupt standards.

When pseudo-intellectual work is rewarded, published, cited, funded, it signals to everyone in the system what the system values.

It trains the next generation in the production of the performance of thought rather than thought itself.

It creates a race to the bottom of credentialed mediocrity.

They make consequential decisions.

The pseudo-intellectual is not contained in the seminar room.

They write the reports that shape policy. They review the drugs that reach patients. They evaluate the technologies that are deployed. They advise the governments that make decisions affecting millions of people.

Their confident wrongness, their inability to know what they do not know, is not an academic problem.

It is a public health problem. It is a political problem. It is a civilizational problem.

They undermine trust in expertise.

This is perhaps the most damaging effect.

When pseudo-intellectuals speak with authority, and are wrong, and are later revealed to be wrong, the damage does not fall only on them.

It falls on expertise itself.

The person who trusted the confident generalist and was burned by their confident wrongness does not conclude: “I should find better experts.”

They conclude: “Experts cannot be trusted.”

This is how pseudo-intellectualism feeds anti-intellectualism.

The fake expert and the expert-denier are not opposites. They are collaborators, each making the other’s position possible.

III. The Difference. What Genuine Thinking Looks Like

It is not enough to diagnose the disease. We need to describe the health.

What distinguishes genuine intellectual work from its simulation?

Genuine thinking is uncomfortable.

Real inquiry goes places you did not expect. It produces conclusions you did not want. It requires you to revise beliefs you held firmly.

If your thinking never makes you uncomfortable, if you always end up where you expected, you are not thinking. You are confirming.

The pseudo-intellectual’s thinking is always comfortable because it is not thinking. It is performance, and the performance is rehearsed.

Genuine thinking fails publicly.

Real intellectual work includes wrong hypotheses, dead ends, failed experiments, retracted papers, revised positions.

The willingness to be publicly wrong, to say I was wrong, here is why, here is what I now think, is one of the clearest markers of intellectual honesty.

The pseudo-intellectual is never wrong, or never admits it, because they were never genuinely committed to a position that could be falsified. Their positions are held for social reasons. Social reasons do not require falsification.

Genuine thinking has limits.

The genuine expert knows the edge of their expertise.

They know which questions they can answer, which they cannot, which they could answer with more work, and which are genuinely open.

They say I don’t know without shame.

“I don’t know” is the most important phrase in intellectual life.

It is also the phrase the pseudo-intellectual can never say, because not knowing is not part of the performance.

Genuine thinking is slow.

Real understanding takes time. Reading carefully. Thinking between readings. Returning to texts. Changing your mind. Sitting with difficulty.

The pseudo-intellectual is always fast, because they are not building understanding, they are assembling presentation.

Presentation can be assembled quickly. Understanding cannot be.

IV. The Institutional Enablers

The pseudo-intellectual does not appear in a vacuum. They are produced and sustained by institutions that have lost sight of what they are for.

The publish-or-perish system rewards quantity over quality, the production of papers over the production of ideas. It creates systematic pressure to produce the appearance of research rather than research itself.

The grant system rewards legibility over importance, the ability to describe your work in terms that a committee will understand and fund, rather than the work that most needs doing.

It rewards the already-established over the genuinely new. It rewards the safe over the risky. It rewards the pseudo-intellectual who knows how to write a grant application over the genuine thinker who has not learned that particular performance.

The conference system rewards presence over substance, the ability to network, to be seen, to deliver a polished twenty-minute talk over the ability to think deeply about a problem over years.

The peer review system has been corrupted in many fields by the same dynamics: reviewers who are not experts in the work they review, who evaluate papers by surface features rather than by genuine engagement with the argument.

These are systemic failures. They produce pseudo-intellectualism at scale.

Fixing them requires institutional courage, the willingness to reward genuine inquiry over productive output, honest failure over performed success, the long slow work of thinking over the rapid production of credentials.

V. The Self-Examination

Here is the hardest part.

Everything I have said about the pseudo-intellectual applies, at different times and in different ways, to every person who has been educated, including me. Including you.

We all perform. We all sometimes deploy vocabulary we have not earned. We all sometimes speak with confidence that exceeds our knowledge. We all sometimes avoid the discomfort of genuine intellectual engagement.

The difference between the pseudo-intellectual and the genuine thinker is not that the genuine thinker never performs.

It is that the genuine thinker knows when they are performing, and is troubled by it, and returns, as often as possible, to the harder work of actually thinking.

The Socratic legacy is precisely this: the recognition that the examined life requires constant examination, not of others, but of oneself.

“The unexamined life is not worth living.”

The unexamined intellectual performance is not worth giving.

Ask yourself:

Do I actually understand this, or do I understand how to talk about it?

Could I explain this argument to a genuinely intelligent person who has never encountered it: explain it so they understand it, not so they are impressed by my familiarity with it?

If someone pushed back on my position, if someone found a genuine flaw, would I be able to engage with the flaw, or would I retreat into jargon?

Have I changed my mind about something important in the last year? The last five years? If not, am I thinking, or confirming?

These questions are uncomfortable. They are supposed to be.

VI. What We Owe Each Other

There is a moral dimension here that I want to state directly.

Knowledge is a public good.

When you claim expertise you do not have, when you occupy an intellectual position under false pretenses, you are not just embarrassing yourself.

You are stealing from the public.

You are taking the social trust that is extended to experts, trust built up over generations by people who did the hard work, who were genuinely right about important things, who earned the authority of expertise,

and spending it on your performance.

Every confident wrong pronouncement by someone with impressive credentials depletes that trust.

We are already in a trust crisis. We are already in a moment where expertise is distrusted, often wrongly, but not always wrongly, by large portions of the population.

The pseudo-intellectual is one of the causes of this crisis.

Not the only cause. Not the primary cause. But a real cause.

You owe the truth to the people who trust you with their attention, their credulity, their decisions.

You owe them your genuine best thinking, not your polished performance of thinking.

If you don’t have genuine thinking to offer, if you have not done the work, then the most intellectually honest thing you can do is silence.

“Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”

Wittgenstein said this about metaphysics. It applies equally to expertise.

If you do not know, if you have not done the work, be silent.

Or say: I don’t know.

These are not failures. They are the beginning of honesty. And honesty is the beginning of thought.

VII. The Standard

I want to end with what I am for, not just what I am against.

I am for the person who reads a paper and asks: does this argument actually work?

The one who meets a new idea and sits with the discomfort of not yet understanding it, instead of folding it into what they already know.

Who changes their mind when the evidence changes, not because it is fashionable, but because thinking requires it.

Who says I don’t know without shame, and means it as an invitation to find out, not the end of the conversation.

Who would rather be right than appear right.

I am for the slow thinker, the one who takes years to write a book because the ideas needed years to develop. The careful reader who marks the margins, returns to the hard passages, argues with the author in their head.

And I am for the honest failure: the one who publishes the result that kills the hypothesis, reports the null finding, says we were wrong, here is what we learned.

The humility I mean is not performed, not the of course I could be wrong that proceeds as if it cannot be. It is lived, earned by being wrong enough times to know it can happen again.

This is not a low standard.

It is the only standard that deserves the name intellectual.

Coda

“The first step to knowledge is knowing what you do not know.”

This is attributed to various people. The attribution is uncertain. The content is Socratic.

The pseudo-intellectual knows everything. That is how you know they know nothing.

The genuine thinker knows what they don’t know, and spends their life, carefully, reducing the territory of ignorance.

Not eliminating it. Reducing it.

The territory of ignorance is infinite. The genuine thinker is at peace with this.

The pseudo-intellectual cannot afford to be…

This is a manifesto, not a verdict. Including against myself. On the days when I perform rather than think. Which is more days than I would like.

item.title: Erotapokriseis X
item.description:
EN:

Hello my dear readers, I’ve been reading your emails with great pleasure. Some of your questions were too thoughtful to disappear into private replies, so I decided to collect a few of them here. Thank you for your kindness, curiosity, and careful reading. :)

TR:

Merhaba sevgili okurlarım,

E-postalarınızı büyük bir keyifle okuyorum. Bazı sorularınız özel cevapların içinde kaybolamayacak kadar düşünceliydi; bu yüzden birkaçını burada bir araya getirmek istedim. Nezaketiniz, merakınız ve dikkatli okumanız için çok teşekkür ederim. Yakında doğum günüm geliyor, keşke orada olsaydım. Çok sevgiler. :)

1) Q: When did the line between knowledge and performance disappear? Question came specifically for this post: The System That Rewards Visibility Over Knowledge

A: When the evaluator changed!

The line between knowledge and performance did not disappear because people suddenly stopped caring about truth. It disappeared when visibility became the currency, and the audience replaced the expert as the judge. Once the reward became reach, the person who knows quietly began losing to the person who performs knowing beautifully. Certainty started to look like competence. Simplicity started to look like clarity. Confidence started to look like truth.

And perhaps the saddest part is that the genuine expert often looks less impressive: more hesitant, more careful, more limited, more willing to say “I don’t know.” But those are not failures of knowledge. Those are signs of it. So the line disappeared when we began rewarding the appearance of knowing more than the slow, private, unglamorous labor of actually knowing.

2) Q: Is Camus’s absurd a coldness toward life, or the final form of honesty?

A: This is totaly my perspective from my readings of Camus : The absurd is not coldness toward life. It is the refusal to comfort ourselves with meanings we did not actually earn. Camus is not asking us to feel less; he is asking us to stop lying about what the universe has promised us. In that sense, the absurd is not despair, but the final form of honesty.

3) Q: I have not read the Camus’s stranger yet. Does The Stranger tell us more about morality, or about society’s fear of authenticity?

A: Both, but more about society’s fear of authenticity.

The Stranger is not asking us to admire Meursault as a moral model; it is showing us how violently society reacts when someone refuses to perform the emotions it expects. He is punished not only for what he did, but for what he failed to pretend.

4) Q: In The System That Rewards Visibility Over Knowledge you describe a system that rewards visibility over knowledge. Have you ever felt the urge to play that game yourself, the pressure to be more visible than you’re comfortable with?

A: Honestly and proudly: never! Not once! Everything I’ve achieved in life, I achieved for myself; I never expected approval, applause, or appreciation from anyone. And the very moment I caught myself expecting it, I stopped myself. That is exactly what makes me Filiz: not bending, not breaking!

This question did not came in Turkish, but I liked to answer it. So here is the Turkish translation!

4) Q: The System That Rewards Visibility Over Knowledge yazınızda bilgi yerine görünürlüğü ödüllendiren bir sistemi anlatıyorsunuz. Hiç o oyunu kendiniz oynama dürtüsü hissettiniz mi, rahat olduğunuzdan daha görünür olma baskısı?

A: Durustce ve gururla, asla! Hic bir zaman! Ben hayatta basardigim her seyi kendim icin basardim kimseden de onay, alkis, appreciation beklemedim. bekledigim an da kendimi durdurdum! Beni Filiz yapan sey bu zaten, egilmemek ve bukulmemek. Gururla!

This question came in Turkish.

5) Q: Bir yıldan fazladır neredeyse her hafta yeni bir yazı çıkıyor, harika bir blog, üstüne okul, iş, go kariyeri, bu cevaplara zaman ayırmanız. Hiç uyuyor musunuz? :)

A: Çok tesekkür ederim, çok şekersiniz! Hakikaten uyuyamıyorum. Vücudum hiç dinlenemiyor. Kansızlığım baya kötü durumda ve Amerika’da sadece 8 kez Iron-IV verdiler ve gerisini sen kendin halletmelisin dediler takviye alarak. Halbuki çok iyi bir sağlık güvencem var! Bazen nefessiz kalıyorum. Bazen bir ayda aldığım tüm demir takviyesini bir adette kaybediyorum. Zor geçiyor biraz. Şu hayatta sağlığımdan başka sorunum yok diyebilirim ama maalesef o da çok büyük sorun!

Yani sorunuza cevabım, uyumak istesem bile uyuyamıyorum!

6) Q: What makes you lose interest in someone immediately?

A: Insincerity.

When the distance between what someone says and what they actually do becomes too wide, something in me quietly shuts down.

7) Q: Is decoherence only a physical problem, or can it also be seen as the universe’s resistance to preserving memory?

A: It is a physical problem, fully. But I like the second framing, as long as we do not take it mystically: the universe is not “resisting” anything. The environment is constantly entangling with the qubit, quietly carrying away information about it until the state is no longer privately itself. In that sense, yes, memory is not free; it has to be paid for, atom by atom. We are allowed to romanticize a little, right? :)

8) Q: Is Stoicism, for you, about disciplining the emotions, or about living without self-deception?

A: I am not a Stoic! But the part of Stoicism I actually value is not going cold, not disciplining emotion into silence. It’s living without self-deception: seeing clearly what is in your control and what is not, what you are actually feeling, and what story you are telling yourself to avoid admitting it. I don’t want to be without emotion. I just don’t want to be governed by illusions.

9) Q: When reading Seneca, what is more disturbing: that he speaks about death, or that he is right about life?

A: That he is right about life. Death is not the disturbing part of Seneca. The disturbing part is how calmly he notices the ways we waste our lives while pretending we’re still waiting for them to begin. He isn’t frightening because he talks about dying. He’s frightening because he makes procrastination look like a moral failure.

10) Q: If life has no inherent meaning, does our responsibility to live well decrease or increase?

A: I think it increases! If meaning isn’t handed to us from the outside, we are not relieved of the responsibility; we are left alone with it. We have to live well not because the universe is watching, but because no one else can do the living for us.

11) Q: Does placing the question of suicide at the center of philosophy make you more pessimistic, or more serious?

A: Hard to answer.

I understand why Camus places that question at the center of philosophy, but I do not personally like making suicide the organizing word for life, death, or meaning. For me, the deeper question is not whether life is worth ending, but whether we can live without lying to ourselves about what life is.

12) Q: Who is more dangerous: someone who uses knowledge as a weapon, or someone who uses it as decoration?

A: Someone who uses knowledge as a weapon! Decorative knowledge is irritating, but usually small. It harms taste, conversation, maybe a little community. Weaponized knowledge is different. It does not just want to be admired; it wants to corner, humiliate, and isolate. It turns intelligence into a room where the other person is left completely alone.

13) Q: Why do some people prefer appearing to understand over actually understanding?

A: I have thought about this a lot. It is a beautiful question.

I think the answer is partly psychological, and partly about survival. Some people learn very early that not knowing is dangerous: it makes you look weak, slow, unworthy, or easy to dismiss. So they begin to perform understanding before they ever feel safe enough to actually understand. And after a while, performance becomes a kind of armor. They are not always trying to deceive others. Sometimes they are trying to survive the shame of being seen as someone who does not know. But of course, the tragedy is that real understanding requires the exact thing they are afraid of: admitting confusion.

This essay was originally published at gulfiliz.github.io.

item.title: The System That Rewards Visibility Over Knowledge
item.description:
There is a system.

It is not a conspiracy. No one designed it with malicious intent. It emerged, the way most destructive things emerge, from the accumulation of individually rational decisions that are collectively catastrophic.

The system rewards visibility.

Not knowledge, not depth, not accuracy. Not the slow, careful, unglamorous work of actually understanding something.

Visibility.

How many people saw it, how many liked it, how many shared it, how many followed, how many subscribed.

The metric is reach, the reward is attention, the currency is recognition.

And the person who knows the most is systematically disadvantaged relative to the person who performs knowing most convincingly.

This is not a peripheral malfunction in an otherwise healthy system.

It is the central operating principle.

I. How the Inversion Happened

To understand the current situation, we need to understand what it replaced.

In the pre-internet intellectual world, knowledge was rewarded, imperfectly, with significant distortions, but substantially.

To become a recognized expert, you needed years of training, peer review, the slow accumulation of a reputation among people who knew the field, and the ability to withstand expert criticism.

This system had serious problems. It was gatekept by existing elites, excluded people without access to institutions, was conservative and slow to accept genuinely new ideas, and was subject to nepotism and network effects (as we have discussed elsewhere).

But it had one important virtue: the people doing the evaluating were the people who knew the most.

Peer review, whatever its failures, involves experts evaluating expert claims. The currency of academic reputation, whatever its distortions, is roughly correlated with expertise.

Then the internet, and specifically social media, changed the evaluators.

Now anyone can evaluate anything. Now the metric is not expert judgment but aggregate attention.

A paper read carefully by 50 experts and found to be important is less visible than a tweet read carelessly by 50,000 people and found to be exciting.

The tweet wins.

Not because the tweet is more correct. Because visibility is now the currency, and the tweet has more of it.

II. The Mechanics of Visibility

Why does the visibility system consistently reward certain things over others?

The first mechanism is simplicity over complexity.

Complex ideas require time to understand. Simple ideas are immediately accessible.

In a system that rewards reach, where the marginal reader has a short attention span and many competing demands, the simple idea always has an advantage.

The complex idea must be simplified to travel. Simplification loses information. The information that is lost is often the most important part.

The viral version of any complex idea is necessarily a distortion.

The second is certainty over uncertainty.

Uncertainty is uncomfortable. “We don’t know” is not a satisfying answer. “The situation is complicated” does not generate engagement.

The confident wrong answer travels further than the hesitant right one.

In expert discourse, the expression of uncertainty is a virtue; it is epistemic honesty, the acknowledgment of the limits of evidence.

In the visibility system, uncertainty reads as weakness. The person who says “I’m not sure” loses to the person who says “I’m absolutely certain” regardless of which one is actually right.

The third is story over argument.

Narratives are processed differently than arguments.

A story activates emotion, memory, identification. An argument requires effortful processing: attention, working memory, logical tracking.

In a system optimized for engagement, story wins every time.

The person who can make a vivid anecdote do the work of a careful argument will reach more people than the person who makes the careful argument.

Even if the argument is better. Even if the anecdote is misleading.

And the fourth, outrage over nuance.

Outrage is the most effective engagement driver in algorithmic systems.

Platforms have discovered, empirically, through optimization, that content producing anger and indignation generates more clicks, shares, and comments than content producing calm understanding.

The nuanced analysis that makes you think differently loses to the outrageous claim that confirms and amplifies what you already feel.

Every platform algorithm optimized for engagement is therefore optimized for outrage. Not by design, but by consequence.

III. The Produced Experts

The visibility system produces a specific type: the produced expert.

The produced expert is not produced by knowledge. They are produced by visibility.

They appeared on the right podcast, wrote the right viral thread, have the right number of followers.

They are invited to the right conferences because they have the right followers because they were invited to the right conferences.

Their credential is their platform. Their platform is their credential.

The circularity is the point.

What are the characteristics of the produced expert?

They are confident on a wide range of topics. The confidence is not proportional to knowledge; it is the performance that produced the visibility in the first place.

Accessibility comes next. Complex ideas are simplified until they can be explained to anyone. What is lost in the simplification is not their concern.

Then there is consistency. They have a brand: a set of positions, a recognizable style, an identifiable perspective. The brand must be maintained. New evidence that complicates the brand is a threat, not an opportunity.

And finally, reactivity. The visibility system rewards being first to respond to events: rapid takes, instant analysis, the hot interpretation of whatever just happened.

The person who waits to think carefully is punished by the person who speaks immediately.

How does this compare to the genuine expert?

The genuine expert:

  • Knows a specific domain deeply
  • Knows the limits of that domain
  • Is uncertain about things outside it
  • Changes their mind when evidence warrants
  • Is uninteresting to the general public on most days

The produced expert:

  • Has opinions on everything
  • Projects confidence uniformly
  • Rarely acknowledges limits
  • Changes their position only when the audience does
  • Is consistently engaging, consistently accessible, consistently present

In the visibility system: the produced expert wins.

IV. The Academic Version

The visibility problem is not only in popular media. It has penetrated academia.

It shows up first in citation metrics.

Academic reputation is increasingly measured by citation counts, h-index, impact factor.

These are visibility metrics; they measure how often work is seen and cited, not how important or correct it is.

Highly cited papers tend to appear in “high-impact” journals, on fashionable topics, from prestigious institutions, by established names.

Low-cited papers tend to appear in specialist journals, on unfashionable topics, from less prestigious institutions, by unknown names.

The correlation between citations and quality is positive but weak.

The correlation between citations and visibility is almost definitional.

The conference circuit operates similarly.

Academic conferences select speakers partly by expertise and partly by the ability to generate interesting, accessible talks.

The person who gives a compelling 20-minute performance is invited back. The person who does the most important work but gives dense, difficult talks is not invited back.

Over time, the conference circuit selects for performance.

The most visible academics are those who have learned to perform: to give the stimulating talk, to generate the quotable phrase, to be the name that draws an audience.

Grant funding follows the same logic.

Grant proposals must be readable by committees that are not specialists in the proposed research.

The proposal must tell a story: here is the big question, here is why it matters, here is why we are uniquely positioned to answer it.

This is a visibility skill, the ability to make work seem important to non-experts.

The person who can tell the story well gets the grant. The person doing the most important work may not be able to tell the story.

And social media has become embedded in academic careers.

Twitter, LinkedIn, Substack: academics are increasingly expected to have a public presence.

The academic who tweets effectively builds a following. The following generates invitations. The invitations generate opportunities. The opportunities generate publications. The publications generate citations.

The visibility loop is now fully embedded in the academic career structure.

V. What Is Lost

When visibility displaces knowledge, specific things are lost.

The first is the slow work.

Some of the most important intellectual work is invisible for years.

Darwin spent 20 years developing the theory of evolution before publishing. He was waiting until he had enough evidence to defend the idea against objection.

The 20 years of preparation generated nothing visible.

In a visibility-rewarded system, 20 years of invisible work is 20 years of career death.

The system cannot accommodate the person who needs decades to be right.

The honest negative result is also lost.

Scientific progress requires knowing what does not work. The null result (we tried this, it did not work) is essential information.

Null results are not published in high-impact journals. They do not generate citations. They do not generate visibility.

So they are not published.

This is the publication bias problem: systematic suppression of negative results because they are not visible enough to matter.

The consequence: replication failures, inflated effect sizes, entire research programs built on results that cannot be reproduced.

The careful qualifier is lost too.

Expertise requires qualification. “This is true in these conditions, with these limitations, contingent on these assumptions.”

The qualification is not weakness. It is accuracy.

In the visibility system, the qualification is weakness. It makes the claim less shareable, less usable, less interesting.

The careful expert is outcompeted by the reckless confident one, not because the reckless one is right but because they are more visible.

And the genuinely novel is selected against.

Genuinely new ideas are initially incomprehensible to most people.

The novel idea requires new concepts: new vocabulary, new frameworks, a restructuring of existing categories.

This takes time to understand. It takes effort. It is not immediately accessible.

In the visibility system, what is not immediately accessible is not shared, is not amplified, is not rewarded.

The genuinely novel is selected against.

What is rewarded: the novel-seeming.

The repackaging of existing ideas in new vocabulary, the old insight made to look new, the familiar made to feel profound.

VI. The Audience’s Complicity

The visibility system does not operate without an audience.

We, the consumers of intellectual content, are complicit.

We choose the stimulating over the accurate, the confident over the uncertain, the story over the argument, the familiar-in-new-clothes over the genuinely new.

Not because we are stupid. Because we are human.

Our cognitive systems are not optimized for evaluating complex arguments under conditions of information abundance.

We are overwhelmed, time-poor, processing more information than any human being in history has processed.

Under these conditions, we use heuristics.

Is this person confident? Then they probably know what they’re talking about. Is this widely shared? Probably true. Is this from a recognizable name? Probably reliable. Does this confirm what I already think? Probably correct.

All of these heuristics are wrong.

Confidence correlates weakly with accuracy, sharing correlates negatively with it, name recognition correlates with visibility rather than knowledge, and confirmation bias is the enemy of truth.

But we use them anyway, because we have to, because there is no time for anything else, because the alternative is paralysis.

VII. The Political Consequences

The visibility system has political consequences that extend far beyond intellectual culture.

Policy is made by the visible.

Policy decisions are influenced by the most visible voices on a topic, not the most knowledgeable ones.

The scientist who has studied the topic for 20 years and communicates with careful qualification is less influential than the pundit who has read three articles on it and communicates with total confidence.

The politician listens to the pundit. The pundit has 2 million followers. The scientist has a university position and a research group of 12.

Public understanding is shaped by the visible.

What the public believes about climate, vaccines, economics, nutrition is shaped primarily by visible communicators, not by domain experts.

The visible communicators have been selected for their ability to communicate, not for their accuracy.

The most effective communicators on contentious topics are often the most wrong, because willingness to simplify and distort is a competitive advantage in the visibility market.

There is, finally, an expert gap.

The visibility system produces a systematic mismatch between public understanding and expert consensus.

The public believes things that experts know to be false. The public disbelieves things that experts know to be true.

This is not primarily an education problem. It is a visibility problem.

The false belief is more visible than the accurate one. The visible wins.

VIII. The Exceptions, and What They Show

There are exceptions to the visibility system.

Some people are genuinely expert and genuinely visible at once. Some platforms reward accuracy and depth. Some audiences seek out genuine expertise. Some corners of the internet maintain standards.

The exceptions matter, not because they refute the general pattern but because they show what is possible.

What do these exceptions have in common?

They have found a niche where the audience is self-selected for caring about accuracy.

Trust accumulates over time, the trust that comes from being right when it was hard to be right, from admitting error, from being specific enough to be falsifiable.

They have accepted smaller reach in exchange for higher quality.

The goal is not to be maximally visible. The goal is to be useful to the people who actually care about what is being said.

This is the only viable alternative within the current system: accept the reach penalty and serve the audience that can bear the truth.

Not an inspiring conclusion. But an honest one.

IX. What Can Be Done

I want to offer something practical, not naive optimism, but concrete possibility.

First, as a producer of knowledge.

Refuse the visibility trap when it requires distortion.

Do not simplify past the point where the simplification is still true.

Qualify when qualification is necessary, even when it costs reach.

Publish the negative result. Admit the error. Say “I don’t know.”

Accept that genuine expertise is rarely viral.

Build a reputation over time with the people who care about accuracy, not a following over weeks with people who care about excitement.

Second, as a consumer of knowledge.

Distinguish between confidence and accuracy. The confident voice is not the reliable one.

Seek the qualifiers: the expert who says “it depends,” “the evidence is mixed,” “I might be wrong.” These are signs of accuracy, not weakness.

Follow the correctors: the people who say “I was wrong about this, and here is why.” These are the most trustworthy voices in any field.

Slow down. The article that requires effort to read is more likely to be accurate than the one that is immediately satisfying.

Be suspicious of your own engagement. If you find something immediately compelling, ask why. Is it compelling because it is accurate? Or because it is well-packaged?

Third, as an institution.

Decouple reward from visibility.

Evaluate academic work by its quality, not its citation count.

Fund the slow work. Fund the null result. Fund the uncharismatic genius who cannot give a good talk but is producing the most important ideas in the field.

Create space for genuine expertise to develop without the constant demand to perform for an audience.

X. The Deeper Problem

Beneath all of this is a philosophical problem that no institutional fix will solve.

There is the problem of evaluating expertise from outside the expertise.

To know that someone is a genuine expert, you need some expertise yourself.

The lay person cannot evaluate the climate scientist’s claim on its technical merits. They can only evaluate the performance: the confidence, the communication skill, the social proof of followers and credentials.

This means: for the non-expert, performance and expertise are indistinguishable.

The produced expert has learned to perform expertise convincingly. The genuine expert may not perform well.

The non-expert, rationally, may prefer the produced expert, because the performance is the only signal available.

This is not stupidity. It is an epistemic constraint.

The visibility system exploits this constraint.

It produces people who are optimized for being indistinguishable from experts without being experts.

And in a world where most knowledge is necessarily second-hand, where we must trust others for most of what we know, this indistinguishability is catastrophic.

Coda

Knowing is not the same as being seen to know.

This sentence should be obvious. In the current system, it is radical.

The person who has spent ten years learning something difficult, who knows it with the precision that only years of work can produce, is systematically disadvantaged relative to the person who has spent ten years learning to appear to know things.

This inversion is not inevitable. It is not natural. It is the product of specific choices, platform design, incentive structures, metric selection, that could be made differently.

They have not been made differently.

The system continues.

And somewhere in it, doing the slow, invisible work, accepting the reach penalty, refusing to distort for the audience, someone actually knows something.

They are not trending.

They are right.

This essay is part of a series on intellectual honesty, epistemic responsibility, and the structures that make genuine knowledge possible.

The previous entry: Against Pseudo-Intellectualism. The next entry: whenever the problem requires it.

item.title: Erotapokriseis IX
item.description:
EN:

Hello, my dear readers, I’ve responded to most of your emails, but I thought I’d answer a few of your questions here as well. Thank you so much for reading and for your thoughtful feedback. It means a lot to me.

TR:

Merhaba sevgili okurlarım, Çoğunuzun e-postasına dönüş yaptım, ancak gelen bazı soruları burada da yanıtlamak istedim. Yazılarımı okuduğunuz ve değerli geri bildirimlerinizi paylaştığınız için çok teşekkür ederim. Hepsi benim için çok kıymetli.

1) Q: Bell’s Theorem forces you to give up one of three things: locality, realism, or free will. Which one do you let go of, and which one do you refuse to?

A: I refuse to give up free will; if something has to die, let it be the innocent little classical realism that thought the world was just sitting there with answers in its pockets. The world can be strange. I can live with strange. :) What I won’t give up is being the one who decides where to look.

This question came in Turkish.

2) Q: “En başarılı teori” dediğiniz Standard Model‘in 25 tane elle girilen parametresi var ve kimse neden tam o değerler olduğunu bilmiyor. İçinizi en çok kemiren hangisi?

A: Higgs kütlesi galiba; çünkü bütün evrenin neden böyle katılaştığını belirleyen sayı orada duruyor ve kimse bana “neden bu?” sorusunun cevabını veremiyor. Hiyerarşi problemi deyip geçiştiriyorlar. Tamam ama neden? :)

3) Q: A stranger at a party tells you quantum computers will break all encryption in five years (Quantum Computing). Before you say anything, what is your face doing?

A: Twitching. :)

P.S. I responded him the long version.

This question came in Turkish.

4) Q: Eski bir Erotapokriseis’te “Plato’yu nepotizm yazımda yerden yere vuracağım” demiştiniz. :) The Philosopher’s Nephew ile vurabildiniz mi, içiniz rahatladı mı?

A: Rahatlamadım, devamke :) Her fırsatta bir daha bir daha :D Bebeğim Aristo için içim hâlâ sızlıyor; o yüzden Platon benden biraz daha çekecek!

5) Q: The holographic principle suggests space itself might emerge from entanglement, that geometry isn’t fundamental. You work with entanglement every single day in error correction. Does that feel plausible to you, or too good to be true?

A: It feels plausible in the dangerous way beautiful ideas do: I do not trust beauty as evidence, but every day entanglement looks less like decoration and more like infrastructure. The honest answer is that I lean yes and distrust myself for leaning. If you haven’t read it, I recommend my own Beautiful But Wrong; this is exactly the kind of gorgeous idea that essay warns me about. Cheers!

This question came in Turkish.

6) Q: Bunca fizik yazısı yazdınız. Hangisini yazarken “vay be” deyip durakladınız, hangisi sizi en çok şaşırttı?

A: Ay, bunu cevaplamak çok zor. Fizik benim yumuşak karnım. Hepsi önemli, hepsi vay be. :D :D Ama silah zoruyla bir tane seçtirseniz: Bell teoremi. Evrenin yerel olmadığının kanıtlanmış olması içimi hâlâ bi şey ediyor. Ne bilmiyorum! :)

7) Q: Where do you place yourself between science and literature?

A: I don’t think I have to place myself between them. That framing assumes they sit on opposite ends of something, and I’ve never felt that. For me they are two faces of the same impulse: the wish to see the world clearly, without pretense.

Science answers “how.” The mechanism, the measurable. Literature answers what it is actually like, what living from the inside feels like. A scientific law can tell me the truth, but it cannot tell me what it was to lose my grandmother. Ivan Karamazov’s question doesn’t get solved in any equation. I carry both because neither is enough on its own. Physics gives me the structure of the world; literature gives me what it means to live inside that structure. And maybe the part I love most: both are looking at the same thing. Seeing why a cyclotomic structure breaks symmetry at exactly that point, and seeing why a Chekhov story aches at exactly that sentence, feel to me like the same kind of understanding. Noticing the pattern beneath the surface. It isn’t a coincidence that Zhivago is both a doctor and a poet. Those two are the same person’s attention, turned in different directions. So I don’t choose. Science tells me how the world works, literature tells me what it is like to be in it. Without one, the other would stay incomplete. That’s just how it is. :)

8) Q: What do you admit you have terrible taste in?

A: Ahahah, what a cute question. When I came to America I noticed something: everyone decorates everything so beautifully. I absolutely don’t get home decor. I’m hopeless at it. So when I bought my first place, I didn’t get any knick-knacks or decorations. Let’s just say it might be the most minimalist home in the world. As an excuse, I get to go “oh those just collect dust, I’m a minimalist.” It’s not like I don’t try when no one’s around, but no, it never works, nothing ever looks right. Even the walls are bare. :) That’s just how I am, what can I do.

9) Q: What is the most attractive intellectual quality?

A: Intellectual humility.

I find it very attractive when someone is intelligent enough to think deeply, but humble enough to know that intelligence does not make them superior. I like people who can say “I don’t know” without feeling diminished by it. For me, the most attractive intellectual quality is not having read the most books, knowing the most theories, or winning every argument. It is the ability to remain serious, curious, and honest in front of truth. I do not like performative intelligence. I do not like people who use knowledge to humiliate others, decorate their ego, or make every conversation a competition. That kind of intelligence feels vulgar to me.

What I admire is quieter: someone who thinks carefully, listens carefully, changes their mind when necessary, and does not need to turn every thought into a performance. A beautiful mind, for me, is not only sharp. It is also disciplined, generous, and humble.

This essay was originally published at gulfiliz.github.io.

item.title: Erotapokriseis VIII
item.description:
EN:

Hellooooggg my dear readers, :) I thought I would open this small corner again for your questions. Some are personal, some are literary, some are philosophical, and some are wonderfully impossible to answer neatly. As always, thank you for reading, questioning, and making this space feel alive!

TR:

Merhaba sevgili okurlarım, Bu küçük köşeyi bir kez daha sorularınıza açmak istedim. Bazıları kişisel, bazıları edebi, bazıları felsefi, bazılarıysa düzgünce cevaplanması imkânsız olacak kadar güzel. Her zamanki gibi okuduğunuz, sorduğunuz ve burayı canlı tuttuğunuz için teşekkür ederim.

1) Q: Small question, but I’m curious: what are you writing all these essays with? Which pen, which ink?

A: Thank you so much, this is a very sweet question. I have a notebook in which I write essays like these, and the name of my notebook is: fragmenta-sképsis-metaxy :) I usually love writing with a fountain pen. But these essays, of course, I write on my computer. I don’t transfer them from the notebook to the computer; I sit down and write. Love!

These days I write in my journal with my Meisterstück, F nib, Pilot Iroshizuku Ajisai, that soft hydrangea blue, in a Rhodia notebook. Cheers!

This question came in Turkish.

2) Q: The Game of Go yazınızda 6-dan olduğunuzu söylüyorsunuz. Hiç KataGo gibi bir yapay zekâya karşı oynadınız mı? Nasıl bir his?

A: Tuhaf bir his. İnsan gibi oynamıyor. Şey gibi düşünün: insanla konuşuyorum diye düşünüyorsunuz ama telefonun karşısındaki ChatGPT :) Anlıyorsunuz yani, insan olmadığını.

3) Q: Nietzsche and the eternal recurrence: this exact life, all of it, the same losses and the same joys, lived again and again forever. Could you say yes to it?

(Amor fati, baby!) :D

This question came in Turkish.

4) Q: Faust ruhunu satıyor, sonra iki cilt boyunca her şeye sahip olup hâlâ tatmin olmuyor, hâlâ daha fazlasını istiyor. Tanıdık geldi mi? :) Siz Faust’un anlaşmasını yapar mıydınız?

A: Filiz’i kendi haline bıraksan, kesin ama kesin aynı anlaşmayı yapardı; ama işte anneannem ve bana verdiği moral compass işleri benim için çok zorlaştırıyor.

5) Q: Nikko got powdered sugar all over her at Café du Monde, I loved that. Honest question: is she a good travel companion or a tiny chaos agent?

A: Ah, Nikko is the cutest. I’m so blessed to have her. She was still a puppy back then, and she was extremely social, also a tiny attention monster :D She wanted everyone to notice her, pet her, love her, basically worship her. So yes, she was adorable, but traveling with her was chaos.

This question came in Turkish.

6) Q: New Orleans yazınız çok tatlıydı. Eve giden bileti yakıp, yerine ömür boyu hayalini kurduğunuz caz şehri. Hayattaki en güzel şeyler hep böyle, plan bozulunca mı geliyor?

A: Evet ya. Hakikaten akışına bırakmak lazım bazen. Çok mu dertleniyoruz acaba..

7) Q: Your Hard Problem of Consciousness essay says the brain isn’t enough to explain experience. Does that gap comfort you or unsettle you?

A: I’m comfortable with uncertainty. I’m comfortable with scientific facts. They’re not there to comfort or discomfort me. The gap is just a gap; my job is not to be soothed by it, but to look at it honestly.

This question came in Turkish.

8) Q: Sartre “özgürlüğe mahkûmuz” diyor. Kötü bir günde bu özgürlük size bir armağan gibi mi geliyor, yoksa bir ceza gibi mi?

A: Özgürlük ceza ya! Kendi hayatını sırtlamak dehşet büyük bir sorumluluk. Çok yorucu. Keşke bir map olsa, ya da birisi benim yerime yaşasa. Rusya’da serflik kalktığında çoğu kişi efendisini bırakıp gitmemiş. Bunu ilk okuduğumda çok rahatsız olmuştum. Ama şu an anlıyorum. Öyle.

9) Q: When are you happiest?

A: One day I’ll come back to this question and really answer it. I’ve been fighting hypothyroidism for a long time now. Every period I lose an incredible amount of blood, and I’m severely anemic. I can’t think the way I used to. I’m not sharp. My hormones are completely upside down. I don’t even have the energy to be happy. The anemia keeps me from sleeping, my body never gets to rest. I can’t remember the last time I was truly happy. Happiness seems to get shorter as you get older. I’m so tired. This turned into venting, I know. I’m very sick right now. But believe me, I’m someone who finds happiness in small things. A tiny kawaii stationery item. A pen that writes beautifully. My dog curling up closer to me at night. Someone I love holding me tightly, and knowing that in that moment I can finally put down the mask of being strong. I haven’t answered your question, but I hope one day I will. Tired, sleepless, anemic, and brain-fogged. With much love.

10) Q: How do you deal with failure?

A: I allow myself to fail! This may sound simple, but it took me a long time to learn. I do not owe anyone constant success. I do not owe anyone a perfect version of myself. I do not owe the world a life without mistakes. Failure hurts, of course. I am not pretending that I am always graceful about it. I am human, after all. Sometimes I cry, sometimes I get angry with myself, sometimes I feel ashamed. Sometimes it really does feel as if everything is over, as if one mistake has swallowed the whole future. But after a while, I try to return to the work itself. I ask what can be learned, what can be repaired, and what must simply be endured. I think failure becomes unbearable only when we turn it into identity. Failing at something does not mean I am a failure. It only means I tried something difficult, and this time it did not work. So I let myself fail. I let it hurt. And then I continue. Quietly, stubbornly, without making a tragedy out of being human.

11) Q: What does a typical Sunday morning look like for you?

A: I try to get out of the house as fast as I can, otherwise I just rot at home. If I’m on my own, I grab my book and head straight to Starbucks, bagel and coffee, and start the day quickly. If I’m with people, on Sundays I prefer going to Eggsellent Cafe (I lived in Carrollton for 4 years and this cafe was near my home, now I moved to Plano but still go there for breakfast!) for a nice breakfast, and sometimes I go with my Turkish friends to places where we can have a proper Turkish breakfast. The point is just to get out of the house. Then I come home and pick up my day where I left off. But if I don’t leave the house, Sunday usually goes by empty for me, and I really don’t like that.

12) Q: Bir insanda zekâ mı, nezaket mi, mizah mı daha tehlikeli biçimde etkileyici?

A: Hiçbiri! Cevap: Merhamet.

item.title: New Orleans — Where Jazz Lives in the Streets
item.description:
I arrived in New Orleans on a December night.

But to explain why I was there, I have to go back to when I was six years old.

There’s a Turkish idiom: “Bana caz yapma!”

Literal translation is: Do not make jazz to me!

In Turkish, it means don’t talk nonsense to me. Don’t ramble. Don’t make excuses. Don’t argue with me. Just be straightforward.

I was about six years old when I first heard this word. I didn’t understand it. Jazz? What does it mean to make jazz? The “jazz” word sounded strange in my mouth. Foreign. Weird. Strange. Cool. Full of air.

Then one night, randomly on TV — on one of TRT’s channels (National public broadcaster of Türkiye), I think — there was a jazz night. A documentary kind of thing.

There was a huge instrument that you blow into. The sound was unlike anything my six-year-old self had ever heard. A saxophone. For some reason, I loved this word, too. :)

Two interesting words for little Filiz!

From that moment on, I started saying I loved jazz music among my friends and adults.

The adults around me just smiled, I don’t think they knew much about it either. And my friends replied with do not make jazz to us, ahahahha.

But I kept saying it anyway. I think I loved it before I understood it.

I love jazz music. I love it a lot.

The Ticket

This past Christmas, I had a ticket from Houston to Amsterdam (a new place to visit, I was super excited!) and then to my hometown İzmir. Ten days! And, come back. I was packed. I was ready…

But I had a health issue and my doctor said the flight might be difficult for me. So I had to burn the ticket (yeah, I always buy the cheapest one and never had an issue!).

And guess where I went instead.

New Orleans, Louisiana!

Wohooooo! Jazz, jazz, jazzz!

A place where jazz plays in the streets, in its soul, in its cafés. And it was legendary. I loved it so much.

French in America

I went to a French-focused school in Türkiye. We learned that Francophone culture was the height of sophistication. We learned to revere France. :)

Then I walked down the streets of New Orleans and heard French. Americans speaking French with American accents. A Parisian would cringe, they always find everything cringe, ahahhha. A nice Parisian(!) would definitely say “you speak sloppy French” to someone from New Orleans. But it was French!

The Food

Legendary!

I ate constantly.

Gumbo. Seafood. So much seafood. Beignets at Café du Monde. Powdered sugar on my face, my hands, my dog Nikko.

I saw fried alligator on a menu. Americans can eat interesting things too, I thought.

Most restaurants and cafés were pet-friendly. This isn’t a common practice in Dallas. For the first time, I had the chance to dine in with my dog.

By the way, seafood pizza is a must try!

There was a place called Luna Pizza just a 30-second walk from the hotel we stayed at. I absolutely loved every pizza I tried there. :)

The Streets

Even though it was Christmas, the streets were quite crowded. Lots of tourists, of course.

I walked the French Quarter street by street. I really enjoyed seeing small balconies in a place other than France, and watching people relaxing on those balconies. The restaurants had put tables out on the streets. It was like a virtual France. I loved it.

There were a lot of signs about voodoo and magic around. New Orleans Ghost Tours were very popular but I didn’t dare to do one. :D

My dog Nikko-chan was with me and she was quite the center of attention. Everyone who passed by asked if they could pet her. Americans are so polite — how could I say no? Of course, the sarcastic Turkish Filiz inside wants to say “don’t make jazz to her,” and the nice American Filiz wants to say “don’t jazz her up” — but since I’m naturalized, I settle for “yeah, sure, go ahead.”

I walked around Riverfront Park all the way to the French Market.

And, I went to the New Orleans Jazz Museum. It was like a gift for little Filizko. I loved it soooo much.

The Three Streets

I had an incredibly good time. Jazz music came out of every street.

There are really 2-3 main streets:

Rampart Street is the one with most of the hotels.

Canal Street is a long street. It took me 4-5 minutes to walk there from the hotel.

And where the real fun happens — Bourbon Street. Whatever you are looking for, it’s here. There are very good cafés on this street, very good restaurants and bars.

I even saw a few strip clubs. :)

I had always seen them in American TV shows, and I smirked when I walked in front of one. Want a quick culture shock? Here we go. The nearly naked women at the door were taking photos with people passing by. What do you expect? Young men being the volunteers for this photo shoot, right? Nooooooo. Even a family with a child in their arms was taking photos. What a culture shock!!! Hey, what is a child doing there at that hour? :D

Anyway, moving on.

Ahahha, could not!

(A big parenthesis: Goodness!!! What a tragedy, really — that woman could have been your daughter! Shakespeare would rise from his grave and write a new tragedy, the finest of all! Actually, let me pause this post and write a serious essay on moral decadence, social decay, the normalization of the absurd! Just kidding.

Jazz, jazz, jazzz!)

The Music

There is no substitute for live jazz.

A bar called 21st Amendment had amazing music. I loved it.

Most restaurants and cafés had live jazz. You didn’t have to go to a bar. The music was just there. In the street.

Every corner had jazz. Every café. Every bar. It didn’t matter where you went. Jazz was playing.

Going Back

The drive back to Dallas took seven hours.

I had burned a ticket home. Instead, I went to a city where jazz lives in the streets, in the cafés, in the restaurants. Everywhere…

I will definitely go back! It is a great weekend getaway activity!

I loved it. I had so much fun!

Below is the photo of Filiz in front of New Orleans Jazz Museum.

Bana caz yapmaaaa! :))
