item.title: Erotapokriseis VII
item.description:
EN:

My dear readers, Thank you for your emails, your questions, your disagreements, and your generous attention! I have replied to many of you already, but some questions kept lingering in my mind after I answered them. Those are the ones I wanted to share here. :)

TR:

Sevgili okurlarım, E-postalarınız, sorularınız, itirazlarınız ve cömert dikkatiniz için çok teşekkür ederim. Çoğunuza zaten dönüş yaptım, fakat bazı sorular cevapladıktan sonra bile zihnimde kalmaya devam etti. Burada paylaşmak istedim bazılarını, çok çok teşekkürler!

1) Q: In Gogol’s Overcoat you say you can’t get through November without thinking about Akaki, and that when people call the story merely funny, something in you closes. That is almost exactly the reaction you describe in My Biggest Red Flag, the withdrawal when someone stays on the surface. Is Gogol a test you quietly give people?

A: Not on purpose, but yes. I don’t hand it to people and watch. It’s just that if you laughed all the way through and felt nothing at “I am your brother,” I learn something I didn’t ask to learn. Akaki isn’t a quiz. He’s a tuning fork. People ring or they don’t.

2) Q: In The Crisis in Fundamental Physics you describe a field that has waited forty years for the anomaly that will crack it open, and you’re entering it anyway. Is that courage, stubbornness, or faith? What do you tell yourself on the days the desert looks endless?

A: Stubbornness wearing faith’s coat, probably. On the days when the desert looks endless, I don’t tell myself a breakthrough is coming. I have no idea if it is. I just tell myself the desert still needs to be mapped, and I’d rather be lost in the right wilderness than comfortable in the wrong one. Most days, that is enough to open the laptop.

This question came in Turkish.

3) Q: Gogol’s Overcoat yazınızda Akaki’nin içtiği değil, içmediği çayları düşündüğünüzü yazmışsınız: kendini küçülterek bir paltonun var olmasına izin veren adam. Sizi en çok yaralayanın onun düşüşü değil, “düşecek bir yeri olmaması” olduğunu söylüyorsunuz. Hiç kendinizi, sadece görülmek için bir “palto” biriktirirken yakaladınız mı?

A: Ah, evet. Utanarak söylüyorum ama evet! Akaki’yi bu yüzden bu kadar yakından tanıyorum; bazen ben de görülmek için bir palto diktim. Tek farkımız şu: benim düşecek bir yerim vardı, onun yoktu. Asıl mesele de bu zaten. Bazılarımız palto kaybedince üşür, bazılarımız yok olur.

This question came in Turkish.

4) Q: The Crisis in Fundamental Physics yazınızda “asıl kriz yanlış teorilere sahip olmamız değil; doğru soruları henüz bulamamış olmamız” diyorsunuz. Bir araştırmacı olarak sizi daha çok ne korkutuyor: yanlış cevabı vermek mi, yoksa hayatınızı yanlış soruya adadığınızı çok geç fark etmek mi?

A: Yanlış cevap beni hiç korkutmuyor; o zaten işin yarısı, bir gün biri düzeltir. Beni korkutan ikincisi: ömrümü güzel ama yanlış bir soruya adayıp bunu en sonda fark etmek. SUSY’ye bütün kariyerini verenler vardı. O yüzden cevaplarıma değil, sorularıma dikkat ediyorum. Yanlış tepeye tırmanmak, yavaş tırmanmaktan beterdir. Bence :)

5) Q: What did you feel the first time you encountered quantum physics?

A: This is such a beautiful question. Thank you for asking it. I’m usually very cautious about scientific hype, so I didn’t come to quantum physics with immediate enthusiasm. I started almost defensively, as if I’d promised myself not to be seduced too easily. I remember thinking, Filiz, what you’re about to learn might betray a lot of the things you thought you understood. And in a way, it did. I think I felt both betrayed and invited. :) It felt aesthetically beautiful to me from the beginning. The mathematics was different, almost strange, but deeply elegant. Looking back, I think the part that stayed with me most is this: quantum physics tells you that the world is not obliged to satisfy human intuition! I still find that incredibly beautiful. Cheers!

This question came in Turkish.

6) Q: Anneanneniz size en çok ne öğretti?

A: Merhameti. ( Daha çok şey yazmak istiyorum ama gözlerim doluyor ve ben şu an kafedeyim ve buradaki tanışlarımın/arkadaşlarımın endişelenmesini istemiyorum.) Çok sevgiler!

7) Q: How is your summer break Filiz?

A: It’s wonderful. The days are beautifully slow. I spend most of my time near the beach with one of my closest friends. I invited you to the Aegean, but you chose to stay in the desert heat of Dallas, so enjoy roasting there. I just submitted a proposal to NASA, and now I am finally chilling a little. :)

8) Q: What quality do you value most in people?

A: Hard question. Can I flip it around and tell you which people I don’t want around me, the ones I won’t keep in my life? Let’s go with that for now :)) I can never love an ungrateful person, and I won’t keep one in my life. If someone is ungrateful, I’ll cut them out, even if they’re the apple of my eye.

Edit August 4, 2025 : Loyalty, honestly. Not the loud kind, just people who remember what you did for them and don’t disappear when it stops being convenient. I can forgive almost anything except ingratitude. Everything else I value probably comes back to that.

9) Q: If I’m ever in Dallas, can I take you out?

A: What makes you think I’m available?

10) Q: I’ve been reading your work since your Medium days. Why did you stop posting there? I still go back and read some of your old pieces sometimes. You had so many readers there. Where did you go?

A: Thanks so much! Ever since Medium became more tied to paid reading, I no longer felt very comfortable writing there. I could never ask people to pay just to read my thoughts. That would not feel very Filiz of me. My purpose in writing has always been to share. There is a Turkish saying: tebdili mekânda ferahlık vardır. I wish I could translate it properly for you, but it means something like, “a change of place brings relief.” So perhaps I did not disappear. I just changed places. With love. :)

And thank you so much for following my journey on different platforms! That means a lot.

This essay was originally published at gulfiliz.github.io.

item.title: Gogol's Overcoat: On Invisibility, Desire, and the Weight of a Name
item.description:
“We all came out from under Gogol’s overcoat.”

This line is attributed to Dostoevsky. Scholars dispute whether he said it. It doesn’t matter.

It is true.

Every Russian writer who came after Gogol (Dostoevsky, Turgenev, Tolstoy, Chekhov) emerged from the literary universe that The Overcoat (1842) created: the universe of the small man, the bureaucratic labyrinth, the city as indifferent monster, the soul crushed by paperwork and poverty until it becomes almost nothing, and then, in the moment of becoming nothing, becomes everything.

I. Gogol Himself

Before the story, the man.

Nikolai Vasilyevich Gogol was born in 1809 in Sorochyntsi, in what is now Ukraine. He died in 1852 in Moscow, having burned the second volume of Dead Souls, his masterwork, years in the making, nine days before his death.

He was forty-two years old.

In the last years of his life, Gogol fell under the influence of a fanatical priest, Father Matvei Konstantinovsky, who convinced him that his literary work was sinful, that laughter was the devil’s instrument, that he must mortify the flesh.

Gogol stopped eating. He burned his manuscript. He turned his face to the wall.

He had spent his career laughing at the world, a laughter that was never entirely comfortable, that always had something desperate in it, something that was not quite laughter.

In the end, the laugh stopped.

What remained: the work. And the work is unlike anything else in literature.

II. The Name

The Overcoat begins with a name.

“In the department of… but it is better not to mention the department. There is nothing more irritable than departments, regiments, bureaus, in a word, any kind of official body. Nowadays every individual considers the whole of society insulted in his person…”

Gogol refuses to name the department. He will name almost nothing precisely: the city is suggested but never confirmed as St. Petersburg, the department is gestures-at but unnamed.

But the protagonist is named. In extraordinary detail.

His name is Akaki Akakiyeviç Başmaçkin.

Akaki, from the Greek ákakos, meaning innocent, guileless, without malice. Twice. Akaki Akakiyeviç, son of Akaki. The innocent son of the innocent.

And Başmaçkin, from the Russian başmak, meaning shoe. The man whose family name derives from footwear.

The name is the first joke. And the first cruelty.

Gogol spends two paragraphs on how this name came to be: the mother’s difficulty choosing, the rejection of other names (Mokkiya, Sosiya, Khozdazat, Trifiliy, Dula, Varakhasiy), the resigned acceptance of the father’s name because there was simply no better option.

“So that is how he came to be called Akaki Akakiyeviç.”

A man who inherits his father’s name because nothing better was available. A man whose family name means shoe. A man who will spend the entire story consumed by a desire for a coat.

Footwear. Overcoat. The man is made of clothing, and nothing else, the story will suggest, until the coat makes him briefly otherwise.

III. The Invisible Man

Akaki Akakiyeviç is a copying clerk in a government department in St. Petersburg.

His job: to copy documents. Not to compose them. Not to summarize them. To copy. He copies with a devotion that goes beyond duty, beyond even enthusiasm, into something that can only be called love.

“It would be hard to find another man who lived so entirely for his work. It was not enough to say that he worked with zeal; no, he worked with love. In his copying he found a varied and agreeable world of his own.”

He has no friends. No family. No social life. When colleagues invite him somewhere, he declines. He has copying to do at home. He carries his copying home in his head, smiling at particular letters as he walks.

He is, at first glance, a comic figure. A man so reduced that his interior life consists entirely of the pleasure of forming letters correctly.

But Gogol will not let us laugh entirely.

The colleagues tease him. They invent humiliations: drop paper on his head, tell him he is to be married, breathe smoke in his face. He does not react. He does not complain.

“Only when the joke became too unbearable, when someone jogged his elbow and prevented him from doing his work, did he say: ‘Leave me alone. Why do you torment me?’ And in those words and in the voice in which they were uttered there was something strange, something that moved to pity.”

A young man, newly arrived at the department, who had begun tormenting Akaki with the others, stops. Suddenly.

“And long after, in moments of great merriment, the figure of the little clerk with the bald patch on his head would appear before him with the words: ‘Leave me alone. Why do you torment me?’ And in these words he could hear the sound of others: ‘I am your brother.’”

I am your brother.

These three words, appearing without warning in the middle of what seemed like a comic story, are the pivot on which the entire story turns.

Gogol has been making us laugh. Now he makes us ashamed of laughing.

IV. The Coat

Akaki Akakiyeviç’s coat is falling apart.

The tailor Petrovich, a one-eyed, pockmarked man who charges more when sober and can be negotiated with when drunk, tells him: it cannot be repaired. He needs a new coat.

The cost: one hundred and fifty rubles. More than Akaki earns in several months.

And here the story transforms.

The coat becomes the object of desire: the single, consuming goal that gives Akaki’s life a shape it never had before.

He saves. He stops drinking tea in the evening. He wears his old coat in the house to preserve it. He walks on tiptoe across cobblestones to save his soles. He stops having his laundry done. Instead he takes it off at home and wears only his dressing gown.

“At first it was somewhat difficult for him to accustom himself to these privations, but after a while it became a habit, and went smoothly enough; he even became quite accustomed to being hungry in the evening; on the other hand, he had spiritual sustenance, for he carried ever in his thoughts the idea of his future coat.”

The coat is his telos, his end, his purpose. The coat gives Akaki Akakiyeviç, for the first time in the story, a future.

A man with no desires has no future. A man with a desire, even this desire, even a coat, has something to live toward.

This is Gogol’s first philosophical move: desire, even trivial desire, is what constitutes temporality. Without wanting, there is only the eternal present of copying.

The coat, when it finally arrives, is described with extraordinary tenderness:

“The coat was carefully examined and found to be in perfect order. Then they brought it out and put it on him… Akaki Akakiyeviç was a connoisseur of fine cloth, and he could not help admiring its quality…”

He walks through the city in his new coat. He is noticed, for the first time in his life, noticed. Colleagues congratulate him. He is invited to a party.

For one evening, Akaki Akakiyeviç exists socially. He has, through a garment, been admitted to the human community.

V. The Theft

Walking home from the party, at the edge of a deserted square, two men stop him.

They take the coat.

The scene is described with almost no detail. A few lines. Abrupt, brutal, over.

The coat is gone.

Akaki reports the theft. He is sent to the police, then to a “Person of Consequence”, a newly promoted official who has adopted the manner of importance through shouting, slowness, and administrative brutality.

The Person of Consequence shouts at Akaki for going through improper channels.

“Do you know to whom you are speaking? Do you understand who stands before you? Do you understand? Do you understand? I ask you!”

Akaki, trembling, leaves. He does not know how he gets home.

He takes to his bed. He develops a fever. He dies.

“And St. Petersburg was left without Akaki Akakiyeviç, as though he had never been in it at all.”

VI. The Philosophical Weight of Disappearance

That sentence, as though he had never been in it at all, is the true center of the story.

Gogol has spent the entire narrative establishing the precise texture of this man’s invisibility. He was always already not there. The coat (the desire for the coat, the having of the coat) briefly made him present. Its removal returns him to absence.

And the city does not notice.

This is not tragic in the traditional sense. Akaki is not a great man brought low by fate. He is a small man who was always low, briefly lifted, and then restored to his original position.

The tragedy is not his fall. It is that there was nothing to fall from.

Hegel wrote about the unhappy consciousness: the awareness of a gap between the self as it is and the self as it ought to be, a gap that cannot be closed.

Akaki has no unhappy consciousness. He is, until the coat, incapable of the awareness that would constitute unhappiness in the Hegelian sense.

The coat gives him this awareness. It shows him what it is to be seen, to be present, to exist socially. Its theft takes this awareness away but leaves behind the knowledge that it existed.

That is what kills him. Not the cold. Not the fever. The knowledge of what he had, briefly, been.

VII. The Ghost

But the story does not end with Akaki’s death.

After his death, a ghost begins to appear in St. Petersburg, near the Kalinkin Bridge, tearing overcoats from passersby.

The ghost is Akaki Akakiyeviç.

“The ghost of the clerk appeared, looking for the stolen overcoat, and under the pretext of the stolen overcoat tearing all sorts of overcoats off the shoulders of all sorts of people.”

The ghost eventually finds the Person of Consequence, who has by now felt some remorse for his treatment of Akaki, and tears the coat from his shoulders.

“The ghost of the clerk appeared to him and said: ‘Ah, so here you are at last! At last I’ve got you by the collar! Your coat is the very one I need! You refused to help me, and have abused me into the bargain! So now give up your coat!’”

The Person of Consequence is terrified. He stops shouting at subordinates. He treats people better.

The ghost, having achieved something, disappears, though rumors persist of it wandering the outskirts of the city.

VIII. What the Ghost Means

The supernatural ending of The Overcoat has been interpreted in two incompatible ways, and the incompatibility is, I think, deliberate.

The social reading: The ghost is justice, or the demand for justice. Akaki in life was powerless, invisible, dismissed. In death he can do what he could not do alive: take back, demand, terrify the powerful. The supernatural gives him the power that the social order denied him.

This reading produces a politically satisfying story: the oppressed, in death if not in life, achieves redress.

The existential reading: The ghost cannot stop. He takes the coat from the Person of Consequence, but this does not bring him peace. He is still seen, still wandering, still tearing coats.

The desire survives death. The wound does not heal by being inflicted on another.

What Akaki could not have in life (recognition, presence, the warmth of being seen) cannot be obtained by haunting. The ghost is not satisfied. The ghost is still wanting.

Gogol does not resolve this. The story ends ambiguously: the ghost still out there, somewhere, still wanting its coat.

IX. Desire, Recognition, and Hegel Again

The deepest philosophical reading of The Overcoat connects to Hegel’s concept of recognition (Anerkennung).

For Hegel, the self is not constituted in isolation: it requires recognition by another self to be fully real. The famous master-slave dialectic: the master is recognized by the slave, but the slave’s recognition is not truly satisfying because the slave is not an equal. Full recognition, genuine selfhood, requires mutual recognition between equals.

Akaki has no recognition. He is seen but not recognized: noticed as an object of mockery, not acknowledged as a subject.

The coat, temporarily, gives him recognition. Colleagues notice him. They smile. They invite him. For one evening, he is the recipient of genuine social acknowledgment.

The theft takes not just the coat but this recognition. And recognition, once felt and then withdrawn, is more painful than its absence.

This is the psychological precision at the center of the story: Gogol understands that deprivation is not simply the absence of something. It is the knowledge of the absence. Akaki before the coat did not suffer his invisibility because he could not conceive of visibility. Akaki after the coat, even for that one evening, has the concept, and therefore the lack.

The overcoat is not a coat. It is consciousness.

X. Gogol’s Laughter

The Overcoat is classified as a comic story.

It begins with jokes. The name is a joke. Petrovich the tailor is a joke. The bureaucratic machinery is a joke.

But the laughter progressively thickens: becomes uncomfortable, becomes uneasy, becomes finally impossible to sustain.

“I am your brother.”

That moment, that sudden apparition of genuine pathos in the middle of a comic scene, is the signature of Gogol’s method.

He is often called the father of Russian realism. He is nothing of the kind. His world is not realistic. It is grotesque, hallucinatory, operating by a logic that is adjacent to realism but fundamentally distorted.

The Nose falls off a man’s face and starts walking around St. Petersburg. Dead souls are purchased as an economic asset. A coat haunts the people who failed to protect it.

Gogol’s grotesque is not surrealism. It is not arbitrary or decorative. It is a way of making visible what realism cannot show: the inner logic of a society so distorted that realism, applied straightforwardly, would produce something that looked like satire.

The only way to show the truth about this world is to make the world even more itself: to take the distortion and amplify it until it becomes visible as distortion.

The coat that becomes a man’s entire soul. The theft of the coat that becomes the theft of a soul. The ghost that haunts because the social order would not give what it owed.

None of this is realistic. All of it is true.

XI. Akaki Akakiyeviç and Us

Why does this story still matter?

Because Akaki Akakiyeviç is not a historical curiosity, a portrait of 19th century Russian bureaucracy, but a recognizable human type that the 21st century produces in extraordinary quantities.

The person whose interiority has been hollowed out by repetitive, meaningless work, who finds in some small, specific object or activity the concentrated meaning that their labor denies them.

The person who is invisible in the social world, who passes through institutions without being seen, who has no advocate, no protector, no one who would notice if they were gone.

The person whose desire for recognition, for the simple acknowledgment that they exist, that they matter, that they are a subject and not merely an object, is met with indifference, bureaucratic obstruction, and finally shouting.

“Do you know to whom you are speaking?”

We know this voice. It speaks in every institution, in every encounter between the powerful and the powerless, in every interaction where someone with status uses that status not to help but to display.

And we know this too: the moment of recognition, however brief, and what it costs to have it taken away.

Gogol wrote this story in 1842. It is set in St. Petersburg. It is about right now. It is about here. It is about the person in the cubicle and the person in the waiting room and the person who has been waiting for an answer for weeks, from an institution that has forgotten they exist.

I am your brother.

Coda: The Coat and the Name

At the end, let us return to the beginning.

The story opens with a name, Akaki Akakiyeviç Başmaçkin, given reluctantly, by default, because nothing better was available.

A man named after footwear, who desires a coat, who briefly has it, who loses it, who dies, who haunts.

The coat and the name are the same thing. Both are coverings. Both are the social self: the self that is visible to others, the self that exists in the social world, the self that can be seen and recognized.

Without the coat, Akaki is just the name: just the formal, bureaucratic designation, the mark in the register, the unit of copying labor.

With the coat, he is briefly a person.

Gogol’s story is about what it costs to be a person: how much of what we are is constituted by how we appear, by how we are seen, by whether someone has looked at us and seen not just a function but a face.

Akaki wanted a coat. What he wanted was to exist.

He existed, briefly. That was enough to destroy him.

That is the story. That is Gogol.

The Teas He Didn’t Drink

There are writers I argue with all my life. Gogol is not one of them. There is no part of him I resist. There is only the wound he opens, and the slowness with which it closes.

Akaki Akakiyeviç lives in me. Whenever it gets cold, whenever I pass someone in a coat, I think of him. Not abstractly. Specifically. I think about the tea he stopped drinking in the evenings to save for the coat. I think about the laundry he stopped having done. I think about him walking on tiptoe across cobblestones to preserve his soles. These are not metaphors. They are the actual privations of an actual person, and they are, I think, the most devastating page in the story, because nothing happens in them. He is just slowly making himself smaller so a coat can exist.

There is no upward ambition in this. He is not trying to rise. He is not climbing toward respectability or status or admiration. He wants the cold to stop reaching him so he can keep doing the only work he loves, which is copying. That the world reads even this, the most modest possible wanting, as a fantasy of mobility says more about the readers than about Akaki. The trap of the story is that the smallest legitimate desire is already too much to be allowed in the kind of world Gogol is describing. He does not want a different life. He wants the one he has, with a coat in it. That is what is denied him.

The coat is not a coat. The essay above says this, and it is right. But I would put it more simply. The coat is the smallest possible token of being a person. And it costs Akaki nearly everything to get it. And one evening of acknowledgment is what he is given before it is taken back. That is enough, knowing what it felt like, to kill him.

There is something else. I find Gogol’s cruelty merciful. The grotesque surface, the absurd registers, the laughter that thickens until you cannot keep laughing, none of this is the writer holding himself above his characters. It is the writer giving us a way into the wound without recoiling from it. If he had written Akaki straight, sentimentally, no one would read past the second page. The comic is the only door into the tragic wide enough for the modern reader to walk through. Gogol knew this. That is why his laughter never feels like a betrayal.

When I think of Akaki I think of his three words: leave me alone, why do you torment me? And the young man at the desk who heard, behind those words, the other words: I am your brother. And then, much later, after Akaki is dead and the city has continued exactly as it was, the ghost on the bridge, still cold, still looking for what was taken. The story is not about a coat. It is about people who lived unseen, and were noticed, finally, only when they were missing.

When people read this story and only call it funny, something in me closes. I cannot get through November without thinking about it.

Further reading:

Nikolai Gogol, The Overcoat and Other Stories (trans. Richard Pevear & Larissa Volokhonsky).

Vladimir Nabokov, Nikolai Gogol (1944). The best book ever written about Gogol.

Dostoevsky, Poor Folk (1846). The direct response to The Overcoat.

Walter Benjamin, “The Storyteller” (1936).

Simone Weil, “Affliction and the Love of God” (1942). On invisibility and suffering.

This essay was originally published at gulfiliz.github.io.

item.title: Erotapokriseis VI
item.description:
EN:

Hello, my dear readers, Every time I receive your questions, I am reminded that writing is never really a monologue. It becomes more interesting when someone reads closely enough to ask back! I’ve answered most of your emails, but here are a few questions I wanted to answer publicly.

TR:

Merhaba sevgili okurlarım, Sizden gelen soruları her okuduğumda, yazmanın aslında hiçbir zaman tam anlamıyla tek taraflı olmadığını hatırlıyorum. E-postalarınızın çoğuna dönüş yaptım, ama bazı soruları burada da yanıtlamak istedim.

1) Q: In Special Relativity you say the deepest wound wasn’t time dilation but the relativity of simultaneity, that there is no fact of the matter about “now.” You’re someone who notices every passing minute. Did losing the universal “now” make your own sense of time feel more precious, or more like an illusion you can no longer trust?

A: More precious, not less. I expected the wound to make time feel fake; instead it made it feel mine. If there’s no universal “now,” then the now I’m in isn’t a clock everyone shares, it’s a thing only I am standing in. That doesn’t cheapen it. It makes it the one thing nobody else is having exactly the way I am.

This question came in Turkish.

2) Q: Special Relativity yazınızda “zaman kutsal değil; ‘şimdi’ dünyanın değil senin özelliğin” diyorsunuz. Ama bütün blogunuz anlara tutunuyor: bir kâğıt turna, bir kahve, bir mürekkep lekesi. Fizik size “şimdi diye bir şey yok” dedikten sonra, anlara hâlâ nasıl bu kadar inanabiliyorsunuz?

A: Çünkü “şimdi”nin dünyaya ait olmaması, bana ait olmadığı anlamına gelmiyor. Fizik onu evrenden aldı, bana geri verdi. Kâğıt turnaya, kahveye, mürekkep lekesine inanıyorum tam da bu yüzden: onlar evrensel değil, benim. Bazen yalnızca bana ait olana tutunmak, en sağlam tutunma biçimi gibi geliyor. Bilemiyorum. :)

3) Q: In Look Up you tell readers: don’t photograph the sky, don’t share it, just receive it. But you run a blog; your whole life is articulating what you see. Why is the sky the one thing you’d rather people stay silent in front of? What does it have that words would only spoil?

A: Because everything else I write about gets better when I put it into words, and the sky gets smaller. I’d rather hand someone the silence than a good paragraph that quietly replaces it. Some things you understand by describing them. The sky you understand by shutting up.

This question came in Turkish.

4) Q: Gökyüzünü Look Up yazınızda “ekranın son büyük panzehiri” diyorsunuz, simülasyonun kolonileştiremediği son gerçek. Post-Truth yazınızda da gerçekliğin çöküşünü anlatıyordunuz. Sizce Andromeda’dan gelen 2,5 milyon yıllık ışık, bir insana hâlâ “bu gerçek” dedirtmeye yetiyor mu, yoksa o da mı bir ekranın arkasında kayboluyor artık?

A: Yetiyor, hem de fazlasıyla. Post-truth gerçekliği tartışmalı kıldı, ama o ışık tartışmaya girmiyor ki; iznini istemeden gözüne çarpıyor. Ekran bize bir şey gösterir, gökyüzü bize çarpar. Farkı da bu: simülasyon bizi izleyici yapar, Andromeda ise şahit. 2,5 milyon yıl yol gelmiş bir foton karşısında insan numara yapamıyor. İyi ki de yapamıyor aslında.

5) Q: Are you in a relationship? I am curious about your love life.

A: I have to admit, I find this question a little funny and trivial! After all these posts, this is what you are curious about? :) I understand the curiosity, but I do not really like sharing my private life on social media, on my blog, or on the internet in general. Some parts of life should remain unlabeled, unposted, and unperformed.

So, respectfully, I will keep that to myself!

6) Q: What is something you simply cannot tolerate in life?

A: Cruelty disguised as intelligence. I cannot tolerate people who mistake being harsh for being honest, or being cynical for being intelligent. There is a particular kind of person who thinks kindness is naïve, humility is weakness, and sensitivity is something to be mocked. I find that unbearable. I also cannot tolerate vulgarity of character, not in the superficial sense but the deeper kind: people who humiliate others, who perform their status, who speak without grace, who turn every room into a stage for their ego. Life is already difficult enough. I do not want to be around people who make it uglier on purpose.

And one more thing, quieter but just as intolerable to me: evasion of honesty disguised as comfort. I cannot stand the kind of reassurance that softens a structural problem instead of naming it, the “it’s going fine” that withholds rather than reveals. When something is broken, I would rather be told plainly than be protected from the truth. I prefer analysis to reassurance, and I find it hard to trust warmth that comes at the cost of honesty. Being shielded from reality, even out of kindness, feels to me like a quiet form of disrespect, both to me and to the truth itself. If you care about someone, you tell them what is actually wrong. Comfort that requires omission is not comfort; it is avoidance wearing a gentler face.

7) Q: Is home a place for you, or more of a feeling?

A: This question looks like a cliché, but it really isn’t. Thank you for asking it. And I think I might be one of the most objective people you could come across in trying to answer it, because of where I’m standing. My answer is this. Home used to be a specific place for me. It was Urla, it was İzmir. Then I lost my grandmother, and now I’m in Dallas. While I’m far away, an illusion forms in me, maybe a defense mechanism: that she is still alive, still there in İzmir. But every time I actually go back to İzmir, it hurts so much. I feel such disappointment, because I see that she isn’t there anymore. So that place isn’t my home either. When I’m there, I can’t bring myself to miss Dallas, but the place I’m in now isn’t home the way it used to be either. I think home is definitely a feeling. Wherever the person you love, the person you love most, happens to be, that is where your home is. Once that person is gone, the place loses its old meaning. That’s just how it is…

8) Q: What do you think you have unusually good taste in?

A: People. I can tell within one conversation whether someone has a real inner life or is performing one, and I have never once been wrong about a person, never! :) And depth. I have very good taste in what is worth my time. I can sense the difference between something that looks profound and something that is, in a book, in a person, in a physics idea. It’s the same instinct every time.

9) Q: Çok popüler olup da sizin hiç sevemediğiniz bir şey var mı?

A: Offf, bir sürü.

(Bir Amerika’li okuyucumda çok benzer bir soru sormuş, O’na verdiğim cevap, siz okuduğunuzda kültür kodlarimizla resone edebilecek mi emin değilim ama Amerika’da en populer en sevemediğim şeyi bir sonraki soruda paylaşiyorum. )

10) Q: What is something very popular that you just cannot get into?

A: Yes. The performance of healing!

I do not dislike healing, of course. I dislike the way it has become an aesthetic, a vocabulary, almost a little costume people wear. Everyone is “protecting their peace,” “setting boundaries,” “choosing growth,” and somehow still being completely unkind. I find that very hard to take seriously.

11) Q: What is something people dismiss that you actually take seriously?

A: Small signs.

The way someone speaks to a waiter. The way their face changes when they are corrected. The little cruelty hidden inside a joke. The tiny hesitation before they congratulate someone else. People dismiss these things as insignificant, but I take them very seriously. Character rarely announces itself dramatically. Most of the time, it leaks out in small moments. :)

12) Q: What are you unapologetically basic about?

A: Coffee shops.

I know it is painfully basic, but I love sitting in a coffee shop with a book, a notebook, and a pen as if I am about to understand the entire human condition between two sips of coffee. Also long walks, bookstores, pretty stationery, and taking pictures of the sky. I refuse to be embarrassed by any of it.

This essay was originally published at gulfiliz.github.io.

item.title: Look Up — A Letter to Anyone Who Has Forgotten the Sky
item.description:
Go outside tonight.

Not with your phone. Not with an app. Not with a plan.

Just go outside, find a dark patch of sky, and look up.

Give it ten minutes. Let your eyes adjust.

What you will see — what has always been there, waiting — will change something in you.

I promise this.

I. The First Astronomers

Before writing, before agriculture, before the city and the state and the law —

there were people who looked up.

We know this because they left marks.

The Lascaux cave paintings in France — 17,000 years old — contain what appear to be star maps: the Pleiades, the Hyades, Orion.

The Nebra sky disk — 3,600 years old, found in Germany — is a bronze disk inlaid with gold: the sun, the crescent moon, the Pleiades cluster.

It is a calendar. A navigational instrument. A ritual object.

Whoever made it understood that the sky had a pattern — that the stars moved in ways that could be tracked, predicted, used.

This is the beginning of astronomy. Not the telescope. Not the equation.

A human being, sitting in the dark, watching the sky move, and thinking: there is an order here.

II. Thales and the Birth of the Question

Around 585 BCE, Thales of Miletus predicted a solar eclipse.

The prediction was correct. The eclipse occurred.

This was not magic. It was the application of Babylonian eclipse records — the Saros cycle of 18 years, 11 days — to predict a future event.

But what made Thales significant was not the prediction.

It was the question beneath it:

What is the sky made of? What are the rules by which it moves? Can we know these rules?

Thales proposed that everything was made of water — wrong, but beside the point.

The point was the move itself: the replacement of mythological explanation (the sun moves because Helios drives his chariot) with natural explanation (the sun moves because of a physical rule that applies everywhere, always).

This is the birth of science. Not experiment. Not mathematics. The question.

The willingness to look at the sky and ask not who is responsible but how it works.

Anaximander, Thales’s student, proposed that the earth floats freely in space — unsupported, held by nothing — because it is equidistant from everything.

This was 2,600 years ago. The idea of a free-floating earth — requiring nothing to hold it up — was as radical then as quantum mechanics is now.

Aristarchus, two centuries later, proposed that the earth orbits the sun.

He was ignored for 1,800 years.

He was right.

III. Hipparchus and the Catalog

Around 129 BCE, Hipparchus of Nicaea compiled the first star catalog in Western history.

He measured the positions of approximately 850 stars. He assigned each a magnitude — a measure of brightness on a scale of 1 to 6.

This scale is still used.

He also discovered stellar precession — the slow wobble of the Earth’s axis that causes the position of the celestial pole to trace a circle over 26,000 years.

He discovered this by comparing his measurements with older Babylonian records.

He noticed that the stars had moved slightly — not relative to each other, but relative to the equinoxes.

From measurements made with the naked eye, with no instruments more sophisticated than a dioptra — a sighting tube — he identified a phenomenon that takes 26,000 years to complete.

The patience this required — the willingness to compare his work with measurements made centuries earlier, to notice a change of fractions of a degree — is one of the most extraordinary acts of scientific attention in history.

IV. Galileo and the New Sky

On the night of January 7, 1610, Galileo Galilei pointed a telescope at Jupiter.

He saw three small stars — in a line, close to Jupiter.

The next night, they had moved.

The night after: different positions.

He watched for weeks. He realized: these were not stars. They were moons — orbiting Jupiter.

He had discovered the first moons of another planet.

But more than that:

He had discovered objects that did not orbit the Earth.

In the Ptolemaic system — the system endorsed by the Church, by tradition, by common sense — everything orbited the Earth. The Earth was the center.

Galileo had found objects that orbited something else.

The center was not holding.

He published his observations in Sidereus Nuncius — The Starry Messenger — in March 1610.

It sold out immediately. It was read across Europe within weeks.

He had also observed the Moon — and found it was not a perfect sphere. It had mountains, craters, valleys.

The celestial bodies were not perfect. They were physical places — rough, irregular, made of matter.

He had pointed his telescope at the Milky Way and found it was not a cloud. It was stars — more stars than anyone had imagined, packed so densely they blurred together.

In one winter, Galileo transformed the sky from a dome painted with lights into a universe of places.

The telescope did not just show more. It showed differently. It revealed that the sky was not a backdrop.

It was a destination.

V. The Celestron and the Texas Sky

I have an advanced Celestron telescope.

And, I live in Texas now.

People do not always know this about Texas: the sky here is extraordinary.

Not in the cities — Dallas, Houston, Austin have light pollution as bad as anywhere.

But drive an hour west of San Antonio. Drive into the Hill Country. Drive to the McDonald Observatory near Fort Davis — one of the darkest sites in the continental United States.

Or just drive to a state park on a moonless night.

The Milky Way appears as a band — not a faint smear but a structure, with dark lanes of dust, with brighter regions and dimmer ones, with the sense of being inside something enormous.

The first time I saw it properly — not from a city, not filtered through light pollution — I sat down on the ground.

Not from weakness. From something that felt like being struck.

The sky I had been looking at all my life was not the sky.

The sky — the actual sky — is something else entirely.

With the Celestron, I can see:

The Andromeda Galaxy — not as a smear but as a structure, with a bright core and faint spiral arms extending. 2.5 million light-years away. The light entering my eye tonight left before Homo sapiens existed.

The Orion Nebula — the birthplace of stars. A cloud of gas 1,344 light-years away, glowing because young hot stars inside it are ionizing the gas. Stars are being born there tonight.

The rings of Saturn — which never, no matter how many times I see them, fail to produce a small gasp. They look fake. They look like a stamp. They are real.

The surface of the Moon — craters, mountain ranges, the dark maria, the ray systems of young impact craters spreading across the surface like cracks in glass.

With my telescope, I can see what Galileo saw on his first night of observation.

I think about this often.

VI. What You Can See With Your Eyes — Tonight

Here is what I want you to know:

You do not need a telescope.

The unaided human eye — dark-adapted, patient, in a reasonably dark sky — can see approximately 5,000 stars.

More than enough.

Let me tell you what is up there, waiting for you.

The Moon

If the Moon is up: look at it.

Not a glance. Look.

The dark regions — the maria, the “seas” — are ancient lava flows, billions of years old, solidified and preserved in the airless cold.

The bright regions are the ancient highlands — the original crust of the Moon, battered by billions of years of impacts.

The line between light and dark — the terminator — is where you can see the most detail. The shadows are long there. Craters that are invisible in full moon leap out in sharp relief.

You are looking at a world. Another world. 384,000 kilometers away. Close enough that, in a dark sky, you can trace its mountains with your naked eye.

The Planets

Five planets are visible to the naked eye: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn.

They have been visible to the naked eye since before history.

Every ancient culture tracked them. They were called “wanderers” — planetes in Greek — because they moved against the fixed stars.

Venus is the brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon. It appears as a dazzling white point — so bright it can cast shadows on a dark night.

It is visible just after sunset in the west or just before sunrise in the east.

Jupiter is the second brightest planet. Its disk is visible to the naked eye if you know what to look for — it does not twinkle like a star. It is steady, bright, cream-colored.

With any binoculars, you can see the four Galilean moons — the same moons Galileo saw in 1610. They shift position from night to night. You can watch them move.

Saturn is dimmer but unmistakable — a warm golden color, steady like a planet should be. With a small telescope, the rings become visible.

But even without — knowing it is there, knowing that those rings exist, that this point of golden light is a world with a ring system large enough to contain several Earths — changes how you see it.

Mars is red. Not subtly red. Unmistakably, immediately red. At opposition — when it is closest to Earth — it is bright enough to read by.

The Stars

The stars have names.

Not catalog numbers — names. Ancient names. Arabic names, Greek names, Latin names.

Betelgeuse — the shoulder of Orion. Arabic: yad al-jawzā’ — the hand of the giant. A red supergiant so large that if placed at the center of our solar system, it would extend past the orbit of Jupiter.

It will explode as a supernova — perhaps tomorrow, perhaps in 100,000 years. When it does, it will be visible in daylight.

Sirius — the Dog Star. The brightest star in the night sky. The ancient Egyptians oriented their temples to it. Its heliacal rising — its first appearance at dawn after a period of invisibility — marked the beginning of the annual Nile flood.

8.6 light-years away. The light you see left when you were in primary school.

Vega — one of the three stars of the Summer Triangle. 26 light-years away. The standard star for photometric calibration — the reference by which other stars’ brightness is measured.

Polaris — the North Star. Not the brightest star. Not particularly impressive. But it sits almost exactly above Earth’s North Pole.

As the Earth rotates, every other star traces an arc across the sky. Polaris barely moves.

Find Polaris. The two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper’s bowl — Dubhe and Merak — point directly to it.

Once you find Polaris, you can find north anywhere on Earth, any night of the year, without a compass.

This is how sailors navigated the world.

The Milky Way

If you are away from city lights — if the sky is genuinely dark —

look for the Milky Way.

It appears as a band of soft light crossing the sky from horizon to horizon.

What you are seeing is the disk of our galaxy — 200-400 billion stars, seen edge-on.

You are inside it. You are looking through the plane of the galaxy — through 100,000 light-years of stars and gas and dust.

The dark lanes within the Milky Way are not gaps in the stars. They are clouds of dust blocking the light of stars behind them.

The center of the galaxy — where a supermassive black hole of 4 million solar masses resides — is in the direction of Sagittarius, toward the south in summer.

The Milky Way is brightest there. Thickest. Most structured.

You are looking at the core of your galaxy.

The Andromeda Galaxy

On a dark night, look in the direction of the constellation Andromeda.

There is a faint smear of light — barely visible to the naked eye, easier with averted vision (looking slightly to the side of it).

This is M31 — the Andromeda Galaxy.

It is 2.537 million light-years away.

The light entering your eye right now left the Andromeda Galaxy 2.537 million years ago — before Homo sapiens evolved.

You are not looking at a photograph. You are not looking at a representation.

You are receiving photons — actual photons, quantum excitations of the electromagnetic field — that have been traveling through space for 2.537 million years and have just ended their journey in your eye.

This is the farthest object visible to the naked human eye.

2.537 million light-years. Without a telescope. With your eyes.

VII. The Practical Guide — How to Start

1. Dark adaptation.

Your eyes need approximately 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to darkness. During this time: no phone, no flashlight.

If you must use light: red light only. Red light does not reset dark adaptation. (This is why astronomers use red flashlights.)

2. Find a dark location.

You don’t need to go far. Any location away from direct streetlights helps. A park, a field, a dark backyard.

For serious observing: find a dark sky site. The Dark Sky Finder website maps light pollution across the country.

3. Learn the constellations.

Start with the ones that are easy and useful.

The Big Dipper — not technically a constellation but an asterism within Ursa Major. Seven bright stars in the shape of a ladle. Visible year-round in the northern hemisphere. Use it to find Polaris (north) and Arcturus (extend the handle’s curve).

Orion — the most recognizable constellation. Visible in winter. The three belt stars are unmistakable. Betelgeuse (red, upper left) and Rigel (blue-white, lower right). Below the belt: the Orion Nebula, faintly visible to the naked eye.

Scorpius — the summer constellation. S-shaped curve of stars with a bright red heart: Antares — “rival of Mars” — another red supergiant, 700 times the diameter of the Sun.

The Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb, Altair. Three bright stars forming a large triangle overhead in summer. The Milky Way passes through it.

4. Get binoculars before a telescope.

10×50 binoculars — 10x magnification, 50mm aperture — will transform your observing.

With binoculars you can see:

  • The Galilean moons of Jupiter
  • The Pleiades cluster in full glory
  • The Andromeda Galaxy as a structure
  • Star clusters, nebulae, double stars
  • The craters of the Moon in sharp detail

A good pair of binoculars will show you more interesting things than a poor telescope.

5. Get an app — but use it before you go outside.

SkySafari, Stellarium, Star Walk — these apps are extraordinary.

But use them to plan. Not to watch.

The goal is to see the sky. Not to look at your phone under the sky.

Plan at home. Note what you want to find. Go outside with the plan in your head. Leave the phone in your pocket.

VIII. Why This Still Matters

In an age of simulation — in a world where Baudrillard’s hyperreality has colonized most of our experience —

the night sky is stubbornly, irreducibly real.

You cannot fake it. You cannot simulate the experience of standing under a genuinely dark sky and seeing the Milky Way for the first time.

The photons are real. The distance is real. The time — the millions of years of travel — is real.

The sky is the last great antidote to the screen.

It requires nothing from you. It demands no subscription, no account, no engagement metric.

It has been there for 4.6 billion years. It will be there after you.

And it is available — free, tonight — to anyone willing to go outside and look up.

IX. A Note on Wonder

The ancient Greeks had a word: θαυμάζειν — thaumazein.

Wonder.

Aristotle said philosophy begins with wonder.

Not with doubt, as Descartes said. Not with method. Not with rigor.

Wonder.

The experience of standing before something that exceeds your categories — that cannot be immediately absorbed, explained, filed away — and feeling not anxiety but openness.

The willingness to be undone by what is larger than you.

The night sky produces thaumazein.

Every time.

For Thales, wondering what those lights were and how they moved.

For Galileo, pointing a tube of glass at Jupiter and finding moons where no moons should be.

For every child who has ever asked, on a camping trip or a dark night in the backyard: how many stars are there?

And been told: more than you can count. More than all the grains of sand on Earth. More than you can imagine.

And felt — not overwhelmed — but enlarged.

This is what the sky does.

It does not make you small.

It makes you aware of how large the world is — and of the extraordinary fact that you are the part of it that can look up, and wonder, and ask.

Coda

Tonight, wherever you are:

Go outside.

Give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust.

Find the darkest patch of sky available to you.

Look up.

Find Polaris. Find Orion. Find the Milky Way if you can.

Find the faint smear in Andromeda — the light that left before your species existed.

Stand there.

Do not photograph it. Do not share it. Do not explain it.

Just receive it.

2.537 million years of travel — for this moment, here, your eyes, open.

That is enough. That has always been enough.

If you want to go deeper:

Timothy Ferris — Coming of Age in the Milky Way (1988) — the best history of astronomy ever written

Carl Sagan — Cosmos (1980) — still the greatest introduction to the universe

Terence Dickinson — NightWatch (1983) — the practical guide to backyard astronomy

Dark Sky Finder: darksitefinder.com

Clear Outside app — for weather and seeing conditions

SkySafari — for planning and identification

And: go outside. Tonight. Look up.

item.title: Erotapokriseis V
item.description:
EN:

Hello again, my dear readers! Some of your questions arrived like letters, some like puzzles, and some like tiny philosophical traps. Naturally, I loved them. I’ve answered many of you by email, but I thought a few of these deserved a place here as well. :)

TR:

Yeniden merhaba sevgili okurlarım, Bazı sorularınız mektup gibi geldi, bazıları bilmece gibi, bazılarıysa küçük felsefi tuzaklar gibiydi, ahaha! Türkiye özlemim sizinle diniyor birazda olsa. Doğal olarak hepsini çok sevdim. Çoğunuza e-posta ile dönüş yaptım, ama bazı soruların burada da yer almayı hak ettiğini düşündüm. Çok sevgiler.

This question came in Turkish.

1) Q: Post-Truth yazınızda post-truth’un “yetişkin-Filiz”i yarattığını, zihninizi olgunlaştırdığını, hatta sizi felsefeye ittiğini yazmışsınız. Tuhaf bir minnet bu: sizi en çok büyüten şey, gerçekliğin çöküşü olmuş. İnsanı olgunlaştıran şeyin çoğu zaman onu en çok korkutan şey olması sizce tesadüf mü?

A: Tesadüf değil. Bizi büyüten şey, üzerine basıp da çatırdayan zemindir birazda bence; sağlam yer insanı sadece taşır, sarsmaz! Beni olgunlaştıran, gerçekliğin çökmesi değildi aslında; çökerken ona dikkatle bakmak zorunda kalmamdı. Tam cevaplayabildim mi sorunuzu emin değilim. Çok sevgiler.

This question came in Turkish.

2) Q: Geometry yazınızda Perelman’ın hem Fields madalyasını hem de bir milyon doları reddedip Petersburg’da sessizce yaşadığını anlatıyorsunuz. Sizce o bir aziz mi, yoksa Epictetus‘un “elimde olanı umursarım, gerisini değil” dersini herkesten iyi öğrenmiş biri mi? Onu anlıyor musunuz, yoksa anlamak istemediğiniz bir yanı mı var?

A: Aziz değil; sadece dersini bizden iyi çözmüş biri. Perelman ödülü reddederken bir şeyden vazgeçmiyor, elinde olmayanı zaten istemiyordu. Anlıyorum onu. Anlamak istemediğim yanı şu: ben hâlâ dünyayı istiyorum, o istemeyebiliyor. Orada beni geçiyor. Aslında bir sürü şeyde beni geçiyorda, çaktırmayalım şimdi! :))

This question came in Turkish.

3) Q: Marcus Aurelius kendine not tutuyordu, yayımlamak için değil. Sizin blogunuz da bir bakıma “kendine notlar”, Fragmenta. Peki siz kime yazıyorsunuz: okura mı, kendinize mi?

A: Ah bir bilsem kime yazdığımı…

This question came in Turkish.

4) Q: Topological Phases of Matter yazınızda “fizik, 20. yüzyıl matematiğinin derin bir sonucunu yeniden keşfetti” diyorsunuz. Fizikle matematik arasında yaşayan biri olarak: doğanın matematiği çoktan biliyor olması size ne hissettiriyor?

A: Tedirgin değil, mahcup hissettiriyor. Çünkü “doğa matematiği biliyor” demek bile bizim kibrimiz; sanki matematik bizim de doğa ödünç almış gibi. Belki de tam tersi: matematik dediğimiz şey, doğayı yeterince uzun süre dikkatle izlemiş insanların aldığı not. O zaman doğa bir şey “biliyor” değil; biz geç anlıyoruz. :)

5) Q: In Beautiful But Wrong you confess you’ve felt Kepler’s divine ecstasy three times, and twice it turned out to be a bug. Before the relief or the heartbreak arrives, how do you now tell a result that’s beautiful-and-true from one that’s beautiful-and-a-bug?

A: I don’t trust the ecstasy anymore; I treat it as a siren, not a verdict. A result is only allowed to stay beautiful after it has survived the ugly tests: null cases, old examples, dumb baselines, and the possibility that I simply made a mistake. Sounds similar,huh? :)

6) Q: In Wittgenstein you refuse his last commandment, “whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent,” and say you want to push at the limit “with a beautiful sentence and see what gives way.” Has a beautiful sentence ever actually made something give way for you, or is that the most romantic lie a writer tells herself?

A: Yes, once or twice, and I’d know it again. A sentence gives way when you read it and something in your chest rearranges before your mind catches up. It’s rare, and most of what I write isn’t it. But it happens, which is why I refuse to be silent. Wittgenstein felt it too; he just called it showing.

7) Q: Plato carved “let no one ignorant of geometry enter” over his door, and you agree: you can’t understand reality without geometry, because reality is structured. But your blog is full of the unstructured, grief, ink, a child’s paper crane, the things that resist the metric. Which is the truer language for you, the geometry or the fragment?

A: Geometry is the truer language for the world. I use structure to understand reality, and fragments to survive being inside it. But, I need to survive, right? I learned this pragmatism from Americans :D

8) Q: Which character in Russian literature do you feel closest to?

A: This is the best question I’ve ever been asked. While answering it, I realized I’d been waiting since my youth for someone to ask me this question. Thank you!!!!

Probably Levin, though my mind understands Ivan Karamazov a little too well.

Levin, not because I resemble him completely, but because I understand that restless desire to live truthfully. Ivan is closer to my mind: the questions, the rebellion, the inability to look away from suffering. But Alyosha is closer to the kind of soul I would like to have.

So perhaps the honest answer is this: my mind is often with Ivan, my longing is with Levin, and my heart would like to become a little more like Alyosha.

Thank you again, hugs!

9) Q: Which fictional villain do you secretly think has a point?

A: Frankenstein’s creature.

Though even calling him a villain feels a little unfair. I do not justify what he does, but I understand the wound he speaks from. To be created, abandoned, feared, and then blamed for becoming monstrous feels like one of literature’s cruelest moral traps. Sometimes the real horror is not the monster. It is the person who creates life and then refuses responsibility for it. And thank you so much for the heartfelt email C.!

( Milton’s satan, Javert, Magneto are also other candidates. Ahahah :) )

10) Q: Have you ever realized you were completely wrong about something and changed your mind?

A: Yes, absolutely!

I have realized I was wrong many times, and I have changed my mind many times: about people, about ideas, about what I thought I wanted, and sometimes about myself. I do not see changing my mind as a weakness. I think there is something beautiful about being able to outgrow your own certainty. Staying loyal to an old version of yourself just because she was once convinced feels much more embarrassing to me.

And I feel the same way about apologizing. I have never seen an apology as a loss of dignity. On the contrary, I think being able to say “I was wrong” is one of the cleanest forms of strength. I have to admit, I do not have much patience for people who cannot apologize. Apologizing is a beautiful thing.

11) Q: What was the most beautiful gift you’ve ever received, the one that made you happiest?

A: My reader from Medium. :) Thanks for the question.

Every gift I’ve ever received has been beautiful and precious to me. I could never put a price on any of them. A smooth, lovely gel pen, a magnet someone picked out while thinking of me, or a pin given with the words “this reminded me of you” would all make me just as happy.

But if I’m being honest, the most unforgettable gift I’ve ever received was a piano. Not because it was expensive. I’ve been given things that were more expensive than a piano. But because of the timing, and the tenderness behind it. I had casually mentioned one day that, as a child, I had always wanted to learn the piano, but never had the chance. The next day, I was given one. It felt like a small, unfinished dream of mine had been heard and gently placed back in my hands.That meant so much to me. It’s still hard for me to describe. (I hate crying!)

This essay was originally published at gulfiliz.github.io.

item.title: Filizko got her masters degree, yay!
item.description:
I finished my master’s in Computer Science at UT Dallas, with a concentration in Intelligent Systems, AI and ML.

It still feels a little strange to write that sentence.

Computer Science was not originally my field. I came in needing eight prerequisite courses just to catch up, which meant that for a while I was basically an undergraduate again: intro lectures, problem sets, basic concepts, and the humbling feeling of learning something from the very beginning.

And somehow, that became one of the best parts.

There is something beautiful about becoming a beginner again, especially years after you thought you were done being one. This degree taught me algorithms, machine learning, artificial intelligence, and systems, yes. But more than that, it taught me patience. It taught me humility. It taught me that starting over is not a failure; sometimes it is exactly how you grow into the next version of yourself.

I was also lucky to learn from professors who truly inspired me: Yi Zhao, Dung Huynh, Yvo Desmedt, and Yapeng Tian. They were not only brilliant teachers, but also wonderful human beings, and I will always be grateful for the way they shaped this part of my journey.

And I did get to walk across the stage.

I graduated with dear friends beside me, and with people I love there to celebrate with me. That made the day even more meaningful. A degree is already something to be proud of, but sharing that moment with people who know what it took to get there made it unforgettable.

So here it is: my master’s in Computer Science.

It was difficult, humbling, unexpected, and beautiful.

I am very proud of this one!

P.S. I started CS with zero programming knowledge. Ahahaha!

Some degrees are not just earned. They are survived, shared, and remembered.

item.title: Erotapokriseis IV
item.description:
EN:

Dear readers, Your emails have been one of the quiet joys of writing here. I cannot always answer everything at once, but I do read them with care. Today, I wanted to bring a few of your questions into this space and answer them in the open. Thank you so much! :)

TR:

Sevgili okurlarım, Burada yazmanın en sessiz ama en güzel taraflarından biri, sizden gelen e-postalar. Her şeye hemen cevap veremiyorum, ama hepsini özenle okuyorum. Bugün bazı sorularınızı buraya taşımak ve açıkça yanıtlamak istedim. Benimle birlikte düşündüğünüz için teşekkür ederim!

1) Q: You’ve now written two essays on how America exiles its thinkers and buys them back with Europe’s approval, The Country That Ate Its Own Geniuses and Why American Intellectuals Are Invisible. You left İzmir to go there. Be honest: are you writing about America, or about a fear for yourself?

A: :) Hehehhe. :). Not enough, heheheheheheheheh :)

P.S. I gave him the long answer in the email without hehehehes :)

2) Q: You admit Epictetus makes you “feel personally attacked” (Epictetus): the test of philosophy isn’t what you can say but what you can bear. By that test, honestly, how are you doing?

A: Terribly! But at least I know it now. :)

This question came in Turkish.

3) Q: The Country That Ate Its Own Geniuses yazınızda Poe, Melville, Dickinson, Ives, hepsi ancak öldükten sonra anlaşıldı. Açık konuşalım: bir yazar olsaydınız sizi anlaşılmamak mı daha çok korkuturdu, yoksa çok geç anlaşılmak mı?

A: İkisi de değil. Beni korkutan, anlaşılmak için yazmaya başladığım gün olurdu.

Ayrıca, Poe geç anlaşıldı ama hiç eğilmeden yazdı; korkulacak şey eğilmek, geç kalmak değil. Çok sevgiler!

4) Q: What quality do you value most in people?

A: Maturity and humility.

I like grounded people. Substantial people. People who have a certain weight to them, not in a performative way, but in the way they carry themselves. People often say that communication is the most important thing: open communication, honesty, saying things clearly. And yes, of course, all of that matters. But I think two people can only really meet each other if they have a similar level of maturity. If you are not standing on the same emotional ground, even honesty becomes difficult. Open communication does not save you. Good intentions get wasted. If you asked me what the people I love and value most have in common, I would probably say this: they are mature in a similar way. They know how to listen. They know when to speak. They do not turn every disagreement into a wound or every silence into an insult. There is a steadiness in them that makes life easier.

The other thing is humility. We all come from different backgrounds, different families, different chances, different kinds of luck. The things we have in life should not be sold as personal virtues. They should be things we are grateful for. The moment someone starts performing their money, their car, their degree, their title, I lose interest. I do not need to know that person further. They still have a long way to go in life. I like people who are humble, who know how to sit among people, how to speak with respect, how not to make themselves the center of every room. The funny thing is, my own humility is often misunderstood. People sometimes read my warmth as romantic interest, or they mistake my gentleness for weakness. Some men, especially, think that because I am kind and warm, I must be in love with them. Others think they can underestimate me. But hell no, cicimmm :). That is my quality. It has nothing to do with you.

5) Q: What quality of yours are you most proud of?

A: This is a beautiful question. I will try to answer it without sounding arrogant.

I think the quality I am most proud of is my self-respect, and the fact that it remains intact no matter who is in front of me, what I feel, or how much I care. For example, I can love someone deeply. I can be willing to do almost anything for the people I love. I am not afraid of effort, loyalty, or sacrifice. But my self-respect is non-negotiable. That is the line.

I know this may sound like a cliché, because everyone likes to think they have self-respect. But for me, self-respect is not something I talk about only when life is easy. It is something that has to work when I am hurt, attached, tempted, or heartbroken.

If I part ways with a friend/partner, for example, I do not stalk them. I do not keep looking back. I do not say this because I never feel the desire to look. Of course I do. I am human! But I know how to stop myself. I may feel the impulse, but I do not obey every impulse. My will is stronger than my curiosity, my longing, and sometimes even my sadness. I have a very strong will. Very strong!

6) Q: What tiny etiquette rule matters a lot to you?

A: I will answer this one as a woman.

I care a lot about whether someone knows how to behave in the presence of a woman. How they sit, how they speak, how much space they take, how they use their hands, whether they make lazy sexist comments or assumptions about her background — these things matter to me. For example, stretching your legs toward a woman, sitting across from her with your legs spread open, flossing your teeth in front of her, or speaking to her with a kind of careless familiarity is not charming. I am not your mother or your sister. The fact that we work in the same place, study at the same school, or belong to the same interest group does not exempt you from basic manners.

I also find it deeply unattractive when men assume that every woman will automatically be impressed by their education, money, title, or status. That kind of confidence does not look powerful to me. It looks a little pathetic. Not in an old-fashioned, performative way. I do not need theater. I just appreciate basic grace, respect, and composure.

7) Q: What do people usually assume about you that is wrong?

A: People usually assume that I am very serious and difficult to approach.

I think I may look a little intimidating from the outside, especially when I am quiet or focused. But once people get to know me, they usually realize that I am much warmer, funnier, and more playful than they expected. I have heard some version of “Oh, you are actually so much fun” many times. :)

8) Q: Does knowledge make a person better, or only more alone?

A: Knowledge only makes a person informed! That is all!

It does not automatically make you kinder, wiser, humbler, or more decent. It only gives you information. What you do with that information is a matter of character.

9) Q: What is your faith?

A: This is a private question, and I do not think the answer really matters that much. Perhaps the better question is whether I believe in God or not. Yes, I believe in God. Whether the God I believe in is exactly the same God everyone else has in mind, I am not entirely sure. But perhaps that is true for most of us. With love. :)

10) Q: If you could fight with one historical figure, who would it be?

A: Kant.

I’m still not entirely over the fact that he shut every door to God, the soul, and metaphysics, only to sneak them back in through morality.

And by “fight,” I don’t mean shouting. I mean a long, serious, unnecessarily passionate argument at a table somewhere.

(I should add that I am not really a fight person. I did not grow up in a loud or combative home; I was raised by my grandmother in a very safe, quiet, and peaceful one. Raised voices, slammed doors, and dramatic arguments are simply not my language. I believe almost anything can be resolved by talking, and if it cannot, I would rather leave than become part of the noise.)

11) Q: What are you a little elitist about?

A: Taste. Not expensive taste, not brand-name taste. I mean the ability to recognize when something has soul. A sentence, a room, a pen, a book, a conversation, even a silence. I am a little elitist about things that are not merely impressive, but alive.

&

Books. Not in the sense of judging people by how much they read. I do not think reading automatically makes someone deep or interesting. But I do become a little suspicious when someone says they read, and then I look at what they read and think, perhaps cruelly, that they might have been better off not reading at all.

What I care about is not the performance of reading, but whether a person has a private life with ideas: a book, a question, an obsession, some little corner of the mind where they go to be alone!
