item.title: The Art of Folding: Paper, History, and the Mathematics of Modular Origami
item.description:
There is a moment, when you fold paper, where something shifts. The material stops being passive. It begins to speak, in angles, in tensions, in the geometry of a crease that, once made, cannot be entirely unmade.

I met origami in Japan, in my twenties.

It started at a hotel. By the elevator, where any other country leaves a toothbrush and Q-tips and a shower cap, they had set out origami paper. Of course they had. Ah, Japan. How unique you are. I grabbed a pack on the spot, and it rode home with me, still sealed.

But the origami that actually stayed with me is a different one.

I was on the Yamanote line, the green loop. A woman got on holding a small child, so I gave up my seat and stood. A little boy, just before his stop, reached up, held out a folded scrap of paper, and bowed. The moment I took it, he bolted off the train. When the doors closed and we pulled away, he was on the platform, smiling, waving.

That little fold is still with me. I use it as a bookmark. A child small enough that the gift fit inside his hands, big-hearted enough to give it to a stranger who was only visiting his country. I am smiling just writing this.

Before I flew home I bought far too much paper, from Daiso, from Loft, from Tokyu Hands. Then, naturally, I did nothing with it. It sat in a corner of the house for a couple of years. Until one night I fell into a random YouTube video, Jun Maekawa folding a modular piece, and for some reason a structure built from many identical units pulled at me far more than any single folded shape ever had.

Modular origami, the kind where dozens or hundreds of units interlock without glue into a single structure, is the form I keep returning to. Not because it is the most beautiful. Not always. But because it is the most honest: every unit must be identical, every join must be precise, and the whole will not hold unless everything is right.

There is no hiding in modular origami.

To understand origami, you must first understand paper!

I. The Invention of Paper

Before paper, writing surfaces were expensive, heavy, fragile, or scarce. Clay tablets. Papyrus. Silk. Bamboo strips. None of these fold.

Paper, thin, flexible, cheap, strong, changed everything.

The invention is attributed to Cai Lun (蔡倫), a court official of the Han dynasty, who in 105 CE presented Emperor He with a new writing material made from bark, hemp, rags, and fishnets.

This is the traditional account. Archaeological evidence suggests papermaking existed in China perhaps two centuries earlier. Fragments have been found dating to the Western Han period (206 BCE – 9 CE). But Cai Lun standardized and improved the process, and the court’s adoption of his method spread it throughout the empire.

The process he developed is recognizably modern:

Fibrous plant material, the bark of mulberry, hemp, bamboo, is soaked, beaten into a pulp, suspended in water, and scooped onto a flat screen. As the water drains, the fibers bond. The sheet is pressed and dried.

The result: a material that is at once strong and flexible, light and durable, and, crucially for origami, capable of holding a crease.

II. Paper Travels West

From China, papermaking spread along trade routes with extraordinary slowness by modern standards, and extraordinary speed by ancient ones.

Korea received papermaking in the 4th century CE. Korean paper, hanji (한지), made from the bark of the mulberry tree (Broussonetia papyrifera), became famous for its exceptional durability. Documents written on hanji have survived a thousand years.

Japan received the technology in 610 CE, according to traditional accounts via the Buddhist monk Damjing from Korea. Japanese papermaking developed into an art form of its own, producing papers of extraordinary variety, texture, and beauty.

The Islamic world acquired papermaking after the Battle of Talas (751 CE), where Arab forces captured Chinese papermakers. Paper mills appeared in Samarkand, then Baghdad, then across the Islamic world. The Arabic word for paper, waraq, entered dozens of languages.

Europe received paper through the Islamic world, with the first European paper mills appearing in Spain and Italy in the 12th and 13th centuries.

By the time Gutenberg invented movable type in 1440, paper was ready for it.

III. Japanese Paper: Washi

The Japanese word for paper is kami (紙). It shares its sound, though not its character, with the word for spirit or god: kami (神).

This is not coincidence, or rather, it is the kind of coincidence that shapes a culture. Paper in Japan was sacred material. It was used in Shinto rituals, folded into ritual forms called shide that still hang in shrines today.

Japanese papermaking, washi (和紙, wa = Japanese, shi = paper), developed its own distinct tradition.

The finest washi papers are still made by hand, using traditional techniques that have changed little in a thousand years.

Among the most celebrated:

Washi (和紙): the general term for traditional Japanese handmade paper, made primarily from three plants: kōzo (楮, mulberry), mitsumata (三椏), and gampi (雁皮). Each produces paper with distinct qualities: kōzo is strong and flexible, gampi is smooth and lustrous.

Yuzen (友禅): not strictly a paper type but a dyeing technique, originally developed for silk kimono fabric in the Edo period by the fan painter Miyazaki Yūzen. The technique, using rice paste as a resist to create precise, elaborate patterns, was later applied to paper. Yuzen paper is used in bookbinding, crafts, and high-end origami.

Chiyogami (千代紙): chiyo means “thousand generations,” gami is the voiced form of kami (paper). Traditional Japanese decorative paper, featuring bold, repetitive patterns derived from kimono fabric designs. Originally produced in Kyoto and Edo. The patterns, cranes, waves, cherry blossoms, geometric forms, are printed using hand-carved woodblocks. Used in traditional crafts and ceremonial wrapping.

Kozo (楮紙): pure mulberry paper, prized for strength. Used in conservation and restoration of artworks worldwide. The Library of Congress uses kozo paper to repair ancient documents.

Momigami (揉み紙): paper that has been crumpled and worked by hand until it achieves a soft, leather-like texture. Used in decorative arts and certain origami techniques.

IV. The Word Origami

Origami (折り紙): ori (折り) meaning “folding,” kami (紙) meaning “paper,” voiced to gami in compound.

The word is surprisingly recent.

The practice of paper folding in Japan is ancient, at least as old as the introduction of paper itself. But for most of Japanese history, the craft was called orikata (折り形, “folded shapes”) or orisue (折り据え).

The word origami in its current sense became standard only in the modern period. Some scholars date its widespread use to the Meiji era (1868–1912) or even later.

Before this, two distinct traditions existed:

Noshi (熨斗): formal paper folding for ceremonial use. Paper folded around gifts, used in wedding ceremonies, attached to sake cups. These were rigid, prescribed forms, not art but ritual.

Tsutsumi (包み): wrapping and folding paper for gifts and formal presentation. The aesthetics of wrapping, the geometry of folded paper, were codified into elaborate systems of etiquette.

The tradition of folding paper for play and artistic expression, closer to what we now call origami, developed alongside these ceremonial forms and was documented in the 18th century work Hiden Senbazuru Orikata (秘伝千羽鶴折形, 1797): “The Secret of One Thousand Cranes,” the first known book of origami instructions.

V. The Crane and the Legend

Senbazuru, one thousand cranes.

The tradition: fold one thousand paper cranes, and your wish will be granted. Some versions say: you will be healed of illness. Some say: you will live for a thousand years.

The legend became inseparable from Sadako Sasaki, a girl who was two years old when the atomic bomb fell on Hiroshima in 1945.

She developed leukemia at twelve. She began folding cranes in the hospital, aiming for one thousand.

She folded 644 before she died. Her classmates completed the remaining 356.

She was twelve years old.

There is a statue of Sadako in the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park. She holds a golden crane. Every year, thousands of children from around the world send origami cranes to be placed at her memorial.

I have stood there. I went to Hiroshima, to the A-Bomb Dome, and into the museum, which was so raw and so unfiltered that I could not make it through all of it; there were rooms I simply could not stay in.

Before I left, I folded a crane for every person I love, and I left them with Sadako.

This is what paper can hold.

VI. The Mathematics of Folding

For most of its history, origami was transmitted as craft, through instruction, imitation, practice.

In the 20th century, mathematicians began to ask: what are the underlying principles?

The result was a new field: computational origami, the mathematics of paper folding.

Huzita-Hatori axioms:

In 1989, Humiaki Huzita formalized the operations possible with a single fold. Later extended by Koshiro Hatori, the complete set of seven axioms defines what can be constructed by folding.

Remarkably: origami is more powerful than compass-and-straightedge construction. With origami, you can:

  • Trisect an angle (impossible with compass and straightedge)
  • Double a cube (impossible with compass and straightedge)
  • Solve certain cubic equations

The fold is a more powerful geometric operation than the compass arc or the straight line.

Flat-foldability:

When does a crease pattern fold flat?

Two necessary and sufficient conditions for a single vertex:

  1. Kawasaki’s theorem: At any interior vertex, the alternating sum of angles equals zero: \(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2 + \alpha_3 - \alpha_4 + \cdots = 0\)

  2. Maekawa’s theorem: At any interior vertex, the number of mountain folds and valley folds differ by exactly two: \(|M - V| = 2\)

These are local conditions: they apply vertex by vertex. Global flat-foldability (whether the entire model folds flat without self-intersection) is a harder problem. It has been proven NP-hard in general.

VII. The Miura Fold

In 1970, Japanese astrophysicist Kōryō Miura developed a folding pattern for deploying large structures in space.

The Miura fold (ミウラ折り) is a method of folding a flat surface into a smaller area using a tessellation of parallelograms.

Its key property: it has one degree of freedom. The entire surface can be opened or closed with a single motion: pulled at opposite corners, the whole sheet expands. Released, it collapses.

No sequential unfolding required. No risk of a panel failing to deploy.

The Miura fold was used in the solar panels of Japan’s Space Flyer Unit (1995). It appears in maps designed to be opened and closed with one hand. It has been proposed for airbags, medical stents, architectural facades.

The fold obeys a beautiful mechanical property:

In the Miura fold, each parallelogram unit is a rigid panel. The folding motion is distributed entirely in the creases. This means the fold can be made from rigid materials, metal, carbon fiber, not just paper.

Origami geometry becoming aerospace engineering.

VIII. Rigid Origami and Deployable Structures

The Miura fold is one instance of a broader field: rigid origami, folding patterns where the faces between creases undergo no bending, and all deformation is concentrated in the crease lines.

This has profound engineering applications.

Heart stents: A flat mesh folded into a small cylinder for insertion, then deployed to hold open a coronary artery. The geometry of the fold must be precisely engineered to achieve the required expansion ratio without tearing.

Space telescopes: The James Webb Space Telescope’s primary mirror, 6.5 meters in diameter, was folded to fit inside the Ariane 5 rocket fairing and deployed in space. The folding sequence was engineered over years.

Soft robotics: Origami-inspired structures that can change shape in response to pneumatic pressure, used in grippers, locomotion systems, and medical devices.

Architecture: Building facades that adjust to light and temperature using origami-inspired kinetic panels.

The mathematics of paper folding, developed in the context of an ancient craft, is now a branch of mechanical engineering.

IX. Modular Origami: The Form I Love

Standard origami produces a single form from a single sheet. Modular origami builds a structure from multiple identical units, modules, that interlock without adhesive.

People ask me which modular form I like best. I don’t have an answer. I love all of it, without exception, the plain Sonobe unit and the crystalline impossibilities alike.

The history of modular origami is relatively recent.

The earliest known modular form is the Sonobe unit, developed by Mitsunobu Sonobe in the late 1960s. A single Sonobe unit is a simple parallelogram-based form. But 12 units assemble into a small stellated dodecahedron. 30 units into an icosahedron. 270 units into a large stellated truncated icosahedron.

The three-dimensional modulars that followed, developed by Tomoko Fuse, Robert Neale, and later the extraordinary Ekaterina Lukasheva, pushed the form into territory that feels less like craft and more like crystallography.

Why modular origami is mathematically deep:

Each unit must satisfy local constraints: the tabs must fit the pockets precisely, the angles must be consistent, the tension must be distributed evenly.

For large models, this becomes a global constraint satisfaction problem.

Consider a 180-unit buckyball, a truncated icosahedron, the shape of a football or soccer ball. 60 pentagonal faces, 12 hexagonal faces. Every unit must be identically folded. Every join must be identically tensioned. The whole structure is held by friction and geometry alone.

If a single unit is folded incorrectly, if a single angle is off by a few degrees, the error propagates. The structure refuses to close.

There is no hiding in modular origami.

X. The Geometry of Assembly

Modular origami maps onto polyhedral geometry.

The most common forms are based on the Platonic solids, the five convex regular polyhedra known since antiquity:

  • Tetrahedron (4 triangular faces)
  • Cube (6 square faces)
  • Octahedron (8 triangular faces)
  • Dodecahedron (12 pentagonal faces)
  • Icosahedron (20 triangular faces)

And the Archimedean solids, 13 convex polyhedra with regular polygonal faces of two or more types, the same arrangement of faces at every vertex.

The truncated icosahedron, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, is the buckyball, the soccer ball, and one of the most beautiful modular origami targets.

Euler’s formula governs all of these:

\[V - E + F = 2\]

Vertices minus edges plus faces equals two. For any convex polyhedron. Always.

When you assemble a modular origami structure, you are physically instantiating this theorem. Every vertex, every edge, every face: your hands have placed them.

XI. Paper as Thought

I want to end not with mathematics but with phenomenology.

There is a psychologist, Mihály Csíkszentmihályi, who gave a name to the state I fall into when I fold: flow. The conditions are exactly his. The task is hard enough to demand all of you, clear enough that you always know the next move, and somewhere in there both the self and the clock disappear.

When I start a modular piece, my hands do not stop until the whole structure is sitting in them. I can fold for five or six hours without looking up. Fifteen minutes has never once happened to me. I forget to eat. I forget to sleep. The only thing that pulls me out is someone saying my name. (The same thing happens over a jigsaw puzzle, the other place my time goes missing.)

There is a small irony in this, at least for me. I am someone who notices time, who feels every minute of it passing. Folding is the one place it stops.

The mind quiets. Not because the task is mindless, it is not, precision is required constantly. But because the precision is physical, not verbal. You are not thinking in words. You are thinking in angles.

The paper has its own logic. It tells you, through resistance and compliance, when a fold is right and when it is wrong. You learn to listen to it.

A large model, 90 units, 180 units, 270 units, takes hours, sometimes days. Each unit is folded identically. The repetition is not tedious. It is meditative. Your hands learn the form so well that by the hundredth unit you are no longer thinking about it.

And then the assembly. The units that were separate become a whole. The structure that existed only as a diagram, or as an image in your mind, becomes physical, becomes holdable, becomes real.

This is not a metaphor for anything. It is itself.

A thing made of paper and time and attention, held together by geometry and friction, that did not exist before you made it.

That is enough.

If you want to start:

Learn the Sonobe unit first, 12 units, one afternoon.

Then Tomoko Fuse’s Unit Origami (1990) for intermediate modular forms.

For the mathematics: Robert Lang’s Origami Design Secrets (2003) is the most complete treatment available. Lang trained as a physicist, a Caltech PhD who worked on lasers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory before leaving to fold paper full time. A fellow physicist gone to paper. I take it as a good omen.

For inspiration: search Ekaterina Lukasheva’s work. Prepare to lose several days.

And a few places to watch:

Jo Nakashima, for clear, beginner-friendly modular tutorials.

Robert Lang, the master himself: one, two, three.

PrwOrigami, the channel I keep coming back to.

Prepare to lose several days.

item.title: The Country That Ate Its Own Geniuses: America and the Intellectuals It Could Not Love
item.description:
Edgar Allan Poe died on October 7, 1849, in Baltimore.

He was forty years old.

The circumstances of his death remain officially unexplained. The medical records were lost, the death certificate lists “phrenitis,” which may mean brain fever, may mean alcohol-related causes, may mean something else entirely.

What is known: he was found, four days before his death, delirious and incoherent, wearing clothes that were not his own, outside a tavern that was being used as a polling place.

He died in a hospital. He was buried in a church cemetery. The funeral was attended by approximately eight people.

In France, at approximately the same time, Charles Baudelaire was translating Poe, obsessively, reverently, with the conviction that he had found the most important American writer and that America had no idea.

Baudelaire was right.

Poe’s reputation in France exceeded his reputation in America for most of the nineteenth century.

The Symbolists, Mallarmé, Verlaine, Rimbaud, read Poe as a founding figure, a philosopher of aesthetic intensity whose work pointed toward everything European modernism would become.

In America: Poe was considered a minor talent, a writer of entertaining gothic stories, a cautionary tale about alcohol and instability.

The country that produced him did not know what it had.

This is not an isolated incident. It is a pattern.

I. The Pattern

Herman Melville published Moby-Dick in 1851.

The American reception: mixed to negative. Too long. Too philosophical. Too much digression. Too strange.

Sales were poor. Melville’s reputation collapsed.

He spent the last decades of his life working as a customs inspector in New York. He wrote poetry that almost no one read. He died in 1891. The obituaries were brief and inaccurate.

One described him as the author of “Typee” and other stories, as if Moby-Dick did not exist.

It was essentially not read for thirty years after his death.

The Melville revival began in the 1920s, driven in part by British critics who recognized what American culture had missed.

Moby-Dick is now considered the great American novel. Melville died thinking he had failed.

Emily Dickinson wrote 1,800 poems.

She published fewer than a dozen in her lifetime, and those, she published anonymously, or had published without her consent, in forms she did not recognize because editors had regularized her dashes, her capitalization, her refusal of conventional meter.

She withdrew from public life and wrote in private, not from shyness, exactly, but from the recognition that what she was doing had no audience available to it.

She was right. Her poems were too strange, too compressed, too formally radical for the American literary culture of her time.

She died in 1886. Her complete poems were published in 1955. The full scholarly edition appeared in 1998.

She is now considered one of the greatest poets in the English language. She died not knowing this.

Charles Ives, the composer who invented techniques that the European avant-garde would not reach for thirty years, worked as an insurance executive.

He composed at night and on weekends. He could not get his music performed. He could not find an audience.

He published his Concord Sonata in 1920 at his own expense, and mailed it, free of charge, to anyone who might be interested.

He received almost no response.

He stopped composing in the 1920s, partially due to health, partially due to the silence that met his work.

He was awarded the Pulitzer Prize in 1947, for a symphony he had written in 1904.

He was seventy-three years old.

The pattern:

American genius arrives. American culture does not recognize it. European culture does, sometimes decades later. American culture eventually adopts what Europe validated.

The genius may or may not live to see it. Often they do not.

II. What Europe Heard That America Missed

Why did Baudelaire hear Poe when America did not?

Why did the British hear Melville when America had forgotten him?

The answer requires understanding what each was doing, and what each required from its audience.

Poe:

Poe was not primarily a writer of horror stories. He was a philosopher of aesthetic experience, of the precise conditions under which art produces its effects, of the mathematics of beauty, of the relationship between form and feeling.

His essay “The Philosophy of Composition” (1846), in which he claims to have composed “The Raven” by working backward from its desired effect, is a theory of artistic production that influenced French Symbolism, Modernism, and, through Valéry, the entire tradition of self-conscious aesthetic theory.

What Poe required from his audience: the willingness to take aesthetic theory seriously, to believe that the how of art was as important as the what, that the form was the content, that the effect was the meaning.

French culture, trained on Descartes and Voltaire, on the tradition of philosophical aesthetics from Boileau to Diderot, was prepared for this.

American culture, trained on Puritan plain style, on the suspicion of ornament, on the pragmatist preference for use, was not.

Poe was asking questions American culture had decided not to ask.

Melville:

Moby-Dick is not a novel in the conventional sense. It is a meditation on obsession, fate, cosmology, the limits of knowledge, the nature of evil, wrapped in the technical language of the 19th-century whaling industry.

It requires its reader to follow Melville into extended digressions on cetology, on the color white, on the metaphysics of the whale, digressions that serve no narrative purpose and every philosophical purpose.

It is a book that trusts its reader to be interested in ideas for their own sake, to follow a thought wherever it goes, even when it goes away from the story.

American literary culture in 1851 was shaped by the domestic novel, the adventure story, the moral tale. It wanted narrative. It wanted progress. It wanted the book to be about what it was about, not to use its subject as a vehicle for cosmological meditation.

Melville was writing a different kind of book, the kind of book that European culture had a category for (the philosophical novel, the essay-novel of ideas) and American culture did not.

Dickinson:

Dickinson’s poems are compressed to the point of requiring active reconstruction by the reader.

The dashes are not decorative. They are structural: they create pauses, ambiguities, unresolved tensions that the poem refuses to resolve.

The slant rhymes aren’t failed craft either. They are a theory of imperfect correspondence: the world does not rhyme cleanly, and the poem should not either.

The capitalization creates hierarchies of meaning that conventional typography flattens.

She was developing a formal system as radical, in its way, as Schoenberg’s twelve-tone technique, a complete rethinking of what the poem is and what it can do.

American literary culture of the 1860s wanted poems that worked, that rhymed, that scanned, that said their thing clearly and moved on.

Dickinson refused all of this.

She was punished with silence.

III. The Flaneur and the Frontier

Walter Benjamin’s flaneur, developed in the Arcades Project, is the figure who makes the modern city legible.

The flaneur walks without destination. They observe without purpose. They read the city the way others read books, finding in the crowds, the storefronts, the architecture, the faces, the text of modern life.

The flaneur produces nothing except attention, a quality of attention that is both pleasurable in itself and, eventually, the source of the deepest cultural knowledge.

Baudelaire was a flaneur. Benjamin was a flaneur. The Parisian café culture was built for the flaneur.

The American frontier:

America had, for most of its history, a frontier.

Not just a geographical frontier, a cultural one. The sense that there was always more land, more opportunity, more future to be seized.

The frontier mentality: movement is progress. Stopping is failure. The person who stays is the person who could not make it.

The flaneur stops. The flaneur is the person who finds more in standing still than in moving forward.

This is the anti-frontier.

The flaneur is the figure that frontier culture cannot accommodate, because the flaneur’s intelligence is the intelligence of the stationary, the patient, the receptive.

The frontier demands the active, the mobile, the productive.

Poe could not move west. His genius required a city, and not the American city of enterprise but the European city of accumulation, of layered time, of the past pressing on the present.

He was, in the wrong country, the right sensibility.

IV. The Specific American Failure Mode

Every civilization fails its geniuses in specific ways.

The Chinese examination system sometimes selected for conformity over originality. The European court system made artists dependent on aristocratic patronage with all the compromises that implied.

America’s failure mode is specific:

It cannot distinguish between the genius who is ahead of the market and the failure who is simply bad.

In a market culture, and America is the purest market culture in history, the test of value is market response.

Does it sell? Does it find an audience? Does it get reviewed well? Does it win prizes?

These are legitimate tests. They are not sufficient tests.

The work that is genuinely new, that requires its audience to develop new capacities, new frameworks, new ways of reading, will fail these tests in the short run.

Not because it is bad. Because the audience for it does not yet exist.

Poe’s audience, the audience that could read him, was European aesthetes who had been trained on a tradition he was completing and transforming.

Melville’s audience, the audience for the philosophical novel, did not exist in 1851 America. It existed in Europe.

Dickinson’s audience, the audience for formally radical poetry, did not exist until the twentieth century.

A market culture has no mechanism for distinguishing the genius ahead of the market from the failure.

Both produce work that doesn’t sell.

The market treats them identically.

V. The Violence of Reception

There is something more troubling than mere neglect.

American culture does not merely ignore its uncomfortable geniuses. It attacks them.

Poe:

Rufus Wilmot Griswold, a minor critic and editor, published a vicious obituary of Poe two days after his death, under the pseudonym “Ludwig.”

It portrayed Poe as a drunkard, a drug addict, a moral reprobate, a man whose life was a cautionary tale about the dangers of artistic excess.

Much of what Griswold wrote was false. Much became the standard account.

For decades, Poe’s reputation in America was shaped by his enemy’s obituary.

The attack was specific: Poe’s failure was not artistic but moral. He failed not because America failed him, but because he failed America, by not being industrious, sober, productive, by not being the kind of artist America approved of.

The genius was blamed for the neglect.

Melville:

The attacks on Moby-Dick were not primarily aesthetic. They were moral.

The book was called godless, irreverent, dangerous. Ahab’s obsession was not a tragedy, it was a warning against pride, against the refusal to accept limits.

The book’s cosmological ambition, its refusal to resolve into comfortable American optimism, was experienced as a threat.

The pattern:

When American culture attacks its difficult geniuses, it does so morally.

Not: this work is aesthetically inadequate. But: this person is morally deficient.

The attack converts artistic judgment into character assassination, and places the responsibility for failure on the artist rather than the culture.

This is the most efficient way to avoid the uncomfortable question: what did we miss?

VI. What Europe Did With American Genius

The European reception of American genius is one of the most instructive episodes in cultural history.

Jazz:

Jazz was created by Black Americans, in New Orleans, Chicago, New York, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

In America: popular entertainment, later seen as low culture, associated with Black life in a segregated society that could not take Black art seriously on its own terms.

In Europe, particularly France: recognized immediately as a new art form, as the most significant American contribution to world music, as a formal innovation comparable to European classical modernism.

Duke Ellington was treated in Paris with a respect he never received at home.

American jazz found its intellectual audience, its flaneur audience, in European cafés and concert halls before it found it in America.

Abstract Expressionism:

Pollock, de Kooning, Rothko, Kline, the New York School of painting, produced work that American culture initially found incomprehensible.

What is this? A child could do it. Where is the skill? What does it mean?

In Europe: recognized as the most important development in painting since Cubism. Greenberg and Rosenberg, the American critics who theorized it, were arguing to an American audience that did not want to listen.

The work eventually won American acceptance, but partly because European acceptance gave it the cultural authority American culture needed before it could take it seriously.

VII. The Poe-Baudelaire Relationship, In Detail

The Poe-Baudelaire relationship deserves extended attention, because it is the purest example of the transatlantic genius exchange.

Baudelaire discovered Poe in 1847. He was twenty-six years old. He wrote to a friend:

“Do you know why I so patiently translated Poe? Because he resembled me.”

Baudelaire spent seventeen years translating Poe’s complete works into French. Five volumes. An obsessive, total project.

What did Baudelaire find in Poe?

The theory of the poem as effect:

Poe argued, in “The Poetic Principle,” that a long poem is a contradiction in terms. The poem must sustain intensity throughout. Length works against intensity. The poem is defined by its effect, the single emotional or aesthetic impression it creates.

This became the foundation of Symbolist poetics, the poem as pure effect, as the distillation of a sensation, as the thing that cannot be said except in the specific way the poem says it.

Mallarmé, Verlaine, Rimbaud, all are working in the space Poe opened.

The artist as theorist:

Poe did not only write poems and stories. He theorized them. He explained, in “The Philosophy of Composition,” how he produced effects, what choices he made and why, what the mathematics of aesthetic impact were.

This was new. The artist as self-aware craftsman, as technician of the soul, this figure, which became central to European modernism, came from Poe.

Baudelaire brought it to France. France brought it to Europe. Europe brought it, eventually, back to America, where it was adopted as a European import rather than recognized as its own.

VIII. The Structural Analysis

Why does this pattern repeat?

Not because individual Americans are less intelligent. Not because American culture is simply philistine.

The reasons are structural.

The market test applied too early:

Genius that is ahead of its time fails the market test in the short run. A culture that applies the market test as the primary measure of value will systematically undervalue what is ahead of its time.

The moralization of aesthetic judgment:

American culture converts aesthetic difficulty into moral failure. The work that is hard to understand is not ahead of its time. It is pretentious. The artist who cannot find an audience is not misunderstood. They are self-indulgent.

This conversion makes it impossible to ask the right question: what does the failure of reception say about us, not about the work?

The absence of a critical infrastructure:

European public intellectuals provide the interpretive infrastructure that allows difficult work to find its audience.

The critic who explains why Poe matters, who provides the framework, the context, the vocabulary that makes the work accessible, performs an essential function.

American literary culture has critics. But the critic who operates in the public intellectual tradition, who writes for a general audience, who shapes public taste, who has the cultural authority to say this matters, pay attention, this figure is rare.

Without this infrastructure, difficult work arrives without introduction. It either conquers immediately, which difficult work almost never does, or it is ignored.

The speed of American cultural life:

The flaneur’s intelligence requires time, time to accumulate impressions, to make unexpected connections, to find the significance in what did not seem significant.

American cultural life moves too fast for this kind of intelligence.

The work that rewards slow reading is disadvantaged in a culture that reads fast.

Dickinson rewards slow reading, each poem requiring minutes of reconstruction.

The culture that produced her wanted to read a poem in thirty seconds and move on.

IX. What Remains

I want to say something about what this pattern means for understanding America, not to condemn it but to understand it.

America built something unprecedented: a civilization on a continental scale, organized around individual freedom and markets, that achieved material abundance beyond anything in human history.

This required specific values: practicality, mobility, optimism, the willingness to move on, the preference for the new over the old, the future over the past.

These values produced wonders.

They also produced a specific relationship with genius, with the kind of intelligence that does not move on, that returns obsessively to the same problems, that sacrifices practical success for aesthetic or intellectual purity.

Poe was this kind of intelligence. Melville was. Dickinson was. Ives was.

They were not failures. They were the wrong shape for the container America had built.

The container was not built wrong. It was built for different purposes.

But a civilization that cannot accommodate its own difficult geniuses, that must export them to be understood and import them back, validated, before it can take them seriously, is missing something.

Not everything. Something specific.

The capacity for the purposeless, for the thought that has nowhere to go except deeper into itself, for the work that serves no function except to be completely itself, this capacity is what the flaneur has and the frontier cannot afford.

America could not afford Poe. France could.

This says something about France. It says something about America.

Both things are true.

Coda

In 1875, for the dedication of Poe’s monument in Baltimore, Stéphane Mallarmé wrote Le Tombeau d’Edgar Poe.

“Tel qu’en lui-même enfin l’éternité le change…”

“Such as into Himself at last Eternity changes him…”

The poem argued that Poe’s true self, the self that America could not see, became visible only in death. That eternity had done what America could not: recognized what was there.

In French, tombeau means two things at once. A tomb. And an elegy, a poem written to honor the dead. Mallarmé meant both.

And here is the part that stays with me.

The stone America raised over Poe’s grave carries only his name and his dates. No line of verse. No epitaph. Nothing.

The tomb made of words came from France. The tomb made of bare stone came from home.

America gave Poe a grave. France gave him a tombeau.

This is the full irony, and it is sharper than the stone.

Further reading:

Baudelaire, “Edgar Poe: His Life and Works” (1852), the essential European reception.

Benjamin, “On Some Motifs in Baudelaire” (1939), in Illuminations, on the flaneur and modernity.

Matthiessen, American Renaissance (1941), on Emerson, Thoreau, Hawthorne, Melville, Whitman; the recovery of American genius.

Lawrence, Studies in Classic American Literature (1923), D.H. Lawrence’s savage, brilliant reading of American writers.

Fiedler, Love and Death in the American Novel (1960), the dark underside of American literary culture.

Wilson, Axel’s Castle (1931), on Symbolism and its American reception.

For Poe specifically:

Quinn, Edgar Allan Poe: A Critical Biography (1941)

Meyers, Edgar Allan Poe: His Life and Legacy (1992)

For Dickinson:

Habegger, My Wars Are Laid Away in Books (2001), the definitive biography.

For Melville:

Parker, Herman Melville: A Biography (2 vols., 1996, 2002)

EN:

Hello, my dear readers, I’ve received many kind and thoughtful messages from you lately. I answered most of them privately, but a few questions felt like they belonged here too. Much love! TR:

Merhaba sevgili okurlarım, Son zamanlarda sizden çok güzel ve düşünceli mesajlar aldım. Çoğuna özel olarak dönüş yaptım, ama bazı soruların burada da yer bulması gerektiğini düşündüm. Çok sevgiler. :)

This reader sent a long email; I’ll try to relay the question as closely as I can to the way they asked it.

1) Q: In Quantum Chromodynamics you write that your mass is “the energy of permanently confined color fields.” That’s almost a spiritual claim dressed as physics. Does knowing that 99% of your body’s mass is field energy actually change how it feels to be in a body, or is it just a beautiful fact?

A: No, and I’d resist the word spiritual. The body stays stubbornly itself; physics doesn’t change how it feels, only the story I tell about the feeling.

2) Q: You close Quantum Chromodynamics with “we have been asking for fifty years.” If you had to bet: will confinement be proven analytically in your lifetime, or do we just keep computing it forever?

A: I don’t know, and I won’t pretend to. You can’t schedule an idea that doesn’t exist yet. I don’t bet on theorems; I shouldn’t! We’d rather keep computing and let it surprise us.

3) Q: In Kant you call him “a troll” for demolishing the proofs of God and the soul and then postulating them anyway for morality. Is that intellectual dishonesty, or the most honest thing he did?

A: Both, and that isn’t a dodge. The trolling is real but it isn’t cheap: he demolished the proofs, refused to pretend reason could recover them, and moved the question into practical reason, out loud. Am I at peace with it? No. But it may be the most honest version of a move that had no honest version.

4) Q: You say his prejudices should make us “deeply suspicious of philosophers who claim their personal limitations don’t affect their universal theories.” Do you turn that same suspicion on yourself when you write?

A: I try to, and I don’t fully trust that I succeed. It is easy to aim that suspicion outward and much harder to catch it in yourself, because your own blind spots are exactly the ones you cannot see. So the honest answer is that I hold the rule over my own writing and assume I am still failing it somewhere I haven’t noticed yet. The most I can do is keep the suspicion switched on and let other people show me where it should have fired.

5) Q: Kant never traveled ten miles and changed everything; you’ve been to Tokyo twelve times and counting. Do you ever secretly envy the man who didn’t need the world to think?

A: No. I don’t envy him for a second. The world is mine, and I’m going to keep wandering it and discovering new places. I’ll even travel on Kant’s behalf.

6) Q: You say folding is the one place time stops for you, you who notices every minute. But you said the same about Go in In Defense of Boredom. Is it the structure you love, or the disappearing?

A: Structure.

P.S. I gave her the long answer in the email.

7) Q: You folded a crane for everyone you love and left them with Sadako in Hiroshima. Will you write on Hiroshima?

A: No. Even if I wanted to, it would be too overwhelming for me to write. It is so hard to put into words. Hiroshima was too graphic for me. It stayed with me for a very long time. For a long while I felt disgust, not so much at science as at knowing, and at the physicists who made it. I hope there is a God. There is no limit to what a human being can do, and no limit to what they cannot.

8) Q: You wrote a whole essay on how America makes its thinkers invisible (/blog/2025/american-anti-intellectualism/) and then you moved there to become one. Has it started working on you yet? Do you catch yourself reaching for the useful answer over the interesting one?

A: Honestly? It’s working a little. I catch myself measuring ideas by whether they’ll go anywhere, and that question would have embarrassed me five years ago. But noticing it is still half the fight. The blog is where I go to not do that. (Ask me again in five years, ahahha!)

9) Q: You celebrate the flaneur and “purposeless presence,” yet you’ve confessed you can’t sit idle for twenty seconds and that boş durma is a curse. Aren’t you more American than you’d like to admit?

A: Ah, Filizko can be neither American nor flaneur. I’m always in the metaxy!

10) Q: In My Biggest Red Flag you admit the intolerance can be “loneliness dressed up as standards,” a way to keep people from getting close enough to notice the depth you demand isn’t always in you. Honestly: how often is that the real reason?

A: So hard to answer, and the difficulty is the tell. Sometimes the standard is real and sometimes it’s a wall with a standard painted on it, and I can’t always see which from the inside. The people who get close anyway are the ones who show me the difference.

11) Q: Your whole blog demands depth from its reader. Is the blog itself a filter, a way of only meeting people who pass the test before they ever reach you?

A: Ah, not at all. I can meet you at whatever depth you want. But getting here was painful. My whole life went by like a teenager’s. Filtre miltre yok, bam bam bam! :)

12) Q: You define depth as “the willingness to be changed by what you encounter.” What is the last thing, a book, a person, an idea, that actually changed you instead of confirming you?

A: While thinking about this, I thought: isn’t being able to have an encounter like that something to be grateful for in itself? Not all of us are lucky enough to run into one. I’ll add it once I find it. I need to think a little. It’s very late now.

Edit 2025/03/19: Found it! Ink, of all things. I switched to an iron-gall ink that keeps changing color for days after it dries, darkening as it oxidizes. Watching a finished page keep changing without me did something quiet to my idea of “finished.” I now distrust the word. Cheers! :)

This question came in Turkish, and the reader is asking me to marry him. I may be the first woman to receive a proposal through a blog.

13) Q: Evlen benimle!

A: Çok şekersiniz. Neyimden böyle hoşlandınız bilemedim ama tahmin ettiğiniz kişi olmayabilirim. Sevgiler. :)

This question came in Turkish.

14) Q: Bu kadar okumak ve derin düşünmek özel hayatınızda sorun çıkartmıyor mu?

A: Çok güzel bir soru bu. Çok teşekkür ederim.

İstediğim kadar kitap okuyamıyorum, çoğu okumam gençlikten. Yani çok okuyan birisi miyim emin değilim. Derin düşünüyor muyum onu da bilmiyorum. Etrafımda sevdiğim ve çok değer verdiğim insanlar var ve bu kişiler tarafından da çok sevdildiğimi ve değerli görüldüğümü biliyorum, sağ olsunlar. Yani olduğum halimle kabul ediliyorum, kimseden de kendimin aynısını asla beklemiyorum. Küçük circle, belki de beni koruyan şey. Sorunuzu cevaplayabildim mi bilemiyorum. Çok sevgiler.

item.title: My Biggest Red Flag: On Being Intolerant of Superficiality, a Confession and a Defense
item.description:
I have a problem.

When a conversation stays on the surface, when it skims and performs and borrows the vocabulary of depth without any of the substance, something in me closes. It isn’t rude, and it usually isn’t even visible. But something withdraws. I get polite where I should be present, courteous where I should be curious, and I keep going through the motions of engagement long after the essential part of me has left the room.

I am intolerant of superficiality.

I have been told this is a flaw, that it makes me difficult, that I expect too much, that not everyone thinks the way I do and I should learn to meet people where they are. All of that is true, and I have tried.

What I want to do here is make a different argument, not against that criticism but alongside it: that the intolerance is also, in its way, right. That it can be a form of respect, and that the refusal to pretend is its own kind of honesty. And that living in the space between the demand for depth and a world that mostly does not supply it is not a pathology. It is a condition.

I. What Superficiality Is, Precisely

I should be careful, because the accusation of superficiality is very often superficial itself, a way of dismissing people for being different, or less educated, or less verbal, or simply interested in other things. That is not what I mean at all.

Think of a farmer who knows the land with a knowledge that has no words, who reads weather and soil and season through decades of it living in his hands. Or a carpenter who understands wood the way a philosopher understands an argument, feeling the grain, anticipating the split, knowing exactly what the material will and will not allow. Or a grandmother who has lived through enough loss to know, without ever once theorizing it, what matters and what does not. None of these people is superficial, and not one of them needs a single abstract word to prove it.

So superficiality is not a lack of vocabulary, or credentials, or cultural consumption. It is the refusal of depth: the active choice to stay on the surface, to be satisfied with appearances, to perform engagement while carefully avoiding any actual encounter.

It can wear the most sophisticated clothes. The reader who has gone through all the right books and used all the right words and never once let any of it disturb a single assumption. The person who treats philosophy as a social credential instead of a live question. The one with confident opinions about everything who has risked nothing on any of them. That is what I mean by superficiality. It is the armor, not the absence of it: the performance of knowing that defends against the vulnerability of not knowing.

II. The Philosophical Pedigree

This intolerance has a long pedigree, and it starts, of course, with Socrates.

His whole method, the elenchus, the cross-examination, the endless questioning, was an intolerance for superficiality turned into a technique. He would not take the first answer, or the comfortable one, and he would not let a conversation settle where it wanted to settle. He pushed, relentlessly, until the person across from him had to admit: I do not actually know what I claimed to know.

It made him deeply unpopular. The people he questioned felt he was making them look stupid, that he was being aggressive, that he was breaking the ordinary rules of polite Athenian conversation. Eventually they executed him for it.

But his intolerance was never contempt for people. It was closer to the opposite. He thought the unexamined life was not worth living, and he meant it less as a judgment of others than as a claim about what a life is for. To live without examination, in his view, was to miss the thing itself, not so much to fail at life as to not quite be living it. His refusal to let people rest in their comfortable unexamination was a kind of love, an unwillingness to leave them asleep.

III. Pascal’s Diversion, Again

We have met Pascal before. His famous observation was that human beings cannot bear to sit quietly alone in a room, and so they reach for diversion, divertissement, anything that lets them escape the confrontation with themselves.

Superficiality is diversion turned into a social institution. The small talk, the performance, the careful steering away from anything that might demand a genuine response, all of it does exactly what Pascal’s hunting and gaming did. It keeps the self from meeting itself, fills the silence before the silence can say anything, and keeps us busy enough that we never quite have to be present.

The person who cannot tolerate superficiality is the one who notices the diversion happening and cannot unsee it. This is uncomfortable for everyone in the room. The one performing the diversion feels seen, and not in a flattering way, while the intolerant one cannot relax into the pretense that would make the whole thing easy. Both end up a little uneasy. Pascal would say the uneasy one is simply closer to the truth, awake to something the comfortable one has decided not to feel.

IV. The Social Cost

I should be honest about what this costs.

The first cost is loneliness. The intolerance narrows the field considerably, because plenty of people do not want depth, or do not have the energy for it, or were never trained toward it, or simply do not think it is worth the trouble, and all of those are perfectly legitimate positions. What it leaves you with, though, is the experience of being alone in rooms full of people. Not alone physically, but conversationally, psychologically: present without being encountered, talking without quite speaking, connected to everyone by proximity and separated from them by depth. It is a strange kind of loneliness, more disorienting than ordinary solitude, because it happens in company.

The second cost is being read as arrogant. The intolerance gets perceived as contempt, and I will not pretend it never is. Sometimes it really is contempt: for the performance of depth with no substance under it, for the name-drop that has not been earned, for the confident wrongness that refuses to question itself. But a great deal of the time it is not contempt at all. It is a different quality of attention, a kind of listening that is waiting for something real and goes visibly flat when the real thing does not come. That disappointment looks like judgment, and gets felt as judgment, even though it is not quite the same thing.

The last cost is the most concrete: the missed connections. The people who would have been wonderful given a little more time, who had depth that needed drawing out, who were performing superficiality only because the situation seemed to call for it, and who in other circumstances would have met me exactly where I was. The intolerance can shut that door before it has any chance to open, and that is a genuine failure, not a virtue in disguise.

V. The Defense, Why It Is Also Right

Against all of that, and I do hold all of it honestly, here is the defense.

The first part is that honesty requires it. There is a familiar social performance that means pretending to be interested when you are not, finding something meaningful when you do not, manufacturing engagement out of pure politeness. I understand why people do it, and I know it is often a kindness. But underneath, it is also a small and socially convenient lie. The intolerance for superficiality is, at its best, simply a refusal of that lie: a refusal to fake an interest I do not have, to pretend a conversation is going somewhere it clearly is not, to let the social script stand in for an actual meeting between two people. There is respect in that. It says: I will not perform for you; I will either be really here or not here at all.

The second part is that it protects something. Every hour spent in a real conversation is an hour not spent performing a shallow one, and this is less a claim about other people than about the plain economics of time and attention. Someone who can sit happily in surface-level talk for hours has those hours to spend. Someone who cannot is guarding something: the capacity for depth, the readiness for a genuine encounter, the attention such an encounter demands. That is not superiority. It is a different way of allocating a finite resource.

The third part is that it is a form of fidelity. Fidelity to the conviction that things actually matter, that ideas have weight, that words are supposed to mean something, that a conversation can change you, and that the person in front of you is usually capable of far more than small talk and deserves to be met at that capacity rather than at the comfortable minimum. Refusing to accept less is, at the very same moment, a refusal to offer less.

VI. The Danger, When Intolerance Becomes Contempt

I also have to name the ways this goes wrong, because it does.

It can curdle into elitism: the belief that depth is available only to a few, that an inability to articulate depth proves its absence, that the vocabulary of profundity is the same thing as profundity. That belief is wrong, and it is itself a kind of superficiality, the superficiality of mistaking the map for the territory, the language for the thought, the performance of depth for depth itself.

It can curdle into impatience, into closing the door before the room has had any chance to show what is in it. Depth is not always immediately on display. People are not always at their best, and anxiety, social pressure, unfamiliar ground, all of these flatten depth in people who genuinely have it. The intolerant person who will not wait simply misses the depth that was there and only needed a little more time.

And it can become loneliness dressed up as standards. “I just cannot tolerate superficiality” makes a very convenient way to avoid asking why connection is hard, why intimacy feels like a threat, why the surface might be preferred not because it is comfortable but because it is safe. This is the hardest one for me to look at directly. Sometimes the intolerance is a way of making sure that no one ever gets close enough to notice that the depth I demand of other people is not always present in me. The person who cannot be met is also the person who cannot be known.

VII. The Between

I called this blog filizinbetween, and between is exactly the right word.

The whole thing lives in a series of gaps. Between the demand for depth and the fact that most social life runs along the surface. Between the loneliness of never quite fitting and those rare, extraordinary moments when someone meets you precisely where you are. Between the failure mode of contempt and the virtue of honest attention, and between the exhaustion of holding the demand up and the impossibility of ever putting it down.

This between is not a problem to be solved. It is a condition to be lived in. Lower the demand in order to resolve it and you lose something; withdraw from people entirely in order to resolve it and you lose something else. The harder path is to keep the demand while holding it loosely enough to still be surprised by depth where you did not expect it, and the harder path here, as almost everywhere, turns out to be the right one.

VIII. What Depth Actually Requires

So what is depth, actually? The question matters, because depth without any content is just another kind of superficiality.

It is not using difficult vocabulary, or having read the right books, or holding the correct opinions, or being able to perform profundity on cue. Depth is the willingness to be changed by what you encounter. The book that rewrites how you think. The argument you can neither answer nor honestly dismiss. The person whose life has made your assumptions about the world suddenly look too small. Depth is the capacity for an encounter, with an idea or a person or the world, that leaves you different from how you came in.

The superficial person encounters everything and is changed by nothing; everything confirms what was already believed, and every conversation ends roughly where it began. The deep person encounters things and is altered by them, sometimes a little and sometimes completely, but always actually.

That is the thing whose absence I cannot tolerate. Not the performance, not the vocabulary, not even intelligence exactly. Only the willingness to be changed, the openness to a real encounter, the refusal to close.

IX. The Gift of the Intolerance

And here is what the intolerance gives back.

When you do find depth, and you do find it, the encounter is extraordinary. A conversation that goes somewhere none of you expected. A person who says something that makes you stop moving. An idea that quietly reorganizes everything around it. The moment when two people are genuinely present to each other, not performing, not managing the interaction, just actually there.

These moments are rare, and the intolerance makes them rarer still, by holding the standard up, refusing the consolation prize, and waiting. But it also makes them far more vivid when they finally come. Someone who is content with the surface does not meet depth the same way, because they were never waiting for it and never turning down the substitute. The person who has sat through performance after performance, who has so often been almost-present but not quite, recognizes the real thing the instant it appears. And it lands with a weight it simply cannot have for someone to whom it was never scarce.

Coda

One last thing: this is a confession, not a prescription. I am not recommending the intolerance, or claiming it is optimal, or suggesting you go and acquire it if you do not already have it.

I am saying that if you do have it, if any of this is recognizable, if you have sat in a room full of people and felt that particular loneliness of being present and still not encountered, then you are not broken. Not arrogant, or at least not only arrogant. Not antisocial, or at least not only that. You are someone for whom depth is not optional, for whom the surface genuinely is not enough, and not as a preference but as something closer to a constitutional fact.

It makes some things harder. It makes the right things more real. The demand is the cost, and the demand is also the gift, and the only honest place to stand is in the between.

item.title: Filizko Went to Beijing for Go Things
item.description:
Filizko went to Beijing for Go things. :)

I won all three of my games!

I’m so happy! So happy! Go has been part of my life for such a long time, but playing in China felt different. In the United States, most people do not even know what Go is. But in China, no explanation was needed. Go was not some strange little hobby I carried around with me. It was understood. It was respected. We were taken seriously there. There was a kind of respect around it that made everything feel bigger, older, and more real.

That meant a lot to me.

I had my teachers, Fan and Thomas, with me. My friends Tanguy, Ben, and Ali were there too, always beside me, making the whole trip warmer than Beijing itself. Every game carried a little bit of everyone who had taught me, helped me, encouraged me, laughed with me, and sat with me through the strange little emotional storms of playing a serious game.

And Beijing was cold!

Very cold.

December in China did not come to play. I could not visit the Great Wall because of the ice and snow, which still breaks my heart a little. But maybe that just means China is asking me to come back. :)

The hardest part was not the freezing Beijing weather. It was sitting in the traditional seiza position (zhengzuo (正坐)) during the Go games!

By the time the game was over, I was not sure whether I had won a match or simply become part of the floor. Let’s just say getting me back up was a team effort. :)

I did get to visit the National Museum of China, and I absolutely loved it. It was magnificent. Truly one of those places where you walk around quietly and feel very small in front of history, in the best possible way. After spending so much time around an ancient game, being surrounded by so much history felt almost too fitting.

The Chinese people I met were incredibly welcoming. I also learned that the Chinese way of showing love is definitely feeding you. Ahahaha. There was always more food, more tea, more “try this,” more “eat more.”. Beijing was freezing, but people kept putting warm things in front of us, so in the end, maybe that was the real weather of the trip.

Huawei was our sponsor, which also made the whole thing feel a little surreal. We stayed in Wangfujing! One moment I was playing Go, the next I was in Beijing, surrounded by people who cared deeply about this ancient game, eating lamb skewers in the freezing cold, and thinking, “Life is so good!” Me being a female also a little shock to most people. A white girl playing Weiqi!

And now, after winning all three of my games, I can finally apply for pro qualification.

That sentence feels unreal too.

Three games. Three wins. One very frozen, very happy Filizko.

I rang in the New Year in a completely different country, and today I’m flying to Tokyo for a learning game. My “little” (ahahha!) gift to myself for winning is Mount Fuji and a short Kawaguchiko getaway. Don’t worry, I’ll enjoy the onsen enough for all of us. :)

So yes, Beijing was cold. I missed the Great Wall. I ate too much lamb. And I came home with something more than three wins. I learned once again that Go is not just a game; it is a language, a culture, a discipline, and sometimes, somehow, a doorway.

And this time, it opened in China.

A: Teşekkür ederim. Yuvarlanıyoruz diyelim. :)

A: I have a blog post about this on Medium. I had been writing there since 2019. I just checked it so I could share it, but it is in Turkish. :)

Maybe I can write a post about it here too!

8) Q: What fountain pen brand would you recommend for a beginner?

A: Thank you for this question.

My first fountain pen was a Pelikan, and I still have many Pelikan pens in my collection. They write beautifully, but I usually find them a little too light. I think I prefer heavier pens, though not Waterman-heavy. :) For a beginner, I would highly recommend the LAMY AL-star. It has a very nice weight in the hand, and I love its simple Bauhaus-inspired design. The body is made of anodized aluminum, so it feels a little more substantial than the plastic LAMY Safari, while still being light enough for everyday writing. It is also very beginner-friendly. You can use LAMY T10 cartridges, which is the easiest option, or you can buy a LAMY Z28 converter and fill it with bottled ink. If you want to make the experience more personal and beautiful, I would suggest trying a Pilot Iroshizuku ink in a color you love. That is one of the pleasures of fountain pens: the pen is only half of the experience; the ink is the other half. Another nice thing about the AL-star is that it has a transparent ergonomic grip, an ink window so you can see when you are running low, and interchangeable steel nibs. You can start with a Fine or Medium nib, and later try Extra Fine, Broad, or even calligraphy nibs without buying a whole new pen.

Just don’t forget to clean your pen with lukewarm water from time to time, especially when changing ink colors. Fountain pens are not difficult to use, but they do like a little care. :)

8) Q: Hayatınızda en çok hangi konuda “aşırı seçici”siniz?

A: Ay ben çok seçici birisiyim o kadar çok şey var ki :)

Sanırım hayatıma kimi aldığıma. Arkadaş, partner, akraba fark etmez; yakınlık benim için kan bağıyla ya da tesadüfle değil, güvenle, incelikle ve sahicilikle kurulur.
