item.title: Chingiz Aitmatov — The Writer Who Carried a Whole World on His Back
item.description:
There is a writer most Western readers have never heard of.

He was born in 1928 in a small village in Kyrgyzstan, so remote that the nearest railway station was a day’s journey away. He wrote in both Kyrgyz and Russian. He was translated into more than 170 languages. He sold hundreds of millions of copies.

In the Soviet Union he was the most widely read living author. Gabriel García Márquez called him one of the greatest writers of the century. Mikhail Gorbachev counted him a personal friend and advisor.

His name was Chingiz Aitmatov.

I should say up front that I can’t write about him from a distance. I was raised by my grandmother, the way the children in his books so often are. His novels are tangled up with the most important person in my life, and with losing her. So this isn’t a neutral recommendation. It’s closer to a confession.

If you haven’t read him, there is a gift waiting for you. Let me try to tell you why.

I. The World He Came From

To read Aitmatov without knowing where he came from is to read him with one eye closed.

Kyrgyzstan, the land between the Tian Shan mountains and the vast steppes of Central Asia, is one of the oldest inhabited places on earth and one of the least known to Western readers.

The Kyrgyz were nomads for millennia, their culture built around movement, horses, the sky, the relationship between the human and the elemental. Their oral tradition, the Epic of Manas, is the longest epic poem in any language, three times the length of the Odyssey and the Iliad combined, and it carried the memory of the people across centuries of conquest.

Then came the Russians. Then the Soviets.

Collectivization destroyed the nomadic way of life. The great Manaschi, the epic singers who had memorized hundreds of thousands of verses, were branded class enemies. The old language, the old stories, the old bond with the land, all of it was being taken apart on purpose.

Aitmatov grew up in the ruins of that dismantling. His father, Törökul Aitmatov, a Communist Party official and intellectual, was arrested in 1937 during Stalin’s purges and shot the following year. Chingiz was nine.

His mother raised four children alone, in a village with almost no men left, all of them taken by the purges or the war. At fourteen, Aitmatov was the village tax collector. At fifteen, secretary of the village council. He carried the weight of adults before he had finished being a child.

This isn’t background. It’s the source of everything he wrote: knowing what it means to lose a father to the state, to watch a culture erased, to carry too much too soon, to love a landscape while it is being destroyed.

II. The White Ship (Белый пароход, 1970)

There is a boy.

He is seven, maybe eight. He lives with his grandfather Momun at a remote forest ranger’s post in the mountains of Kyrgyzstan. His parents are gone, separated, absent, unreachable. He has a school bag, and he treasures it.

He has three friends: a pair of binoculars he uses to watch the distant world, a stone shaped like a fish, and a white ship he can see far away on the Issik lake below. He has invented a game. He will turn into a fish, swim down the river to the lake, find the white ship, and tell his father, who he believes is on that ship, everything that has happened.

I have to stop here, because this is where the book stopped being a book for me and became a mirror.

I was raised by my grandmother, the way this boy is raised by his grandfather. I learned my töreler, my customs, the old right and wrong of things, from her, exactly the way Momun teaches the boy. And I had a game almost identical to his. I grew up in a house on the Aegean. The whole sea opened up from our balcony, and I spent my entire childhood watching the ships go by. I used to tell myself: if I can count more than ten ships before they pass, my wish will come true (I do not remember my wishes!). The boy had his white ship on the Issik lake. I had the Aegean, the sea I fell in love with as a child. It was my white ship.

And the school bag. The boy’s whole heart is in that bag. When I was six I got my first one, green, with the Lion King on it, and I fell so completely in love with it that I wanted school to start immediately just so I could carry it. I have never forgotten that feeling, and Aitmatov had already found it and put it in a book before I was even born.

So, the boy. He lives in two worlds at once. The forest post, with its adult cruelties and small corruptions, and the world of myth: the world of the Horned Mother Deer, who in Kyrgyz legend brought the ancestors of the Kyrgyz back to life after enemies had wiped them out. She is the spirit of the forest, the principle of regeneration, the promise that destruction is not the last word. Momun tells the boy this story, and the boy believes it, not naively, but with a child’s full capacity for mythic truth.

Then Orozkul, the boy’s uncle by marriage, the brutal, drunk, resentful man who runs the post, kills a deer. Not just a deer. The last deer in the forest, against every prohibition the grandfather has ever taught. And Momun, gentle, frightened, compromised, helps him do it.

The boy watches his grandfather butcher the deer. The man who gave him the myth helps destroy it.

There is no rescue. No Horned Mother Deer returning. The boy walks into the river.

“I won’t return,” he said to himself. “It’s better to be a fish, it’s better to be a fish.”

When I first read that, I didn’t read it as despair. I said to the boy, almost out loud: you’re free now. Because life is like that. Some people’s burden is unbearably heavy while they are still children, and this is the novel of a child who answers his disappointment by drowning himself in his own dream.

What it does

Aitmatov said he agonized over that ending. His editors wanted him to change it, to give the boy a rescue, a hope, a Soviet future. Soviet literature was supposed to end in forward motion, in the promise of the new Soviet man. He refused.

The ending isn’t a celebration of death. It’s a statement about what happens when the sources of meaning, the myth, the story, the grandfather’s love, are corrupted from the inside. The boy doesn’t die because the world is cruel. He dies because the person who gave him the myth helped kill it. That is the precise, unbearable betrayal at the center of the book: not the cruelty of enemies, but the weakness of love. Momun loves the boy. Momun is also weak. Both are true at once, and it is their being true at once that breaks everything.

This book has no good guys and bad guys. It has innocence, and just as much pain. It has the world of one small child, which may be more meaningful than all of ours. And the characters are so sincere, so alive, so much like us. Which of us hasn’t flared up like Orozkul? Which of us hasn’t railed against fate like Aunt Bekey? Which of us hasn’t begged forgiveness like Grandfather Momun? And which of us, head to toe in innocence, hasn’t waited for our own white ship?

The one I keep arguing with is Momun. Half the book I wanted to shake him. Raise your voice, old man. Rebel. Break the chains. And the maddening thing is that the one or two times he does raise it, even slightly, both Orozkul and the grandmother flinch and back off. But it never lasts. Isn’t that exactly how it goes? You work yourself to the bone, you stay quiet, you try to make yourself useful to people, and as long as you never raise your voice you get crushed, looked down on, never paid back for what you gave. Sometimes you have to raise it. Sometimes you have to act for what you believe, or you end up like Momun, destroying the thing you love with your own hands.

There is a line in it I underlined: the one who wants to cover his own shame smears it on the faces of others. That is Orozkul exactly.

The book is short, a novella really. You can read it in an afternoon. It will stay with you for decades.

III. The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years (И дольше века длится день, 1980)

This is his masterpiece. It is, and I’ll say it without hedging, one of the great novels of the twentieth century, and one of the least known in the West.

The title comes from a Pasternak poem, Unique Days (Единственные дни). The line is И дольше века длится день, “and the day lasts longer than a century.” The novel’s Russian title is essentially that line: The Day Lasts Longer Than a Century.

It is also my grief book. I started it while my grandmother was still alive and finished it after she was gone. By the time I read the last page, the person who raised me, the person who gave me my töreler the way Momun gave them to that boy, was no longer in the world. I cannot separate this novel from that. For a while I would fall into certain sentences and stay there for hours.

The book takes place over a single day and night: the day Yedigei Zhangel’din, a worker at a small railway junction in the Kazakh steppe, has to bury his lifelong friend Kazangap. But the single day holds a whole century. Yedigei’s journey to the burial ground, across the flat enormous steppe on a camel named Karanar, opens out into memory: his whole life, his friendship with Kazangap, the history of the junction, of the steppe, of the Kazakh people.

Yedigei has lived here for decades. He arrived after the war, stayed, raised children, buried friends, watched the world change while the steppe stayed exactly where it was. He is not a hero in any conventional sense. He is a man of the steppe: patient, sturdy, with a memory that holds everything and a grief that cannot be said quickly.

The junction is called Boranly-Burannyi, the Windy Place, the Place of Blizzards. Trains pass through it east to west and west to east, carrying everyone and everything, connecting and separating in the same motion.

“Trains in these parts went from East to West, and from West to East… On either side of the railway lines lay the great wide spaces of the desert - Sary-Ozeki, the Middle lands of the yellow steppes. In these parts any distance was measured in relation to the railway, as if from the Greenwich meridian… And the trains went from East to West, and from West to East…”

This is the passage I lost myself in. It looks like nothing. It is one of the most resonant openings in modern literature: the steppe as crossroads, the junction as the point where all directions meet and none of them is home. I read it over and over in the weeks I was grieving, the trains going and coming, going and coming, while one particular person stayed gone.

Another line I underlined, and I no longer remember exactly what undid me in that moment, but I marked it hard: terrible things can happen to people too. A person left alone with contradictions he cannot overcome is shaken to the depths, and he can tell no one, because no one can help him. It is like a terrible landslide. You see the danger, and you can do nothing.

The Mankurt

Woven through the novel is the legend of the Mankurt.

In Aitmatov’s retelling of the old Zhuan legend, enemy warriors who took prisoners would sometimes perform a procedure to destroy a captive’s memory, to make him forget his name, his family, his language, his self. They shaved his head, wrapped it in raw camel hide, and left him in the desert sun. As the hide dried it shrank and tightened, causing unbearable pain. Some it killed. Some it drove mad. The ones who survived came out as Mankurts: human bodies with no memory of ever having been human. Perfect slaves. Obedient, tireless, with no will and no history.

They couldn’t be freed, because they didn’t know they were enslaved. They had no self to free.

In the legend, a Mankurt kills his own mother when she comes to rescue him, because he doesn’t recognize her, because the word mother means nothing to him, because being a son requires a self that can stand in relation to a mother, and his is gone.

Aitmatov wrote this in 1980, at the height of a Soviet cultural policy that was systematically erasing minority languages and histories. The Mankurt is not really a metaphor. It’s a description. A people made to forget their language is being Mankurtized. A culture whose epics are filed away as dangerous is being Mankurtized. A child taught that her grandparents’ world was backward and primitive is being Mankurtized.

The mother in the legend, Naiman-Ana, rides out calling her son’s name. He doesn’t know her. He kills her. Her white headscarf, lifting into the air as she falls, becomes a white bird that flies over the steppe forever, calling: remember whose child you are, remember your name.

That image gets into you and never leaves. And I think I understand now why it lodged so deep. Everything I am that is worth keeping, my language, my customs, the small old rules of how to be a person, came from my grandmother. To forget her would be to be Mankurtized. So I don’t. The bird is still calling, and I am still answering.

The science fiction frame

The novel’s second strand is extraordinary, and largely unknown even to people who have read the book, because it was cut from many editions.

While Yedigei crosses the steppe, two cosmonauts, one Soviet and one American, aboard a joint space station, make contact with an alien civilization: Lesnaya Grud, the Forest Breast, a planet of beings of remarkable intelligence and goodwill. The cosmic beings want to make contact with Earth. The Soviet and American governments, terrified of what that contact might reveal or disrupt or give to their own citizens, refuse. They build Parity, a joint barrier around the Earth to keep any contact out. The cosmonauts, unable to obey the order to cut off the civilization that has opened itself to them, are stranded, unable to come home and unable to go on.

The parallel isn’t subtle, and it isn’t meant to be. The steppe and the cosmos, the burial and the barrier, the forgetting of the Mankurt and the refusal of contact, are all the same story. The story of power choosing ignorance over knowledge, isolation over connection, control over the frightening freedom of knowing more than you knew before.

IV. The Scaffold (Плаха, 1986)

In Turkish it’s published as Dişi Kurdun Rüyaları, “The Dreams of the She-Wolf,” and honestly that title is the truer one, because the wolves are the soul of the book, and I notice I left their dreams out the first time I tried to write about it.

By 1986 Aitmatov was writing differently. The Scaffold is his most ambitious and most uneven novel, a book that reaches for everything and doesn’t entirely hold together, but whose best moments are among the greatest things he wrote.

It opens, magnificently, with wolves. Akbara and Tashchainar, a she-wolf and her mate, on the Central Asian steppe. The wolves aren’t symbols. They are wolves, specific and particular, with their own perceptions and fears and desires, and Aitmatov gives us their inner life, and the she-wolf’s dreams, with a directness that is genuinely astonishing.

The wolves are hunting, raising cubs. Then the Soviet narcotics operation arrives to harvest the wild marijuana growing on the steppe. Helicopters, men with guns, chaos. The antelope herd stampedes and is slaughtered. The cubs are killed. Akbara and Tashchainar survive, and lose litter after litter to human activity, not to cruelty exactly, but to indifference. The people don’t hate the wolves. The wolves simply do not exist inside the frame of what matters to the people making the decisions.

That is the moral argument running under the whole book: not that people are evil, but that the circle of what counts has been drawn too small, and a world where wolves and their cubs don’t count is a world where eventually nothing will.

I underlined one question in it that I still don’t have an answer to: why does evil, almost every single time, come out stronger than good?

Alongside the wolves there is a human story: a young man searching for God in the Soviet steppe, a drug addict, a Christ figure, a party official.

The novel isn’t perfectly built. It’s too long, too various, too ambitious. But the wolves are perfect. And the image of Akbara, having lost everything, finally taking a human child, not out of malice but out of a grief with nowhere else to go, will not leave you.

V. The Place That Connects Two Worlds

All of Aitmatov’s novels share a geography, not a literal one but a mythic one.

A vast open landscape, steppe or mountain or lake, in which the human figure is small against enormous forces: time, history, the state, the cosmos. A railway or a river or a white ship in the distance, the possibility of elsewhere. A story inside the story, a myth or a legend or a song, holding the truth the present can’t hold directly. And a moment of loss that is somehow also, in a way that is not consolation but is not the opposite of consolation either, a moment of clarity.

Aitmatov understood something about loss that most writers flinch from: that some losses are not healed, not transformed, not made meaningful. They are simply real.

The white ship does not return. The Mankurt does not remember. Akbara does not stop grieving.

But the telling, the fact that someone sat down and found the exact words for these irreversible things, is its own kind of answer. Not to the loss. To the silence the loss leaves behind. I know that silence. This is the writer who filled it for me.

VI. Language and Double Vision

Aitmatov wrote in two languages, Kyrgyz and Russian, and the bilingualism was not incidental. It gave him a kind of double vision, the ability to live in two cultural worlds at once, to see each through the other, and to find in the gap between them the space where literature happens.

His Kyrgyz gave him the oral tradition, the epic cadences, the particular bond between the human and the natural, the way time moves in a nomadic culture, not in a straight chronological line but in layers, the past still present in the present in a way literate cultures tend to suppress.

His Russian gave him the great tradition of the Russian novel, a literary language honed by Pushkin and Tolstoy and Dostoevsky and Chekhov, two centuries of forms built for thinking about suffering and meaning.

The result is a prose unlike anyone else’s, vast and intimate at the same time, moving between myth and the texture of an ordinary day with a naturalness that feels inevitable afterward and is, in practice, extraordinarily hard to do.

People sometimes reach for “magical realism.” It isn’t quite right. García Márquez’s magic comes from excess, the world overfull with impossible things. Aitmatov’s myth comes from depth: the world exactly as it is, but seen through a longer time, a deeper history, a different relationship to the sacred. The Horned Mother Deer doesn’t break the laws of nature. She is the law of nature, seen from inside a tradition that never split the human off from the natural in the first place.

VII. What He Knew

Aitmatov died in 2008, in Nuremberg, of pneumonia. He was seventy-nine. He had outlived the Soviet Union, served as Kyrgyzstan’s ambassador to several countries, and watched his country become independent and then struggle to work out what independence even meant after centuries of being someone else’s territory.

What his books say to me, over and over, is not that grief will be healed, or that it has a hidden meaning, or that it will pass. It is something quieter and harder and, in the end, more bearable: that the steppe is wide enough to hold it. The landscape, vast and indifferent and enduring, receives what the human can’t contain. The wind takes it. The grass absorbs it. The white bird keeps flying overhead, calling a name that someone, somewhere, still remembers.

And then there is the line I carry around with me, the one that I think actually made me who I am. He wrote, simply:

“Yes, there will be winter, there will be cold, there will be snowstorms. But then there will be spring again.”

I read that as a younger person and never put it down. It is the whole of him in one sentence. The winter is real. He never once pretends it isn’t. And the spring is real too.

VIII. Where to Begin

If you haven’t read Aitmatov, begin with The White Ship. It is the shortest, the purest, the most devastating, and it will tell you almost immediately whether his world is your world. For most people who meet it, the answer is yes, an almost embarrassing, total yes, as if the book had been waiting for them in a language they didn’t know they spoke. It was for me.

Then The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years. Read it slowly. Let Yedigei’s journey take its time. Let the steppe do what the steppe does.

Then The Scaffold, knowing its flaws, reading past them for the wolves and their dreams.

Then Farewell, Gulsary, the story of a man and his horse, which is to say a story about loyalty and about growing old in a world that is growing old in a different direction than you are. And if it takes hold of you the way it took hold of me, go on to Jamila and Mother Earth, and then you will simply have read all of him, which is one of the better things that can happen to a person.

When you’ve read them all, sit for a while with the image of a white bird over the steppe, a headscarf, a mother’s voice, calling a name that must not be forgotten.

Remember whose child you are. Remember your name.

One last thing, and it is the truest one.

I am Turkish, and the Kyrgyz are my kin. Our languages are close enough that we can sit across from one another and understand each other, the way cousins do without even trying. The Horned Mother Deer is not only a Kyrgyz saint. She is holy to all the Turkic peoples, the same sacred mother under different names across the same enormous map. When Aitmatov tells these stories, he is not reporting on a distant culture for outsiders. He is telling mine.

So he is not really, for me, “the most important writer you may never have read.” He is something much closer than that. He is the one who carried our tradition up out of the silence the Mankurts were built for. He is my ata, my ancestor. He is the one who still knows my töre on the days I have half-forgotten it.

My grandmother taught me the traditions. Aitmatov wrote them down so I would never lose them.

Further reading:

Chingiz Aitmatov, The White Ship (trans. Mirra Ginsburg)

Chingiz Aitmatov, The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years (trans. John French)

Chingiz Aitmatov, The Scaffold (trans. Arch Tait)

Chingiz Aitmatov, Farewell, Gulsary (trans. John French)

item.title: Filizko Became an American Citizen!
item.description:
Filizko became an naturalized American citizen, yay!

I still do not know how to write that sentence without smiling a little. :)

I came to the United States in 2015, with a suitcase, a student visa, an accent, and no real idea of what my life would become. I did not know then that this country would become such a large part of my story. I did not know that one day I would build a life here, study here, work here, make friends here, miss home from here, and eventually call this place home too.

Becoming an American citizen felt strange in the most beautiful way.

It was not a sudden transformation. I did not become a different person in that room. I was still from İzmir. I was still Turkish. I was still carrying my first language, my childhood, my grandmother, my memories, and all the places that made me who I am.

But something did change!

After all these years, America was no longer only the country where I studied, lived, and tried to figure things out. It became my country too.

I know that sounds simple, but it meant a lot to me.

It meant that the life I had been slowly building here had become real in a new way. The years of paperwork, uncertainty, waiting, learning, adapting, and starting over had quietly turned into belonging. Not the kind of belonging where you forget where you came from, but the better kind, the kind where you get to carry more than one home inside you.

So yes, I became an American citizen. On Halloween, of all days, which somehow made it even more fun to remember. :)

I am Turkish. I am from İzmir. And now, I am also American.

Some life updates are too big to explain neatly. This is one of them!

But I am grateful.

And I am proud!

P.S. I was so happy, so I forgot to take photos from the celebration with my loved ones. Whole Texas Roadhouse was happy that day! :) I am attaching here the naturalized people’s home countries. It’s indeed a melting pot, huh? And also President Biden’s heartfelt letter. I am not crying, you are crying :))

P.P.S. Anneanneciğimin yazması boynumdaydı. Kendisi zaten hep kalbimde! (On this beautiful and important day, I wore my dear grandma’s scarf around my neck. She was, as always, in my heart.)

item.title: Erotapokriseis I
item.description:
EN:

Hello, my dear readers, After moving from Medium to here, I thought — and worried — that I might lose some of you. But seeing your emails made me so happy, and honestly, a little emotional. I’ve responded to all of them, but I thought I’d answer a few of your questions here as well, continuing our tradition of erotapokriseis! Thank you for always writing to me, reading me carefully, and sometimes asking questions that are much harder than they first appear. It means a lot to me. Cheers!

TR:

Merhaba sevgili okurlarım, Yazılarımı okuduğunuz ve değerli geri bildirimlerinizi paylaştığınız için çok teşekkür ederim. Hepsi benim için çok kıymetli.

1) Q: In your Pushkin essay you say one must learn Russian to read him fully. Have you?

A: I haven’t started learning Russian yet. But it is one of the things I most want to do. I won’t die without learning it!

2) Q: The whole story turns on your grandmother saying “I didn’t expect that from you” and hanging up. That’s brutal. Did it feel like love at the time, or only later? Tokyo

A: Oh no, it may not have come through in the English version. The hazards of thinking in Turkish and writing in limited English. My grandmother was the person who pushed me one step forward all my life. I learned how to push from her. It was said entirely out of love. Growing up, my greatest fear was disappointing her. In that moment I simply knew she was right, and I ran outside. And when she called again three or four hours later, she only asked how the outing had gone. She didn’t even ask whether I was still in the café. She knew that what she had said was an action word for me. :) I always felt deeply loved by her. Even if I had stayed in that café for three days, even if I had committed the most terrible crime in the world, her love for me was unconditional.

This question came in Turkish.

3) Q: Bir gününüzü nasıl geçiriyorsunuz?

A: Teşekkür ederim bu soru için. :) Acaba hangi yazımla ilgili soru gelecek diye merak ederken, e-mailinizde İzmir’den bahsetmeniz, ortak tanışlarımız üzerine yazmanızı okumak beni çok mutlu etti.

Filiz bir gününü nasıl geçirir? Şu an master’ımın son yılındayım, hem okuyup hem de çalışıyorum. Günlerim dolu dolu geçiyor. Kendim için yapmak istediğim çoğu şeyi yapamıyorum aslında. Yaz tatili için İzmir’e gitmiştim ama Amerikan vatandaşlık başvurum için geri çağrıldım, tatilim yarıda kesildi; azıcık keyifsizim. Dallas benim için çok sıcak bir yer. Urla’mı ve deniz kenarını bırakıp geldiğim için azıcık mutsuzum.

Onun dışında Dallas’taki Filiz’in bir günü, sabah kalkıp bazen elini yüzünü bile yıkayamadan okula koşmakla geçiyor. Lisans eğitimim dışında bir alanda master yaptığım için de alan değişimi benim için çok kolay değil. Ama elimden geleni yapıyorum. Hafta sonlarım biraz daha güzel geçiyor diyebilirim. Sevdiğim restoranlara gidiyorum. Sevdiğim insanlarla vakit geçiriyorum. Ama hafta içim felaket. :)

This question came in Turkish.

4) Q: Büyükanneniz neredeyse her yazınızda beliriyor — Tokyo‘da, can sıkıntısı yazısındaki “boş durma”da, Yaşamaya Değer Mi sorusunun ardında. İlk filozofunuz o muydu?

A: Bir gün anneannem üzerine yazacağım. :) Anneannem en iyi arkadaşımdı! Beni hayatta en inspire eden kişi o. Evet, özgür bir düşünür olmayı ondan öğrendim; tüm duygularımı kabul edebilmeyi, sevdiğim şeylerin peşinden koşabilmeyi, duygusal regülasyonu, merhameti, sevmeyi, koşulsuz sevebilmeyi, çok çalışmayı, yaptığım her işe ruhumu koyabilmeyi. Hepsini ondan öğrendim. Sorunuza cevap: hayır, anneannem ilk filozofum değildi. O sadece hayatı tüm gerçekliğiyle kucaklayan bir insandı. İyi ki vardı. :)

5) Q: You wrote “I do not like wasted words, but here I will scatter them freely.” Do you still think the scattering isn’t waste? Beginnings

A: Well, you wrote to me after reading them. So do you think they could be a waste? :) Much love.

6) Q: Boş durma came to you almost as a curse in In Defense of Boredom. Do you really want to be free of it, or would you not be you without it?

A: I don’t like wasting my time, but it’s true that it really has become a curse. Sometimes I struggle with it, I’ll admit. I have almost no tolerance for sitting idle. I feel as if I’m losing something. I think I took the context my grandmother taught me a little too far, and combined with my own character, it truly turned into a curse. I’m trying to cope with it. But I can’t say I get much pleasure out of the idle time I do spend!

item.title: In Defense of Boredom: Why Doing Nothing Is the Most Radical Act Left
item.description:
I can’t sit still.

I mean it literally. I am someone who cannot do nothing for twenty seconds. If there is nothing to do, I will invent something. If the house is already clean, I will clean it again. Empty time makes me itch, and then it makes me angry at myself for being idle, which is a special kind of talent.

I didn’t choose this. I inherited it. Boş durma, don’t sit idle, was practically a household law when I was growing up, and I absorbed it so completely that now, decades later, an unused hour feels like a small theft. Time passing without being spent on something makes me anxious. Time is, if I’m honest, my obsession.

The proof is old. When I was a child and my grandmother told me to sit still for a minute, I would lift my toes inside my shoes, one by one, then put them back down. My one secret motion, the one I was sure she couldn’t see. When she caught me, I froze. The second she turned her head, I started again, faster this time, as if I had to win back the seconds I’d lost holding still. I was maybe six. I’m telling you this as a confession, because honestly not much has changed.

So when I say I tried to do nothing yesterday and lasted about twenty seconds before my hand was already in my pocket reaching for something, please understand: this is not a think-piece written from above. It is a field report from inside the problem.

And here is the part that confuses even me. I play Go. Competitively. I will sit at a board for eight hours, stare at a single position for ten minutes doing nothing but thinking, and feel completely calm. The same person who can’t last twenty seconds on a bench. I have been turning that contradiction over for a long time, and I have started to think it is the whole point.

But let me back up.

I. They Took It On Purpose

Boredom is being engineered out of existence, and not by accident.

Every app, every feed, every notification system is built around one goal: making sure you never have an empty second.

The infinite scroll exists so the feed never ends, so that the moment you hit the bottom and boredom might creep in, more appears.

Autoplay exists so the gap between episodes, that little pause where you might decide to stop, never happens.

Notifications are timed to catch you exactly when your attention starts to drift, and reel it back.

None of this is a side effect. It is the product.

The whole business model depends on swallowing your empty time, because every bored moment is a moment you are not scrolling, not watching, not generating the attention these companies sell. Boredom is bad for business. So boredom has to go.

People like me, by the way, were the easiest customers they ever had. I came pre-trained to hate the empty second. They barely had to show up.

II. What Boredom Actually Is

It helps to be precise about what we’re defending, because boredom is not the same as emptiness.

Boredom is the gap between how much stimulation your mind wants and how little the room is actually giving it. It is restlessness, dissatisfaction, the itch of a mind hunting for something to do and finding nothing good enough. (I know this one intimately. See above.)

It is unpleasant. That is exactly the point.

That discomfort is a signal. The mind is telling you it has run out of things to receive and now has to make something instead.

And if you are bored, genuinely, uncomfortably bored, and you do not reach for your phone, something does start to happen.

The mind begins to move on its own. It wanders back to problems you’d shelved. It makes connections you weren’t trying to make. It produces images and ideas out of its own materials instead of waiting to be fed.

This isn’t mystical. It’s just what an unoccupied brain does when you finally leave it alone.

There’s even a name for the machinery behind it. The default mode network: the set of brain regions that light up when you are not focused on some external task.

It’s associated with things like:

  • self-referential thought
  • seeing things from someone else’s perspective
  • creative ideation
  • thinking about the future
  • pulling your experiences together into a story

It is most active when you are doing nothing in particular. When you are bored.

So when we fill every gap with input, we are quietly switching it off, and we stop integrating, stop imagining, stop making our own meaning. We become consumers of meaning instead of producers of it.

III. A Surprisingly Young Word

Here is something that surprised me: “boredom” as a word is barely older than the railroad. It first shows up in English around the 1850s, right alongside the rush of industrial life.

Before that, most lives ran on seasonal time, communal time, religious time. There was hard labor and there was rest, and the rest wasn’t really boredom in our sense. It was structured emptiness, filled with talk, with stories, with slow work done by hand.

Industrial time invented a new thing: hours that were neither work nor real rest, time that simply had to be filled, time whose emptiness felt vaguely threatening.

The Victorians were genuinely anxious about idleness. The devil makes work for idle hands. Empty time as a moral hazard.

I recognized that immediately, because I grew up with its descendant. Boş durma is the same instinct, handed down through a Turkish grandmother instead of a Victorian pulpit. Idleness is suspect, time must be used, sitting still is something you have to justify. The terror never went away. It just got passed around, and eventually it got monetized.

The attention economy didn’t invent our discomfort with empty time. It inherited it, the way I did, and then made it far worse than any Victorian could have dreamed.

IV. Pascal Would Have Diagnosed Me on Sight

In the 17th century, Blaise Pascal wrote the line that has been following me around for years:

“All of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.”

The first time I read it I laughed, and then I felt caught. Because that is me. That is the toe-wiggling six-year-old, just grown up.

Pascal’s point was that we cannot stand to be alone with ourselves, so we run: into distraction, into company, into endless activity. He called it divertissement, diversion. Not entertainment in the harmless sense. Flight.

And we flee, he thought, because of what is waiting when we finally stop: our own mortality, the smallness of everything we cling to, the question of who we even are when we are not performing or producing or consuming.

I don’t have to share his answer to that question (his was God) to admit he nailed the diagnosis. We cannot sit quietly in a room alone.

And here is the thing I have only recently understood: it isn’t because there is nothing in that quiet room. It is because there is too much.

V. The Cure That Makes You Sicker

This is where Baudrillard comes in, whom I’ve been reading lately.

He described the hyperreal: a world where the simulation has quietly replaced the real thing.

And one job the hyperreal does, maybe its main job, is to manage our boredom.

The simulation is always more exciting than the room you are actually in. The show is more dramatic than your day. The feed is more interesting than your ceiling. The game is more stimulating than just existing.

So the hyperreal “cures” boredom by handing you a version of reality that has been engineered to be more vivid than reality, tuned precisely to the reward circuits in your brain.

The trouble is that the cure is the disease.

Every time you reach for the phone when the silence starts to creep in, you take the cure, and you teach yourself to need it again.

You get a little less able to sit with the emptiness, a little more dependent on the simulation, a little worse at making your own thoughts.

The attention economy isn’t just selling you distraction. It is slowly removing your ability to live without it.

VI. The Part With the Studies

The research here is getting harder to wave away. A few that stuck with me:

Attention restoration theory (Kaplan, 1995). You have two kinds of attention. The directed kind, focused and effortful, is a limited tank that drains. The involuntary kind, the soft diffuse awareness you get in a forest or staring at water, is what refills it.

Boredom in a natural, unstructured setting flips you from the first into the second, and that is restorative. Boredom medicated by a phone flips you nowhere. It just keeps you in effortful mode on a cheaper stimulus, so the tank never refills.

Mind-wandering (Smallwood & Schooler, 2015). The loose, undirected thinking that happens when you are bored turns out to correlate with better creative problem-solving. The wandering mind makes the strange connections. The mind that is always pointed at a screen can’t wander, so it doesn’t.

The phone on the desk (Ward et al., 2017). People did cognitive tasks with their phone either face-down on the desk, in a pocket, or in another room. They performed measurably better with it in another room. Face-down and silent wasn’t enough. Just knowing it was there ate part of their minds.

Now, here is my own complication. By all of this I should be a cognitive disaster, and in everyday life maybe I am. But I play Go, and at a board I can sit perfectly still inside a single position for ten minutes, thinking, and feel nothing but calm. Eight hours of it. The same person who can’t manage twenty seconds on a bench.

For a long time that looked like a contradiction. I don’t think it is anymore. Go isn’t doing nothing. It is stillness with walls around it, stillness pointed at something.

And it turns out I can hold still almost indefinitely as long as the stillness has a job.

That both comforts me and worries me. It comforts me because it means the capacity is in there somewhere. It worries me because the thing I still can’t do is the other kind, the open kind, the stillness with no walls and no task. The kind this whole essay is about.

VII. What People Make in the Empty Spaces

Let me be concrete about what the empty time is actually for.

Newton. When the plague closed Cambridge in 1665, he went home to his mother’s farm at Woolsthorpe and spent about eighteen months with no colleagues, no students, none of the usual machinery of a working life.

In that quiet he worked out calculus, the law of universal gravitation, and the foundations of optics.

Arguably the most productive year and a half in the history of science, and it happened in something very close to enforced boredom.

Darwin. His method, by his own account, was walking. He had a gravel loop at Down House he called the Sandwalk, his “thinking path,” and he would circle it doing nothing but turning problems over. Not reading, not writing. Walking and thinking. He counted it among his most productive hours.

Proust. In Search of Lost Time, seven volumes, the longest novel in the Western tradition, was written by a man in a cork-lined room, mostly in bed, with almost nothing coming in from outside.

The whole engine of the book, the involuntary memory, the madeleine in the tea, the uneven paving stones, is basically a theory of what an unstimulated mind does when you leave it alone.

It goes backward. It recovers. It finds, in the empty moment, the full weight of everything already lived.

And that recovery needs silence. It needs the absence of input. It needs, precisely, the thing I keep running away from.

None of which, I’ll admit, is especially comforting to someone whose response to a free afternoon is to go clean a house that is already clean.

VIII. There’s a Political Cost Too

This is the argument I rarely hear anyone make, so let me make it.

The attention economy is not politically neutral.

When every empty moment of yours gets filled with content that has been optimized for engagement and outrage and tribal signal, you are not exactly a free citizen. You are a node in a system whose profits flow to whoever owns the algorithm. Your attention is the product, and your opinions, shaped by whatever you have been shown, are the output.

Real independent thought needs the opposite of all this. It needs the ability to be alone with your own mind long enough to consider something, doubt it, reconsider, and arrive somewhere slowly, instead of reacting in the fast emotional spasms that feeds are built to trigger.

Hannah Arendt wrote about exactly this. She described thinking as a kind of two-in-one dialogue of the self with itself, and treated it as the ground of any moral or political life.

“The sad truth is that most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be good or evil.”

Her most famous idea, the banality of evil, comes down to thoughtlessness. Not stupidity. Thoughtlessness: the failure to stop, to sit with the question, to be alone for one moment with what you are actually doing.

And the attention economy manufactures that thoughtlessness at industrial scale. It is not neutral.

IX. So I’m Practicing. Badly.

I am not going to tell you to throw away your phone. I am telling you what I am trying to do myself, which is smaller and somehow much harder.

I am practicing being bored. On purpose.

It is not meditation, though it is a cousin. It is not a “digital detox,” though that is a cousin too. It is just scheduled appointments with emptiness.

Sit somewhere. No phone, no book, no music, no podcast keeping me company. Ten minutes, ideally. Twenty seconds, realistically, at least at the start, because remember who you are dealing with.

And when the discomfort shows up, and it shows up fast, the job is not to run from it.

I sit with it. I watch what my mind does with nothing to chew on. I notice the thoughts that arrive without being invited, the problems I have apparently been carrying around without ever giving myself the room to feel them.

I am, I promise you, only at the very beginning of this, and I am bad at it. Trying to do nothing turns out to be full-blown existential dread for me. Genuinely. :D

But every so often, for a few seconds, the panic loosens, and I notice that boredom isn’t the monster I had built it into.

It is just a space. A space where something can happen that cannot happen anywhere else, as long as you can stand to stay in it.

X. The Most Radical Thing Left

In a world built for total stimulation, doing nothing on purpose starts to look like a small act of resistance.

Not a revolution. Not a fix for anything structural. Just a refusal: to be one more node in the attention network, to hand over your empty time, to let your capacity for solitude and daydream and the slow movement of thought quietly waste away because a system profits from its absence.

The Greeks had a word for what waits on the other side of that refusal: ἀταραξία, ataraxia. Usually translated as tranquility, or undisturbedness. Not the absence of thought, but the presence of a self that is gathered and quiet and available to its own deepest resources.

It was something you had to practice. You had to go and meet the emptiness on purpose. You had to be willing, in our terms, to be bored.

Seneca put it plainly: “Retire into yourself as much as you can.”

William James, much later, said the thing I most need to hear: “The faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will.”

Over and over again. That is the whole practice. Losing the attention, bringing it back. Losing it, bringing it back.

So here is where I have landed, as a lifelong member of the can’t-sit-still club.

I still catch myself wiggling my toes, metaphorically, in every quiet minute, trying to win back time I haven’t actually lost. Boş durma is still in there, in my grandmother’s voice, and it probably always will be.

But I am learning, slowly and badly, to sit in the empty room anyway. To let the hour go unspent. To do, for a few unbearable and then somehow bearable seconds, absolutely nothing.

Try it with me. Put the phone down. Sit somewhere. Let the boredom come, and don’t flee.

See what it brings.

That’s the assignment.

item.title: Pushkin — The Man Who Invented Russian Literature
item.description:
Every Russian writer who came after him owes him a debt that cannot be repaid.

Dostoevsky said: “We all came from under Pushkin’s overcoat.”

Wait, that was actually Gogol’s overcoat. :)

But it fits Pushkin just as well. Maybe even better.

Because Pushkin did not just write great literature. He created the language in which Russian literature would be written.

Before Pushkin, Russian literary language was a chaotic mixture: Church Slavonic, French borrowings, bureaucratic formulas, folk speech, with no agreed standard and no single voice.

After Pushkin, there was Russian!

It wasn’t really invented. It was more like crystallization, the way a supersaturated solution, touched at a single point, turns to crystal all at once.

Pushkin was that touch.

I. The Life

Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin was born in Moscow on June 6, 1799.

Russians call him Alexander Sergeyevich, by the patronymic, the way you’d talk about someone you actually know.

His ancestry was complicated and he was proud of it: on his mother’s side, he descended from Abram Petrovich Gannibal, an African prince brought to Russia as a child, who became a general and a favorite of Peter the Great.

Pushkin wrote about Gannibal. He was not embarrassed by his African ancestry. In an era of rigid Russian aristocratic identity, this itself was a kind of provocation.

He was educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, a new institution founded by Alexander I to produce the new Russian intelligentsia.

He was a difficult student. He was also, by eighteen, already recognized as the greatest poet in Russia.

His first major poem, Ruslan and Lyudmila (1820), was published when he was twenty-one. It was both scandalous and celebrated. Critics found it too irreverent and too playful; everyone found it brilliant.

Then came the exile.

His early poems, Ode to Liberty and The Village, contained political sentiments that the Tsar found unacceptable. He was exiled from St. Petersburg: first to the south (Kishinev, Odessa), then to his family estate at Mikhailovskoye, in the northern countryside.

Six years of exile.

He wrote constantly. (Spasibo, Sasha!)

The southern exile produced the Southern Poems: The Prisoner of the Caucasus, The Fountain of Bakhchisaray, The Gypsies. Romantic and Byronic and, frankly, brilliant.

Mikhailovskoye produced the bulk of Eugene Onegin, Boris Godunov, and some of his greatest lyric poetry.

Strangely, exile didn’t silence him. It concentrated him.

He was eventually pardoned by Nicholas I, who then became, in effect, his personal censor. Every major work needed the Tsar’s approval.

This arrangement was humiliating. Pushkin accepted it because he had no choice.

He married Natalya Goncharova in 1831, a woman of extraordinary beauty and, by most accounts, limited intellectual interests. Pushkin was besotted. (Honestly? A little jealous of a love like that.) The marriage produced four children and, eventually, a duel.

II. The Duel

On January 27, 1837, Pushkin fought a duel with Georges-Charles de Heeckeren d’Anthès, a French officer serving in the Russian imperial guard and the adopted son of the Dutch ambassador.

D’Anthès had been pursuing Natalya Pushkina publicly for over a year. Anonymous letters, their authorship never firmly established, had mocked Pushkin as a cuckold.

Pushkin was consumed by jealousy and rage. He was also, by most accounts, worn down: by debt, by the censorship, by the daily humiliation of his position.

He challenged d’Anthès.

He knew he would probably lose.

D’Anthès was a young, experienced military officer in his prime. Pushkin was thirty-seven, in poor health, and no real duelist.

D’Anthès fired first. The bullet entered Pushkin’s abdomen.

Pushkin, wounded, steadied himself and fired. He hit d’Anthès in the arm, a glancing wound. D’Anthès survived.

Pushkin was carried home. He died two days later, on January 29, 1837.

He was thirty-seven years old.

On his deathbed, he said to his books: “Прощайте, друзья.” Farewell, friends.

Russia went into mourning. The announcement that ran in the papers said only: Солнце нашей поэзии закатилось. The sun of our poetry has set.

Nicholas I, fearing a public demonstration, had the funeral moved secretly, at night.

D’Anthès was expelled from Russia. He returned to France and lived to be ninety-three. (Of course he did.)

III. What He Did to the Russian Language

To understand Pushkin’s linguistic achievement, you need to understand the situation he inherited.

18th century Russian literature was written in a language almost no one spoke: a formal, Latinized, Church Slavonic idiom that was prestigious and dead.

At the same time, educated Russians spoke French among themselves. Russian was for servants.

There was a war over this, the Shishkov vs. Karamzin debate, between those who wanted to purify Russian by returning to its Church Slavonic roots and those who wanted to modernize it along French lines.

Pushkin resolved this debate by ignoring it.

He wrote in a language that somehow managed to be all of these at once:

  • Rooted in living spoken Russian
  • Capable of the highest poetic expression
  • Free from artificial archaisms
  • Absorbing of foreign influence where natural
  • Flexible, precise, musical

He didn’t give anyone a theory of the language. He simply showed what it could do.

When Eugene Onegin appeared, when Russians actually read it, they recognized something:

This is how Russian sounds when it is fully itself.

The linguist Roman Jakobson wrote that Pushkin’s verse had achieved something virtually unique in literary history: the coincidence of the ideal poetic language with the living, spoken language of its time.

None of this was accidental. It was the work of a lifetime.

IV. Eugene Onegin — The Novel in Verse

Eugene Onegin (1823-1831) is Pushkin’s masterwork.

It is both a novel and a poem. It is written in a stanza form Pushkin invented specifically for it, the Onegin stanza: fourteen lines, iambic tetrameter, rhyme scheme AbAbCCddEffEgg (uppercase = feminine rhyme, lowercase = masculine).

It does for Russian verse roughly what the Shakespearean sonnet does for English: it fits its purpose so well that it feels like it was always there.

The plot, briefly:

Eugene Onegin is a young St. Petersburg dandy: bored, fashionable, already sick of everything. He inherits an estate in the countryside. He befriends Vladimir Lensky, a young Romantic poet, idealistic, in love with Olga Larina.

Olga’s sister is Tatyana: bookish, dreamy, raised on French Romantic novels, completely unlike the social world around her.

Tatyana falls in love with Onegin. She writes him a letter, one of the most famous letters in world literature, confessing her love with complete, devastating honesty.

Onegin turns her down. Gently, but clearly. He isn’t capable of love, and he says so.

At a party, bored, Onegin flirts with Olga to provoke Lensky. Lensky challenges him to a duel.

Onegin kills Lensky.

He leaves. Years pass.

When Onegin runs into Tatyana again, now a princess, married to a general, moving in the highest society, he falls desperately in love with her.

He writes to her.

She meets him. She tells him: she still loves him. She will always love him.

And she will not leave her husband.

“But I was given to another — and I shall be faithful to him forever.”

The novel ends.

V. Tatyana — The Most Important Woman in Russian Literature

Dostoevsky, in his famous Pushkin speech of 1880, called Tatyana the ideal of Russian womanhood: her sacrifice, her fidelity, her dignity.

He was right that Tatyana matters. But I think he read her wrong.

She isn’t really an ideal of self-sacrifice. She’s the moral center of the novel for a different reason: she’s the only character who actually changes.

At the start of the novel she’s a girl who has confused novels with reality, projecting her romantic fantasies onto Onegin, a man she barely knows.

Her letter is beautiful. It’s also naive. She is in love with an idea, not a person.

His rejection is cruel. Looking back, it’s also a kind of gift.

When we meet Tatyana again, years later, she has become herself. The dreaming girl is gone; what’s left is a clear-eyed woman with no illusions.

She tells Onegin: “I love you — why should I dissemble? — But to another I was given; To him I shall be faithful forever.”

People read this as resignation. I don’t. To me it’s integrity. (God, I love her for this.)

She knows what she felt, and what she still feels. And she knows who she has decided to become.

Pushkin’s sympathy is entirely with her.

And not because fidelity is some conventional virtue. Pushkin was never a conventional moralist. It’s because her refusal is an act of self-possession.

She won’t be the object of Onegin’s belated desire, and she won’t repeat the mistake of her youth: letting passion override judgment.

She is, in the end, more free than Onegin.

VI. Onegin — The Superfluous Man

Onegin gave Russian literature one of its central types: the superfluous man (лишний человек).

He’s intelligent, educated, capable of feeling. He just can’t sustain it: not action, not love, not commitment.

He’s bored by everything. Pushkin even has a word for it: хандра, khandra, Russian spleen, which he says is just like the English kind, only worse. He destroys what he touches, not out of malice, but because he can never quite be present, or take anything seriously, or risk himself.

He kills Lensky out of social cowardice, not malice. He doesn’t want to look afraid to duel, so he lets his friend die to protect appearances.

He rejects Tatyana, the one person who might have saved him from himself, because he’s honest enough to know he can’t love her the way she deserves.

Years later he finally feels something. Tatyana’s transformation wakes something real in him, and it’s already too late. Tatyana isn’t being cruel. The truth is simpler: Onegin can’t be trusted with what he claims to want.

Tatyana knows this. Onegin, in the final scene, may finally know it too.

The superfluous man, Pechorin in A Hero of Our Time, Oblomov in Goncharov’s novel, Rudin in Turgenev, they all descend from Onegin.

Dostoevsky spent his career arguing with this type.

VII. The Lyrics

The novel and the long poems made Pushkin famous. The short lyrics are what made him immortal.

Pushkin wrote several hundred lyric poems: love poems, political poems, meditations on death, nature poems, occasional verse, translations.

They are almost untranslatable.

There’s a precision and a music to them that English simply can’t reproduce.

But let me try to gesture at what they do.

“I loved you once…“ (1829):

Я вас любил: любовь ещё, быть может, В душе моей угасла не совсем; Но пусть она вас больше не тревожит; Я не хочу печалить вас ничем.

I loved you once: perhaps that love Has not entirely died within my soul; But let it not disturb you any longer; I have no wish to cause you any grief.

Eight lines. Iambic pentameter. The most famous love poem in the Russian language. (I have these eight lines memorized. So does half of Russia.)

What it does:

It says goodbye without bitterness. It admits the feeling without demanding anything back, and it lets her go without punishing her for it.

“May God grant you another love you so — As tenderly and truly as I loved you.”

The final lines are the most astonishing part: the speaker wishes the woman he loves to be loved as well as he loved her. By someone else.

It isn’t resignation, and it isn’t martyrdom either. It’s the highest kind of love there is: the kind that wants the other person’s happiness more than its own survival.

In eight lines.

VIII. The Political Poet

Pushkin’s political poetry is less known in the West but central to his legacy in Russia.

Ode to Liberty (1817), written when he was nineteen, attacked tyranny head-on:

“Autocratic villain! I hate you, your throne, Your death, the death of your children — I see with cruel joy.”

This got him exiled.

The Village (1819), on serfdom:

“Here torment-lordship drags along, Without feeling, without law, Appropriated by violent rod The labor, property, and time of the farmer.”

Also exiled.

But Pushkin’s political poetry is more complex than simple opposition.

He wasn’t a revolutionary, at least not in the Decembrist sense, and he wasn’t a democrat. What he believed in was enlightened monarchy: a Tsar who governed by law and reason.

His political ideal was Peter the Great, the modernizing autocrat who dragged Russia into the modern world.

He wrote a poem in defense of Tsar Nicholas I after the Decembrist uprising.

This mix, a real hatred of tyranny sitting next to a real belief in monarchy, made him hard to categorize in his own time. It makes him just as hard to use politically now.

Both Soviet and post-Soviet Russia have tried to claim him. He doesn’t really belong to either. He belongs to the language.

IX. The Translation Problem

Nabokov spent years translating Eugene Onegin into English.

The result, four volumes (two of them pure commentary), is one of the most extraordinary works of literary scholarship ever produced.

It is also, by almost universal agreement, unreadable as a poem.

Nabokov made a decision: absolute fidelity to meaning over any attempt at verse form. He translated word by word, preserving every nuance of the Russian at the cost of all music.

He argued this was the only honest approach, that any attempt to reproduce the verse would inevitably distort the meaning.

Other translators, Johnston, Falen, Mitchell, have gone for verse instead. Their versions read better. They’re also less faithful.

The lesson: Pushkin is the most Russian of writers because his genius lives in the specific music of his language.

To read Pushkin fully, to really understand why Russians put him where they put him, you eventually have to learn Russian.

This is both a challenge and an invitation.

X. Why He Still Matters

On June 6, Pushkin’s birthday, Russians gather at his statues across the country and recite his poetry.

Not because anyone organizes it. It just happens. People who have memorized hundreds of his lines (Russian schoolchildren learn Pushkin the way English children once learned Shakespeare) stand at the statues and say the lines out loud.

This happened under the Tsars. It happened under the Soviets. It still happens now, after them.

There’s a phrase Russians use for him: наше всё. “Our everything.” Not a poet you admire from a distance. Something closer to family.

It happens because Pushkin gave Russians something no one can take from them: a language that is finally, fully itself, and a literature that begins with him and runs through everyone after. A way of speaking about love, death, freedom, and time that is Russian in the deepest sense. Not in a nationalist or ideological way, but in a way that lives in the language itself.

“And for a long time yet I shall be loved by people For having woken gentle feelings with my lyre, For having, in my cruel age, extolled freedom And called for mercy toward the fallen.”

He wrote this in 1836. One year before the duel.

He already knew what he had made, and that it would outlast him.

He was right about that too.

Start with the lyrics — any translation, just to hear the subjects. Then Eugene Onegin — Johnston’s verse translation is the most readable; Nabokov’s prose translation is the most accurate. Then The Bronze Horseman — the greatest short poem in the Russian language. Then, if you can, learn Russian. You will not regret it.

item.title: Tokyo — Or, How I Spent Three Hours in a Starbucks Because I Was Too Scared to Leave
item.description:
I arrived in Tokyo at 1 AM.

I was twenty-three years old.

I had never been to Japan.

I had never been anywhere quite like Japan.

I knew this theoretically.

Japan is different, people said.

Japan is unlike anywhere else, people said.

People were not wrong.

But theory and Shinjuku Station at 6 AM

after a sleepless night on a bus

are different categories of experience entirely.

I. The Bus

My first mistake: the bus.

I landed at Haneda late at night — too late, I reasoned, to navigate an unfamiliar city to my hostel. I would sleep at the airport. I would take the bus in the morning.

This was a reasonable plan. It ignored one fact:

Tokyo has a train system so comprehensive, so frequent, so efficient,

that there is essentially no hour of the day at which you cannot get from anywhere to anywhere with minimal effort.

The bus was unnecessary. The bus was slow. The bus was, however, where I slept — deeply, completely, with the total surrender of someone who has been awake for twenty hours.

I woke up to a voice. “Shinjuku! Shinjuku!”

I grabbed my bag. I was off the bus before I was fully conscious.

I stood on a pavement in Tokyo and I had been awake for maybe thirty seconds.

My first thought, I am not exaggerating, was:

Am I still on Earth?

II. Shinjuku at Dawn

Shinjuku does not ease you in.

I came from a country where cities go to sleep at night.

This one clearly never had.

Shinjuku at 7 AM is already the most intense place you have ever been.

The scale: incomprehensible.

Buildings that seem to keep going up past the point where buildings should reasonably stop.

Signs everywhere, in scripts I couldn’t read, advertising things I couldn’t identify.

It was so grand. So crowded. So not of this world.

I got scared. Actually scared. Everyone was already out and moving,

like they all knew exactly where to go.

And the sound. Not loud, but everywhere. A city-sound I had never heard before.

I walked for about ten minutes in pure shock,

and then I did what any reasonable person does

when the world stops making sense:

I ducked into the first café I saw.

III. The Café ( And the Bell I Did Not Know About)

It had a coffee logo. This was sufficient qualification. (Hoshino Coffee to be specific!)

I sat down. I waited.

No one came.

I waited longer. I began to wonder if I had, somehow, become invisible. I was still in shock.

Then I noticed there was a little bell on the table. You’re supposed to press it.
I pressed it, very timidly.

In Japan, you don’t wait to be served. You ring the bell. The system makes perfect sense.

I had been sitting there for ten minutes, waiting to be served the European way, while the staff politely pretended not to notice my confusion.

The waitress came, also very timidly —
like she could tell
I didn’t know what I was doing
and was being gentle about it.

I tried to order a sandwich.
She said breakfast hours.

And that’s where I saw it. :) And now, you will see it too!

IV. Eggslut

I should explain.

I was hungry. I had been awake, with brief intervals of bus-sleep, for approximately twenty-two hours. I was raised in a culture where breakfast is a serious meal. A real one.

Turkish breakfast: multiple cheeses, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, eggs prepared several ways, bread, butter, honey, jam, tea, possibly more tea, and the general understanding that one does not face the world without first sitting down properly.

I opened the menu.

I saw many things I did not recognize.

And then I saw, in English:

EGGSLUT

I stared.
Is this… food?
Is this a real thing?
You can just write that on a menu?

I ordered it.

Of course I ordered it.
I had been awake and unfed
for almost 24 hours.
What else was I going to do. Reader, it was the size of my palm.

A small vessel. Soft egg. Something creamy. Something bread-adjacent on the side. 1/3 of a bread slice.

Exquisite, probably. Breakfast, technically.

I ate it in 3 bites. A dollhouse breakfast.
I ordered coffee. I sat there for a while, charmed and starving at the same time — which, honestly, is how Tokyo made me feel for the rest of the trip.

V. Three Alphabets (In One Sentence??)

Okay I should explain.

On the plane,
trying to be a responsible traveler,
I had learned that Japanese
has three writing systems:

Hiragana: 46 characters, for native Japanese words and grammar.

Katakana: 46 characters, for foreign loanwords.

Kanji: thousands of characters, borrowed from Chinese.

Fine. I had, on the plane, memorized hiragana and katakana. This took approximately twenty minutes. I was pleased with myself.

Then I walked outside into Shinjuku.

The signs were using all three at once.
In the same sign.
Sometimes in the same word.

I had assumed — naively, adorably —
that one sentence would use one alphabet.

Nobody warned me they’d use all three in one sentence, sometimes in one word, like it was the most normal thing in the world.

I stared at signs. I recognized some characters. I understood nothing.

(Kanji. It was kanji. A lot of kanji.)

VI. Sutābakkusu (スターバックス)

I panicked.
I had no internet.
No Google Translate.
No way to decipher anything.

So I decided:
I need something familiar.
I need Starbucks. ( Me, a slave of the capitalism, ahahha, I should write about this later!)

Not for the coffee —
for the green logo.
For the reassurance
of something I know exists on Earth.

I walked into Tokyo Station. ( 2nd biggest mistake after bus) :D

Tokyo Station is not a station.

It’s an underground city.

Platforms, passages, shops, restaurants, all of it humming away below ground,

and everyone moving through it knows exactly where they’re going.

I did not!

I looked for the green mermaid. I could not find it.

I stopped people. “Starbucks?” I said. With, I hoped, an international intonation that communicated friendly tourist, not threat.

“Sumimasen,” they said — excuse me — and walked away. Politely and kept walking.

In Japan, stopping a stranger on the street is not the done thing. This is not rudeness. It’s just not what you do here. I didn’t know that yet.

I kept trying. I showed people my phone with “Starbucks” typed on it.

Eventually: two young girls in school uniforms who looked at me, looked at my phone, and said, with great enthusiasm:

“Sutābakkusuuuuu!”

Yes! That! Yes!

“Coffee?” I said.

“Hai! Hai! Kohiiidesu!”

They walked me there.

I sat in that Starbucks for two-three hours.

I was too scared to go back out into the station.
I was too scared to go into the crowds.
After sleepless night and tiny eggslut, it was too much for me.

VII. Anneannem and The Phone Call

At some point in the early afternoon, I called my grandmother to say good morning —
it was morning in Turkey by then.

She answered immediately — she always answered immediately — and asked how I was.

“Anane,” I said, “this place is nothing like Turkey. It’s nothing like Korea either.”

Korea had been my second country. Japan was my third. My grandmother was keeping track.

She asked what I meant.

I tried to explain Shinjuku — the scale, the density, the signs, the feeling of having arrived on a different planet that happened to also have coffee.

She listened.

Then she said:

“You’re in one of the safest countries in the world. And you’re hiding in a café.”

A pause.

“I didn’t expect that from you.”

And she hung up. :))

I sat for a moment.

I said to myself, out loud, almost:

Kalk! Kalk! Kalk! ( Get up! Move! ) You are in Tokyo!

Then I put my phone in my bag, picked up my jacket, and walked out into Tokyo.

VIII. Kabukichō

My hostel was in Shinjuku, in the back streets near Kabukichō — the entertainment district, and also the heart of yakuza territory. Organized crime, in the most orderly country in the world.

This is a specific combination.

Kabukichō at night: neon on every surface, lights in colors that have no names in English, pachinko parlors emitting their specific metallic roar, host clubs with men in elaborate suits standing outside calling to passersby, restaurants with plastic food displays that look more real than food.

The yakuza, I had been told, were very much present. They were also, apparently, completely uninterested in a confused twenty-three-year-old from Turkey who was clearly lost and clearly harmless.

No one bothered me. Not once. Not for the entire trip.

I walked the back streets of Kabukichō at midnight feeling, for the first time that day, completely safe.

IX. Shibuya Crossing

Shinjuku at night is a completely different creature
from Shinjuku at dawn —
still overwhelming,
but now the overwhelm was inviting
instead of terrifying.

I walked from Shinjuku to Shibuya.

This is approximately 3 kilometers. I did not know this at the time. I found out afterward. At the time, I was simply walking — following the density of people, the brightness of the lights, the general principle that interesting things are where people are going.

Shibuya Crossing is famous. You have seen photographs. The photographs are accurate. They are also completely useless.

The photographs show: an intersection, many people, neon lights.

What the photographs cannot show: the precise moment when the lights change — when traffic stops — when the crossing opens — and from every direction at once, hundreds of people begin to walk, weaving between each other, and somehow nobody collides.

I stood on the edge and watched it happen.

Then I walked into it.

The crowds moving like water around me.
No one bumped into me. No one stopped. The flow just took me in — one confused foreigner — and kept moving.

I made it to the other side.

I turned around and watched the flow come back.

And somewhere in the middle of that crossing —
between one wave of people and the next —
I fell in love with Tokyo.

Completely.
Irreversibly.
The kind of love
where you don’t even argue with yourself about it.

I thought: I don’t understand anything about this city.
I thought: I want to understand everything about this city.
I thought: I am coming back.

All three turned out to be true.

X. Twelve Times

I have been back to Japan twelve times since that morning!

Twelve!

I did not plan this. Nobody plans this.

You just go once, and then some part of you keeps finding reasons — a conference, a layover, a friend visiting, a week free in July, a no reason at all — and one day you look up and realize you have a favorite konbini, a favorite train line, a specific bench in a specific park where you always sit.

I know the train system now — which is, as I suspected on the bus, completely sufficient and slightly miraculous. A map that initially looks like someone dropped a bowl of noodles and then, over time, reveals its logic — a logic so refined that missing a train is a minor inconvenience rather than a crisis.

I know the food. I know the silence — the specific quality of Japanese public quiet, the way a city of 14 million people can feel, in certain moments, hushed.

I know the parks — Yoyogi on a Sunday, where every subculture has its own corner, all of them sharing the same park.

And most importantly, I know the toilets! :)) God knows how scary they are the first time!

And I know the thing I felt that first morning in Shinjuku —

standing on the pavement with my brain not yet fully operational,

looking at a city that did not fit

any category I had —

the thing I felt was not just disorientation.

It was the particular feeling of encountering something genuinely,

structurally different from everything you know!

That is what Tokyo gave me on the first morning —

before I found the café, before eggslut,

before the bell I didn’t press,

before sutābakkusu,

before my grandmother told me to stop hiding.

item.title: Beginnings
item.description:
I’ve never been good at introductions.

I think in fragments.

I question everything (including the questioning). And I live, perpetually, in the metaxy — the in-between.

This space is not a blog.

Not quite. It’s closer to a commonplace book, or a garden… Things planted at different times, growing at different speeds, not everything blooming at once.

You’ll find equations here.

And philosophy. Research logs written at 2am.

Travel notes from cities that felt like they already knew me.

Thoughts on ink, on Go stones on a board, on the shape of paper folded into something unexpected.

No schedule.

No algorithm to please. Just the honest accumulation of a mind that can’t quite stop noticing things.

I do not like wasted words. But, here I will scatter them freely.

This is fragments, skepsis and metaxy!

item.title: Başlangıç
item.description:
Bir şeyler birikiyor içimde uzun zamandır. Notlar, sorular, kırıntılar. Defterlere yazılanlar, kitap kenarlarına hızlıca düşülenler, gece geç vakitlerde telefona kaydedilen yarım cümleler…

Bunların bir yeri olsun istedim.

Fragmenta — kırıntılar demek.

Sképsis — sorgulamak.

Metaxy — arada olmak, Platon’un arasında dediği yer.

Fizikçiyim. Ama aynı zamanda Rus edebiyatına aşık biri, dolmakalem koleksiyoncusu, Go oyuncusu, modüler origami yapan, yıldızlara bakan, İzmir’den taa uzaklara gelen gelen birisi.

Sürekli evini özleyen, her özlediğinde kendisini kitaplara veren…

Bu alan tüm beni barındıracak, ne demekse tüm ben :).

Formüller de olacak, şiir de. Türkçe de olacak, İngilizce de.

Düzenli olmayacak, kronolojik olmayacak. Sadece dürüst olacak!

Anneanneciğimin mutfağından taşınan bir şey var içimde hâlâ, sorularla büyüyen, denizle büyüyen bir şey.

Burası onun yeri!
